Worth being intentional about that, since it'll fire more/larger flatten orders than a nonzero target would.\n\n2. **`evaluate()`'s unpause condition (`notional <= target_notional`) still works fine at 0** \u2014 it just means \"only unpause once fully flat,\" which is what you'd want.\n\n3. **One real gap for a \"flatten\" mode: `fire_flatten` returns early if `pos == 0`**, which is correct, but there's no explicit check for what happens if `known_price` is stale/None while `desk_position != 0` \u2014 you'd just sit paused forever with no flatten firing until DESK_STATE next updates. Probably fine given quoter publishes on every driver tick, but worth knowing it's a soft dependency.\n\n4. **Single F-in-flight-at-a-time (`hedging_in_flight`) plus escalation ramp** means a full flatten from a large position might take several retries/escalating prices rather than one shot, especially if size is capped by `pos_lim`. With target=0 you're asking for a bigger single clear each time, so escalation working correctly matters more here than in the small-trim case.\n\nSo: setting target to 0 does what you want mechanically.                             "description": "Draft NOTES.md for the trading desk submission",
                            "path": "/home/claude/NOTES.md",
                            "file_text": "# NOTES\n\n## Design decisions\n\n- **Front-month (AAH6) traded via mean reversion.** The mover bot's target\n  selection is a symmetric bounded random walk (target clipped around a\n  fixed center, direction a fair coin flip, step size independent of\n  direction), which guarantees the front-month price is positive-recurrent\n  around a known mean. This made mean reversion a natural, verifiable\n  strategy rather than a directional bet: entries are armed against the\n  mover's sweep, exits ladder back toward the estimated true mean, gated by\n  a z-score entry threshold.\n- **Back-month instruments (piggybacks) traded via stale-ladder crossing.**\n  A back-month LP bot reprices its ladder around the front-month's fair\n  value plus a fixed offset, but only reposts when the rounded center\n  crosses an integer boundary. Between the front-month moving and the LP's\n  repost landing, the LP's resting ladder is briefly stale relative to the\n  freshly-implied center. The quoter crosses that stale side (fill-and-kill\n  only, no resting orders) once it's identified as mispriced.\n- **Clustering assumption:** front-month/back-month clusters are discovered\n  at runtime (lagged correlation between instruments), with the assumption\n  that each cluster contains exactly one front-month instrument (identified\n  by dominant single-aggressor volume share) and one or more back-months.\n- **Taker was disabled.** The provided taker traded non-directional\n  contracts with no consistent edge in this DGP (prices bounce around a\n  mean rather than trend), so running it would only add noise/risk without\n  a plausible source of profit. Silencing it was a deliberate scope\n  decision, not an oversight.\n- **Hedger is a separate process**, independent per instrument (no\n  cross-instrument netting), using a dollar-notional risk cap so\n  differently-priced instruments sit on a consistent risk footing. It\n  reconstructs desk position purely from watching fill messages (no\n  cooperation needed from the quoter/taker for position tracking).\n- **Quoter/hedger coordination uses two separate KV buckets** (DESK_STATE,\n  written by the quoter; HEDGE_STATE, written by the hedger) rather than one\n  shared blob. This was specifically to avoid the two processes clobbering\n  each other's fields on a read-modify-write, or one process missing a\n  field update because it partially overwrote the other's data.\n\n## Assumptions\n\n- Treated the underlying data-generating process as stationary: half-life\n  is a single fixed constant estimated once from a captured sample, not\n  recalibrated live. Given more time, incremental live recalibration would\n  be the natural next step rather than trusting a frozen estimate for the\n  full grading run.\n- Assumed bot behaviour (mover walk mechanics, LP requote pattern, taker\n  behaviour) observed in the sim environment will hold in the grading\n  environment. Nothing in the strategy re-derives these mechanics live\n  beyond the warmup clustering/half-life pass.\n- Assumed each discovered cluster contains exactly one front-month\n  instrument (single dominant aggressor) \u2014 clusters with no dominant\n  instrument are left untraded rather than guessed at.\n- `max_tps` in EX_META was never resolved \u2014 its meaning is still an open\n  assumption and nothing in the system currently rate-limits against it.\n\n## Hurdles\n\n- **Rel-recovery and crossing wasted significant time.** An earlier design\n  tried to recover each piggyback's price offset from the LP's own\n  requote bursts in order to cross profitably, but this required winning a\n  timing race against causality itself (NATS gives no cross-subscriber\n  delivery-order guarantee, so the LP's decision-time fair value and a\n  live-read fair value aren't reconcilable). Mean reversion\n  ended up being a strategy that was actually possible to reason about\n  correctly, which is a large part of why it was adopted over crossing.\n- **Learning NATS and C++ simultaneously was a real cost.** This was a\n  first C++ project, so basic patterns (pointer-to-pointer out-params,\n  manual resource cleanup, no exceptions, blocking vs. async request\n  patterns) all had to be learned alongside the actual trading logic.\n- **Working with an AI coding assistant had its own failure mode.**\n  Imprecise descriptions of intent led to the assistant producing code that\n  didn't match what was actually needed, which sometimes wasn't caught\n  until later.                 "uuid": "01a066be-f265-7c2e-bfe6-8ba7aae282f4",
                "text": "Here's the piggyback trading logic as it exists in `skeleton.cpp`, walked through end to end:\n\n## 1. Identification (during `WARMUP`)\n\n- Every `A` (add) message on every instrument, from every sender, gets bucketed per-sender into `lpIdCandidates[sender]` (`handleMd`, the `type == \"A\"` branch) \u2014 separate buy/sell price vectors, plus a `lastAddTime`.\n- `pollLpIdQuietGaps()` runs every mainLoop tick during warmup. For each instrument not yet locked, it checks every sender's candidate: if quiet for more than `kLpIdQuietGap` (0.1ms) since their last Add, it's judged via `checkLpPattern`.\n- `checkLpPattern` sorts buys descending / sells ascending, pairs them level-by-level into per-level centers `mid(buy_i, sell_i)`, and requires **every level's center to agree with the mean center within `kSymmetryToleranceTicks`**. Pass \u2192 this sender is provisionally locked as `st.lpSender` for that instrument, with `lpLockedLevels` and `lpLockedCenterMean` recorded. Fail \u2192 candidate discarded, sender gets a clean shot on their next burst.\n\nThis matches your memory's \"driver-agnostic, self-referential ladder symmetry\" redesign \u2014 no `fv(driver)` involved at this stage at all.\n\n## 2. Role/rel assignment (`runDiscovery`, end of warmup)\n\n- Instruments are clustered via lagged correlation (`bestFit`/`pearsonR`/`UnionFind`), then within each cluster the instrument with one dominant aggressor (mover share \u2265 `kMoverDominanceShare`) becomes `DRIVER`; everything else in that cluster becomes `PIGGYBACK`.\n- For each piggyback, the provisional LP lock from step 1 is reconciled:\n  - No lock \u2192 `rel` stays unset, piggyback never quotes (just a WARN).\n  - Locked sender **is** the cluster's mover \u2192 discarded as a false positive (mover can look symmetric early in its walk), `rel` unset.\n  - Otherwise \u2192 confirmed: `pst.rel = lpLockedCenterMean - driverMeta.ref_price`.\n\n## 3. Live requoting trigger\n\n- Only fires from **driver bbo ticks** (`handleBbo`, `Phase::LIVE && st.role == DRIVER` branch): for every piggyback in the same cluster with a `rel` set, compute `newCEst = round(driverFv + rel)`. If it changed from `pst.cEst`, call `onPiggybackCenterChanged(pst)`.\n- Piggybacks have **no independent trigger** \u2014 their own book's A/E/C messages update `bidPx`/`askPx`/`fv` via `handleMd`\u2192`handleBbo`... actually wait, checking again: `handleBbo` is keyed off the `ex.bbo.<feed>` subject, which fires for *every* instrument's own bbo changes, not just the driver's. So a piggyback's own bbo tick *does* call `updateFv(st)` \u2014 but for `st.role == PIGGYBACK`, `updateFv` explicitly does nothing (per the comment: \"this function only fires on THIS instrument's own bbo update... piggyback c_est actually needs to be recomputed on the DRIVER's bbo tick instead\"). That part checks out.\n\n**Profitability of the specific bet:** \"post best ask, then buy back lower on the bid\" is a bet that price will fall after you sell. Being first doesn't make that bet correct \u2014 it just means you get filled *first*, on a directional guess that has no reason to be right more than half the time. Speed wins you queue priority for a fill; it does nothing to make the direction of that fill favorable. You've been treating \"I got there first\" as if it were itself the edge, but arriving first at a coin-flip is still a coin-flip \u2014 it just resolves faster and with size behind it.\n\nSo the actual question isn't \"how do I skew better\" \u2014 it's **what is the source of directional edge that justifies picking a side at all**, before any quoting logic gets written. So there's no directional edge versus the driver's next move; the driver has already moved by the time you compute `cEst`.\n- The LP is going to reprice its own ladder to sit around the new `cEst` too, just slower. That's not a bet, that's an observable arbitrage: if `cEst` moved up, their resting asks are now too cheap relative to fair value. Lifting *their* stale ask (not posting your own ask and hoping) is the actual edge \u2014 you know it's underpriced right now, not \"I think price might fall.\"\n\nSo the redesign isn't \"post best ask, hope to buy back lower\" \u2014 it's **cross the LP's stale resting side that's now mispriced**, sized to what's actually resting there, the instant `cEst` moves and before they cancel it.                             "new_str": "// Fires on every driver-implied center change (handleBbo, cEst recompute).\n// Not a passive requote. The LP hasn't seen this driver tick yet, so its\n// resting ladder on this piggyback is still priced at the OLD center \u2014 a\n// known, observable mispricing, not a directional guess. If the LP's stale\n// bid/ask is now on the wrong side of the fresh cEst, cross it with an F\n// (fill-and-kill) sized to what's actually resting there, and move on. This\n// replaces the old passive two-sided quote, which was (a) symmetric with no\n// edge, and (b) a same-side directional bet (\"sell high, hope to buy back\n// lower\") that had no basis for being right more than half the time.\n//\n// Edge condition, per side:\n//   - resting ASK is stale-cheap if askPx <= cEst - tick (LP is offering\n//     below where fair value now sits -> lift it)\n//   - resting BID is stale-rich if bidPx >= cEst + tick (LP is bidding\n//     above where fair value now sits -> hit it)\n// Both can't be true at once for a sane two-sided book (that would mean\n// bid > ask), so at most one side crosses per call. A single-tick minimum\n// edge avoids crossing on noise when cEst only moved by a rounding wobble.\nstatic void onPiggybackCenterChanged(InstrumentState& pst) {\n    long long tick = pst.meta.ticksize > 0 ? pst.meta.ticksize : 1;\n    long long c = static_cast<long long>(std::llround(*pst.cEst));\n\n    bool crossed = false;\n\n    if (pst.askPx >= 0 && pst.askVol > 0 && pst.askPx <= c - tick) {\n        // LP's resting ask is stale-cheap relative to fresh cEst: buy it.\n        long long size = std::min(pst.askVol, kPiggybackSize);\n        if (size > 0) {\n            requestAdd(pst, 'B', pst.askPx, size, ReqKind::PGYB_CROSS, -1, 'F');\n            DiscoveryLog << nowNs() << \",piggyback_cross_fire,\" << pst.feed\n                         << \",side=B stale_ask=\" << pst.askPx << \" cEst=\" << c\n                         << \" size=\" << size << \"\\n\";\n            crossed = true;\n        }\n    } else if (pst.bidPx >= 0 && pst.bidVol > 0 && pst.bidPx >= c + tick) {\n        // LP's resting bid is stale-rich relative to fresh cEst: sell it.\n        long long size = std::min(pst.bidVol, kPiggybackSize);\n        if (size > 0) {\n            requestAdd(pst, 'S', pst.bidPx, size, ReqKind::PGYB_CROSS, -1, 'F');\n            DiscoveryLog << nowNs() << \",piggyback_cross_fire,\" << pst.feed\n                         << \",side=S stale_bid=\" << pst.bidPx << \" cEst=\" << c\n                         << \" size=\" << size << \"\\n\";\n            crossed = true;\n        }\n    }\n\n    if (!crossed) {\n        DiscoveryLog << nowNs() << \",piggyback_no_edge,\" << pst.feed << \",cEst=\" << c\n                     << \" bid=\" << pst.bidPx << \" ask=\" << pst.askPx << \"\\n\";\n    }\n\n    // No passive quotes posted here at all: we only ever act when there's an\n    // observable stale-price edge to take, and the F either fills or dies\n    // immediately, so there is nothing left resting afterward that a future\n    // pgBidId/pgAskId cancel would need to clean up.\n}"

This\n// replaces the old passive two-sided quote, which was (a) symmetric with no\n// edge, then (b) a same-side directional bet (\"sell high, hope to buy back\n// lower\") that had no basis for being right more than half the time.\n//\n// Edge condition, per side:\n//   - resting ASK is stale-cheap if askPx <= cEst - tick (LP is offering\n//     below where fair value now sits -> lift it)\n//   - resting BID is stale-rich if bidPx >= cEst + tick (LP is bidding\n//     above where fair value now sits -> hit it)\n// Both can't be true at once for a sane two-sided book (that would mean\n// bid > ask), so at most one side crosses per call.                 "text": "```python\nimport csv\nfrom collections import defaultdict\n\nrows = list(csv.DictReader(open('pnl.csv')))\n\ncash = defaultdict(float)      # realized cash flow per feed\nqty = defaultdict(float)       # running position per feed, recomputed independently\nlast_price = {}                # last traded price seen per feed, for mark-to-market\n\nfor r in rows:\n    feed = r['feed']\n    vol = float(r['vol'])\n    price = float(r['price'])\n    ev = r['event']\n    last_price[feed] = price\n\n    if ev == 'piggyback_cross_buy_fill':\n        cash[feed] -= vol * price\n        qty[feed] += vol\n    elif ev == 'piggyback_cross_sell_fill':\n        cash[feed] += vol * price\n        qty[feed] -= vol\n    # entry_fill (driver) handled separately below, since the CSV doesn't\n    # log side directly for it -- we infer buy/sell from the position\n    # column's delta instead.\n\n# entry_fill: infer side from the change in the logged 'position' column\nby_feed = defaultdict(list)\nfor r in rows:\n    by_feed[r['feed']].append(r)\n\nfor feed, frows in by_feed.items():\n    prev_pos = 0.0\n    for r in frows:\n        if r['event'] != 'entry_fill':\n            continue\n        vol = float(r['vol'])\n        price = float(r['price'])\n        pos = float(r['position'])\n        delta = pos - prev_pos\n        prev_pos = pos\n        side = 'B' if delta > 0 else 'S'\n        if side == 'B':\n            cash[feed] -= vol * price\n            qty[feed] += vol\n        else:\n            cash[feed] += vol * price\n            qty[feed] -= vol\n\nprint('Per-feed realized cash flow, ending open qty, mark price:')\ntotal_realized = 0\ntotal_mtm = 0\nfor feed in sorted(cash):\n    c = cash[feed]\n    q = qty[feed]\n    mp = last_price[feed]\n    mtm = q * mp\n    print(f'{feed}: cash_flow={c:.2f}  open_qty={q:.0f}  last_px={mp:.0f}  '\n          f'mtm_open={mtm:.2f}  total={c+mtm:.2f}')\n    total_realized += c\n    total_mtm += mtm\n\nprint()\nprint(f'Sum cash flow (pure realized, no mark): {total_realized:.2f}')\nprint(f'Sum with open positions marked at last traded price: {total_realized+total_mtm:.2f}')\n```\n\nTwo things worth flagging about this code, so you don't treat it as more rigorous than it is:\n\n1. **It ignores the `position` column entirely for the cross fills** and recomputes `qty` from scratch by summing vol with sign per event type \u2014 I did that deliberately, to independently verify the logged `position` column rather than just trust it.                         "extracted_content": "#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Hedger: keeps the desk's front-month (AAH6) position from getting large.\n\nPolicy (per task.md's risk framing \u2014 a large position even briefly is the\nthing to avoid, a small one sitting around is fine):\n\n  - Reconstructs desk position purely by watching ex.md.<FEED>.* fill\n    messages and checking whether the quoter's or taker's sender shows up\n    as either party to an execution. No cooperation needed from those\n    processes.\n  - Dead zone: |position| <= FLATTEN_THRESHOLD -> do nothing. This is the\n    quoter's mean-reversion thesis playing out; don't pay spread for noise.\n  - Past the threshold: fire an F (fill-and-kill) order sized to bring the\n    position back to +/-FLATTEN_THRESHOLD, priced N ticks through the book\n    where N ramps up (quadratically by default) between FLATTEN_THRESHOLD\n    and HARD_STOP, so bigger excursions get priced deep enough into the\n    book to guarantee a full sweep.\n  - Reacts per-event (on every fill and every bbo tick), not on a timer,\n    since \"promptly\" is the whole point.\n\nOnly handles AAH6 (the driver) for now, matching the quoter's current\nscope. Extending to piggybacks is future work once the quoter trades them.\n\"\"\"\nimport asyncio\nimport os\nimport random\n\nimport nats\n\nNATS_URL = os.environ.get(\"NATS_URL\", \"nats://127.0.0.1:4222\")\nSENDER = os.environ.get(\"HEDGER_SENDER\", \"PYHGR001\")\nQUOTER_SENDER = os.environ.get(\"SENDER\", \"QUOTE01\")       # matches quoter's $SENDER\nTAKER_SENDER = os.environ.get(\"TAKER_SENDER\", \"PYTKR001\")\n\nFEED = os.environ.get(\"HEDGE_FEED\", \"AAH6\")\n\n# --- Risk policy knobs (tune freely) ---------------------------------------\nFLATTEN_THRESHOLD = float(os.environ.get(\"HEDGE_FLATTEN_THRESHOLD\", \"20\"))  # dead-zone edge\nHARD_STOP = float(os.environ.get(\"HEDGE_HARD_STOP\", \"100\"))                 # max-urgency point\n\n# ticks-through-book ramp: N(pos) = MIN_TICKS + (MAX_TICKS - MIN_TICKS) * t^RAMP_POWER\n# where t = clamp((|pos| - FLATTEN_THRESHOLD) / (HARD_STOP - FLATTEN_THRESHOLD), 0, 1)\n# RAMP_POWER = 1.0 -> linear; > 1.0 -> gentle early, steep near HARD_STOP (quadratic at 2.0)\nMIN_TICKS = float(os.environ.get(\"HEDGE_MIN_TICKS\", \"1\"))\nMAX_TICKS = float(os.environ.get(\"HEDGE_MAX_TICKS\", \"15\"))\nRAMP_POWER = float(os.environ.get(\"HEDGE_RAMP_POWER\", \"2.0\"))\n\nTICKSIZE = int(os.environ.get(\"HEDGE_TICKSIZE\", \"1\"))    # placeholder; replaced by fetch_meta() at startup\nREF_PRICE = 0                                             # placeholder; replaced by fetch_meta()\nBAND = None                                                # placeholder; None = unclamped until fetched\nPOS_LIM = None                                             # placeholder; None = unclamped until fetched\n\n\ndef clamp(x, lo, hi):\n    return max(lo, min(hi, x))\n\n\ndef ticks_through(position_abs: float) -> float:\n    \"\"\"How many ticks through the book to price the F order, given the\n    current |desk position|. Dead zone below FLATTEN_THRESHOLD is handled\n    by the caller (this is only ever invoked once we've decided to act).\"\"\"\n    span = HARD_STOP - FLATTEN_THRESHOLD\n    if span <= 0:\n        return MAX_TICKS\n    t = clamp((position_abs - FLATTEN_THRESHOLD) / span, 0.0, 1.0)\n    return MIN_TICKS + (MAX_TICKS - MIN_TICKS) * (t ** RAMP_POWER)\n\n\nclass Hedger:\n    def __init__(self, nc):\n        self.nc = nc\n        self.oid = random.randint(0, 80_000_000)\n\n        self.best_bid = None\n        self.best_ask = None\n\n        # Desk position (quoter + taker), reconstructed from fills. This is\n        # what the risk policy watches -- separate from the hedger's own\n        # trading, which is just the tool used to bring it back down.\n        self.desk_position = 0\n\n        # Hedger's own position/fills, tracked separately so its own book\n        # is visible (and could itself be folded into \"desk\" later if the\n        # brief's \"taker+quoter+hedger together\" wants it counted too --\n        # see note in on_own_fill).\n        self.own_position = 0\n        self.own_fills = 0\n\n        self.send_lock = asyncio.Lock()\n        self.hedging_in_flight = False  # simple guard against overlapping F sends\n\n    def next_oid(self):\n        self.oid += 1\n        return f\"{self.oid:08d}\"\n\n    def mid(self):\n        if self.best_bid is None or self.best_ask is None:\n            return None\n        return (self.best_bid + self.best_ask) / 2.0\n\n    # --- market data -------------------------------------------------------\n\n    async def on_bbo(self, msg):\n        f = msg.data.decode().split()\n        if len(f) < 6 or f[1] != FEED:\n            return\n        self.best_bid = None if f[2] == \"-\" else int(f[2])\n        self.best_ask = None if f[4] == \"-\" else int(f[4])\n        await self.maybe_hedge()\n\n    async def on_md(self, msg):\n        \"\"\"ex.md.<FEED>.* -- everyone's activity on the feed. We only care\n        about E (execution) messages here, filtered by sender.\"\"\"\n        f = msg.data.decode().split()\n        if len(f) < 8 or f[1] != \"E\":\n            return\n        incoming, resting = f[2], f[3]\n        vol = int(f[4])\n        px = int(f[5])\n        # incoming/resting are \"sender:orderid\" -- split off the sender.\n        in_sender = incoming.split(\":\", 1)[0]\n        rs_sender = resting.split(\":\", 1)[0]\n        aggressor_side = f[7] if len(f) > 7 and f[7] else None\n\n        for sender, tag in ((in_sender, \"in\"), (rs_sender, \"rs\")):\n            if sender in (QUOTER_SENDER, TAKER_SENDER):\n                # Determine this party's side: the aggressor side is given\n                # directly for the incoming party; the resting party is on\n                # the opposite side.\n                if aggressor_side is None:\n                    continue\n                side = aggressor_side if tag == \"in\" else opposite(aggressor_side)\n                signed = vol if side == \"B\" else -vol\n                self.desk_position += signed\n            elif sender == SENDER:\n                self.on_own_fill(tag, aggressor_side, vol)\n\n        await self.maybe_hedge()\n\n    def on_own_fill(self, tag, aggressor_side, vol):\n        if aggressor_side is None:\n            return\n        side = aggressor_side if tag == \"in\" else opposite(aggressor_side)\n        signed = vol if side == \"B\" else -vol\n        self.own_position += signed\n        self.own_fills += 1\n        # NOTE: if the desk-wide definition in task.md (\"taker + quoter +\n        # hedger together\") should include the hedger's own trades in the\n        # thing being kept low, fold this into desk_position too:\n        # self.desk_position += signed\n        # Left separate for now since the hedger's own fills are the\n        # corrective action, not the exposure being corrected -- worth\n        # revisiting if double-counting turns out to matter.\n\n    # --- hedging policy ------------------------------------------------------\n\n    async def maybe_hedge(self):\n        pos = self.desk_position\n        if abs(pos) <= FLATTEN_THRESHOLD:\n            return\n        if self.hedging_in_flight:\n            return\n        if self.best_bid is None or self.best_ask is None:\n            return\n\n        target = FLATTEN_THRESHOLD if pos > 0 else -FLATTEN_THRESHOLD\n        excess = pos - target  # positive -> desk too long, need to sell |excess|\n        side = \"S\" if excess > 0 else \"B\"\n        size = int(round(abs(excess)))\n        if size <= 0:\n            return\n        # Sparing use of position_limit: a hard backstop so a bad\n        # reconstruction/bug can't send an absurd size, not something the\n        # policy is tuned around (20/100 already dwarf it).\n        if POS_LIM is not None:\n            size = min(size, POS_LIM)\n\n        n_ticks = ticks_through(abs(pos))\n        tick_offset = int(round(n_ticks)) * TICKSIZE\n        if side == \"S\":\n            price = self.best_bid - tick_offset\n        else:\n            price = self.best_ask + tick_offset\n\n        # Sparing use of band: only a final safety clip into the tradeable\n        # range (ref_price +/- band per PROTOCOL.md), never a driver of\n        # urgency/pricing -- that's ticks_through() off the live bbo alone.\n        if BAND is not None:\n            lo, hi = REF_PRICE - BAND, REF_PRICE + BAND\n            clamped = clamp(price, lo, hi)\n            if clamped != price:\n                print(f\"[hedger] price {price} clamped to band [{lo},{hi}] -> {clamped}\",\n                      flush=True)\n            price = clamped\n\n        await self.send_hedge_order(side, size, price, pos, n_ticks)\n\n    async def send_hedge_order(self, side, size, price, pos_before, n_ticks):\n        async with self.send_lock:\n            self.hedging_in_flight = True\n            oid = self.next_oid()\n            body = f\"{SENDER} A {FEED} {oid} {side} {size} {int(price)} F\"\n            print(f\"[hedger] pos={pos_before} -> F {side} {size} @ {price} \"\n                  f\"(ticks_through={n_ticks:.1f})\", flush=True)\n            try:\n                await self.nc.publish(f\"ex.req.{SENDER}\", body.encode())\n                await self.nc.flush()\n            finally:\n                self.hedging_in_flight = False\n\n\ndef opposite(side):\n    return \"S\" if side == \"B\" else \"B\"\n\n\ndef parse_meta(value: str) -> dict:\n    \"\"\"EX_META KV value is space-separated key=value pairs (PROTOCOL.md).\"\"\"\n    out = {}\n    for kv in value.split():\n        if \"=\" not in kv:\n            continue\n        k, v = kv.split(\"=\", 1)\n        out[k] = v\n    return out\n\n\nasync def fetch_meta(nc, feed: str):\n    \"\"\"Read EX_META's ticksize/ref_price/band/position_limit for `feed` via\n    JetStream KV. Falls back to env-var/None defaults if the bucket/key\n    isn't reachable, so the hedger can still start (defensively) rather\n    than crash on a KV hiccup.\"\"\"\n    try:\n        js = nc.jetstream()\n        kv = await js.key_value(\"EX_META\")\n        entry = await kv.get(feed)\n        meta = parse_meta(entry.value.decode())\n        ticksize = int(meta.get(\"ticksize\", TICKSIZE))\n        ref_price = int(meta.get(\"ref_price\", 0))\n        band = int(meta[\"band\"]) if \"band\" in meta else None\n        pos_lim = int(meta[\"position_limit\"]) if \"position_limit\" in meta else None\n        print(f\"[hedger] EX_META {feed}: ticksize={ticksize} ref_price={ref_price} \"\n              f\"band={band} position_limit={pos_lim} (raw: {entry.value.decode()})\",\n              flush=True)\n        return ticksize, ref_price, band, pos_lim\n    except Exception as e:\n        print(f\"[hedger][WARN] failed to read EX_META for {feed}: {e!r}; \"\n              f\"falling back to ticksize={TICKSIZE}, band/position_limit unclamped\",\n              flush=True)\n        return TICKSIZE, REF_PRICE, BAND, POS_LIM\n\n\nasync def main():\n    global TICKSIZE, REF_PRICE, BAND, POS_LIM\n    nc = await nats.connect(NATS_URL)\n    print(f\"[hedger] connected to {NATS_URL} as {SENDER}\", flush=True)\n\n    TICKSIZE, REF_PRICE, BAND, POS_LIM = await fetch_meta(nc, FEED)\n\n    h = Hedger(nc)\n\n    await nc.subscribe(f\"ex.bbo.{FEED}\", cb=h.on_bbo)\n    await nc.subscribe(f\"ex.md.{FEED}.*\", cb=h.on_md)\n\n    print(f\"[hedger] {SENDER} watching {FEED}, hedging desk position from \"\n          f\"quoter={QUOTER_SENDER} taker={TAKER_SENDER} \"\n          f\"(dead_zone<= {FLATTEN_THRESHOLD}, hard_stop={HARD_STOP}, \"\n          f\"ramp_power={RAMP_POWER})\", flush=True)\n\n    while True:\n        await asyncio.sleep(3600)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    try:\n        asyncio.run(main())\n    except KeyboardInterrupt:\n        pass"

--- hedging policy ---------------------------------------------------\n\n    async def evaluate(self):\n        \"\"\"Called on every fill and every backstop tick. Decides whether to\n        trip/clear the pause flag and whether to fire a flatten order.\"\"\"\n        if self.known_price is None:\n            return  # nothing to price against yet, quoter hasn't published\n\n        notional = self.notional()\n\n        if not self.paused and notional > HEDGE_CAP_USD:\n            self.consecutive_attempts = 0\n            await self.publish_pause(True)\n\n        if self.paused:\n            target_notional = HEDGE_TARGET_USD\n            if notional <= target_notional:\n                # Back under target -- clear to flat behavior, unpause.\n                self.consecutive_attempts = 0\n                await self.publish_pause(False)\n                return\n            await self.fire_flatten(target_notional)\n\n    async def fire_flatten(self, target_notional: float):\n        if self.hedging_in_flight:\n            return  # one F in flight at a time per instrument; let it land first\n\n        pos = self.desk_position\n        if pos == 0 or self.known_price in (None, 0):\n            return\n\n        # How many lots to shed to bring notional down to target_notional,\n        # preserving current sign (we're reducing magnitude, not flipping).\n        target_lots = target_notional / abs(self.known_price)\n        target_pos = target_lots if pos > 0 else -target_lots\n        excess = pos - self.meta.band, self.meta.ref_price + self.meta.band\n            clamped = max(lo, min(hi, price))\n            if clamped != price:\n                print(f\"[hedger] {self.feed} price {price} clamped to band [{lo},{hi}] -> {clamped}\",\n                      flush=True)\n            price = clamped\n\n        self.consecutive_attempts += 1\n        await self.send_hedge_order(side, size, price, pos, escalation)\n\n    async def send_hedge_order(self, side, size, price, pos_before, escalation_ticks):\n        async with self.send_lock:\n            self.hedging_in_flight = True\n            oid = self.next_oid()\n            body = f\"{SENDER} A {self.feed} {oid} {side} {size} {price} F\"\n            print(f\"[hedger] {self.feed} pos={pos_before} known_price={self.known_price:.1f} \"\n                  f\"-> F {side} {size} @ {price} (escalation_ticks={escalation_ticks:.1f}, \"\n                  f\"attempt={self.consecutive_attempts})\", flush=True)\n            try:\n                await self.nc.publish(f\"ex.req.{SENDER}\", body.encode())\n                await self.nc.flush()\n            finally:\n                self.hedging_in_flight = False\n\n\nclass Hedger:\n    \"\"\"Owns all three per-instrument trackers and the shared subscriptions/\n    dispatch.                 "uuid": "01a06573-5020-77e8-a5ee-d83c7995353d",
                "text": "Good call \u2014 let's think it through rather than jumping to code.\n\n**What \"risk\" actually means here.** The brief is explicit: the danger isn't a small position sitting around, it's a *large* position for even a second. So the hedger's real objective function isn't \"get to zero\" \u2014 it's \"keep |exposure| bounded, continuously, with urgency that scales as exposure grows.\" A hedger that flattens perfectly but slowly after a spike has already failed the brief once the spike happened.\n\nThat reframes the design question. It's not \"how do I compute the desk's net position\" (that's just bookkeeping) \u2014 it's \"what's my *policy*: at what exposure do I start acting, how hard do I act, and on what instrument.\"\n\n**Three sub-questions, in order of how much they matter:**\n\n**1. Per-instrument or netted?**\nDo AAM6 and AAU6 exposure partially cancel because they're correlated with AAH6, or does each instrument's position count as independent risk?\n\nThe honest case for *not* netting: netting requires trusting a rel/offset estimate. If that estimate is wrong or stale, you could convince yourself you're flat when you're not \u2014 and given mem2.md's whole saga of rel-recovery being abandoned as unreliable, that's a real failure mode, not a hypothetical. Since the brief's cost function is about tail risk on a bad market move, and correlation isn't perfect insurance against a bad move, the conservative choice is: **treat each instrument's position as its own risk bucket**, hedge each independently, don't rely on netting to \"cancel out\" exposure between instruments. Simpler, and doesn't inherit the fragile part of the abandoned design.\n\n**2. What triggers action, and how hard?**\n\"Promptly reduce\" plus \"keep it low continuously\" suggests not a single hard cap with panic-liquidation at the edge, but a graduated response: the further |position| is from zero, the more aggressively you cross the spread to shed it. Near zero, do nothing (don't pay spread for noise). Past some threshold, start working out passively-but-urgently. Past a harder threshold, IOC/market it off regardless of price. This is continuous, reacts per-fill (event-driven, not polled on a timer \u2014 matches \"promptly\").\n\n**3. Hedge on the same instrument, or use the driver?**\nGiven #1 (no netting, no cross-instrument trust), hedging on the *same instrument that has the exposure* is the natural fit \u2014 no rel-conversion risk, no execution risk from trading a different, indirectly-related instrument. The driver-hedging idea only made sense under the old netting design; without netting, it doesn't add anything and adds a dependency (driver liquidity, correlation-in-the-moment) for no benefit.\n\n**Net shape:** independent per-instrument position trackers (reconstructed from fills on all three sender IDs \u2014 taker, quoter, hedger \u2014 since the brief says all three count), each with its own urgency curve, each hedging on its own book.\n\nDoes that match how you're thinking about it, or do you want to push back on the no-netting call specifically?",

                "text": "Netting, quickly: if you're trading multiple correlated instruments, instead of tracking \"I'm +5 lots AAM6\" and \"I'm -3 lots AAH6\" as two separate risks, you convert everything into equivalent units of one reference instrument (using each piggyback's rel/offset relative to the driver) and add them up into a single number \u2014 \"net driver-equivalent exposure.\" The appeal is efficiency: if your AAM6 long and AAH6 short roughly cancel in driver-equivalent terms, you don't need to hedge either one, just the small residual. The cost is that it only works if your rel/offset conversion is accurate *right now* \u2014 stale or wrong, and you think you're flat when you're not. Since you're only trading the driver at the moment, this is moot \u2014 there's nothing to net, only one position to watch. Good excuse to defer it cleanly rather than build machinery you don't need yet.\n\nYour framing \u2014 hedger as the seat that reels in the quoter's position \u2014 is the right shape, and it's simpler than what I was overengineering toward. A few things worth pinning down on top of it:\n\n**It's not just \"opposite and equal,\" it's opposite and *sized by urgency*.** If the hedger always fully offsets the quoter 1:1 immediately, the desk is always flat and the quoter can never actually hold the position its mean-reversion thesis wants it to hold \u2014 you'd be fighting your own strategy. The brief's language (\"small position for a while = low risk, large position even briefly = high risk\") suggests a dead zone: below some size, let the quoter run its position, no hedger action. Past that, the hedger starts leaning against it, harder as it grows. That's a curve, not a switch.\n\n**How the hedger sees the quoter's position.** Since there's no DESK_STATE, the clean way is: hedger subscribes to `ex.md.AAH6.*`, watches `E` messages, and whenever the quoter's sender ID appears as either the incoming or resting party, updates its own running tally of the quoter's position. Same mechanism you'd use for the taker later \u2014 just filtered by sender ID. No cooperation needed from the quoter process at all, matches \"how they coordinate is up to you, you already have a message bus.\"\n\n**Order type for the hedge itself.** Given the risk framing is about *not sitting on a big position*, the hedger's own fills should probably be marketable (`F`, fill-and-kill) rather than resting limits once it's decided to act \u2014 a resting hedge order might not fill in time to matter, and a stale one left resting is itself a small version of the same risk.                 "text": "Good, let's back up \u2014 I was using \"urgency\" loosely and it's worth pinning down what it actually *is* mechanically, since right now it's just a word.\n\nWhen the hedger decides \"the quoter's position is too big, I need to reduce it,\" it has to send an `F` (fill-and-kill) order. That order needs two numbers: a **size** and a **price**. \"Urgency\" is just shorthand for how those two numbers respond to how bad the position is.\n\nThere are really only two levers:\n\n**1. Size of the hedge clip.** How many lots does the hedger try to offload in this one order? A small position (say, 25) might only need a clip of 2-3 lots to nudge it back down. A position of 90 might need a much bigger clip \u2014 maybe even the whole thing \u2014 because it needs to come down *now*, not over several small steps.\n\n**2. How aggressively it's priced.** An `F` order needs a limit price \u2014 it fills what it can up to that price, then kills the rest. If you price it right at the current best bid/ask, it might only partially fill (there may not be enough resting volume at the very top of book) and the remainder gets cancelled, leaving you still exposed. If you price it several ticks *through* the book (i.e., a sell priced well below the current bid), it'll walk down and eat multiple price levels to guarantee the full size gets filled \u2014 at the cost of worse average execution price (more slippage).\n\nSo \"urgency\" = as the position gets worse, the hedger sends **bigger clips**, priced **more aggressively into the book**, so it's more certain to actually get the size off in one shot rather than nibbling at the touch and hoping.\n\nAt position 25: maybe a small clip, priced just past the touch (cheap, but not guaranteed to fully fill).\nAt position 95: maybe the whole excess, priced deep enough to guarantee a full sweep even if it costs several ticks of slippage \u2014 because the alternative (staying at 95) is the thing you're actually trying to avoid.\n\nDoes that match what you had in mind, or were you picturing urgency doing something else \u2014 like how *often* the hedger checks/acts, rather than the size/price of each action?",

Per PROTOCOL.md, executions arrive on `ex.md.<FEED>.<SENDER>` as `E` messages, or you can subscribe to `ex.md.<FEED>.*` for everyone's activity on a feed. That's not wrong to have, but it's secondary \u2014 the primary thing the hedger needs to track is **the desk's (quoter's) position**, which is a completely separate running total from the hedger's own fills. Dead zone below FLATTEN_THRESHOLD is handled\n    by the caller (this is only ever invoked once we've decided to act).\"\"\"\n    span = HARD_STOP - FLATTEN_THRESHOLD\n    if span <= 0:\n        return MAX_TICKS\n    t = clamp((position_abs - FLATTEN_THRESHOLD) / span, 0.0, 1.0)\n    return MIN_TICKS + (MAX_TICKS - MIN_TICKS) * (t ** RAMP_POWER)\n\n\nclass Hedger:\n    def __init__(self, nc):\n        self.nc = nc\n        self.oid = random.randint(0, 80_000_000)\n\n        self.best_bid = None\n        self.best_ask = None\n\n        # Desk position (quoter + taker), reconstructed from fills. This is\n        # what the risk policy watches -- separate from the hedger's own\n        # trading, which is just the tool used to bring it back down.\n        self.desk_position = 0\n\n        # Hedger's own position/fills, tracked separately so its own book\n        # is visible (and could itself be folded into \"desk\" later if the\n        # brief's \"taker+quoter+hedger together\" wants it counted too --\n        # see note in on_own_fill).\n        self.own_position = 0\n        self.own_fills = 0\n\n        self.send_lock = asyncio.Lock()\n        self.hedging_in_flight = False  # simple guard against overlapping F sends\n\n    def next_oid(self):\n        self.oid += 1\n        return f\"{self.oid:08d}\"\n\n    def mid(self):\n        if self.best_bid is None or self.best_ask is None:\n            return None\n        return (self.best_bid + self.best_ask) / 2.0\n\n    # --- market data -------------------------------------------------------\n\n    async def on_bbo(self, msg):\n        f = msg.data.decode().split()\n        if len(f) < 6 or f[1] != FEED:\n            return\n        self.best_bid = None if f[2] == \"-\" else int(f[2])\n        self.best_ask = None if f[4] == \"-\" else int(f[4])\n        await self.maybe_hedge()\n\n    async def on_md(self, msg):\n        \"\"\"ex.md.<FEED>.* -- everyone's activity on the feed. We only care\n        about E (execution) messages here, filtered by sender.\"\"\"\n        f = msg.data.decode().split()\n        if len(f) < 8 or f[1] != \"E\":\n            return\n        incoming, resting = f[2], f[3]\n        vol = int(f[4])\n        px = int(f[5])\n        # incoming/resting are \"sender:orderid\" -- split off the sender.\n        in_sender = incoming.split(\":\", 1)[0]\n        rs_sender = resting.split(\":\", 1)[0]\n        aggressor_side = f[7] if len(f) > 7 and f[7] else None\n\n        for sender, tag in ((in_sender, \"in\"), (rs_sender, \"rs\")):\n            if sender in (QUOTER_SENDER, TAKER_SENDER):\n                # Determine this party's side: the aggressor side is given\n                # directly for the incoming party; the resting party is on\n                # the opposite side.\n                if aggressor_side is None:\n                    continue\n                side = aggressor_side if tag == \"in\" else opposite(aggressor_side)\n                signed = vol if side == \"B\" else -vol\n                self.desk_position += signed\n            elif sender == SENDER:\n                self.on_own_fill(tag, aggressor_side, vol)\n\n        await self.maybe_hedge()\n\n    def on_own_fill(self, tag, aggressor_side, vol):\n        if aggressor_side is None:\n            return\n        side = aggressor_side if tag == \"in\" else opposite(aggressor_side)\n        signed = vol if side == \"B\" else -vol\n        self.own_position += signed\n        self.own_fills += 1\n        # NOTE: if the desk-wide definition in task.md (\"taker + quoter +\n        # hedger together\") should include the hedger's own trades in the\n        # thing being kept low, fold this into desk_position too:\n        # --- hedging policy ------------------------------------------------------\n\n    async def maybe_hedge(self):\n        pos = self.desk_position\n        if abs(pos) <= FLATTEN_THRESHOLD:\n            return\n        if self.hedging_in_flight:\n            return\n        if self.best_bid is None or self.best_ask is None:\n            return\n\n        target = FLATTEN_THRESHOLD if pos > 0 else -FLATTEN_THRESHOLD\n        excess = pos - target  # positive -> desk too long, need to sell |excess|\n        side = \"S\" if excess > 0 else \"B\"\n        size = int(round(abs(excess)))\n        if size <= 0:\n            return\n\n        n_ticks = ticks_through(abs(pos))\n        tick_offset = int(round(n_ticks)) * TICKSIZE\n        if side == \"S\":\n            price = self.best_bid - tick_offset\n        else:\n            price = self.best_ask + tick_offset\n\n        await self.send_hedge_order(side, size, price, pos, n_ticks)\n\n    async def send_hedge_order(self, side, size, price, pos_before, n_ticks):\n        async with self.send_lock:\n            self.hedging_in_flight = True\n            oid = self.next_oid()\n            body = f\"{SENDER} A {FEED} {oid} {side} {size} {int(price)} F\"\n            print(f\"[hedger] pos={pos_before} -> F {side} {size} @ {price} \"\n                  f\"(ticks_through={n_ticks:.1f})\", flush=True)\n            try:\n                await self.nc.publish(f\"ex.req.{SENDER}\", body.encode())\n                await self.nc.flush()\n            finally:\n                self.hedging_in_flight = False\n\n\ndef opposite(side):\n    return \"S\" if side == \"B\" else \"B\"\n\n\nasync def main():\n    nc = await nats.connect(NATS_URL)\n    print(f\"[hedger] connected to {NATS_URL} as {SENDER}\", flush=True)\n\n    h = Hedger(nc)\n\n    await nc.subscribe(f\"ex.bbo.{FEED}\", cb=h.on_bbo)\n    await nc.subscribe(f\"ex.md.{FEED}.*\", cb=h.on_md)\n\n    print(f\"[hedger] {SENDER} watching {FEED}, hedging desk position from \"\n          f\"quoter={QUOTER_SENDER} taker={TAKER_SENDER} \"\n          f\"(dead_zone<= {FLATTEN_THRESHOLD}, hard_stop={HARD_STOP}, \"\n          f\"ramp_power={RAMP_POWER})\", flush=True)\n\n    while True:\n        await asyncio.sleep(3600)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    try:\n        asyncio.run(main())\n    except KeyboardInterrupt:\n        pass\n"

But to not bet on that, I added a second detection path: in `handleMd`, when `type == \"E\"` and the aggressor (`inSender`) is the identified `moverSender`, it now also calls `onMoverTargetRevealed` using the execution price and the aggressor-side field (`toks[7]`, confirmed against `PROTOCOL.md`'s `<incoming> <resting> <volume> <price> <matchid> <B|S>` layout). So now you get the walk signal from both the resting remainder (`A`) and from each fill during the sweep (`E`), whichever arrives.\n\n**2. Mover ID vs seed orders \u2014 no bug found.** `aggressorVolume` is only incremented from the *incoming* (aggressor) side of `E` messages, so `MOVER001`'s passive seed resting orders never pollute it \u2014 only genuine sweeps do. Warmup is `kWarmupPeriod = 120s`, not 60s, so timing headroom is more comfortable than you estimated.                 "text": "Yeah, that's exactly the right way to think about it \u2014 mean reversion isn't a replacement for market making here, it's an input to it. Let me lay out how they fit together.\n\n**Market making gives you the mechanism.** You quote both sides, you profit from being crossed on the spread, and your baseline risk is inventory: every fill moves your position away from flat, and if the market moves against that inventory before you can offload it, you lose more than you made on the spread. That's the core problem market makers solve \u2014 not \"what's fair value\" (you already know that exactly here) but \"how do I manage the position I accumulate.\"\n\n**Mean reversion answers the positioning question, not the pricing question.** You don't need it to tell you where fair value is \u2014 you already have `fv(driver)` and `c = fv(driver) + rel` exactly, no estimation involved. What MR gives you is a *view on your inventory risk*: if price is currently far from 600 (or far from `600+rel` for a piggyback), you know with certainty it's going to revert eventually. That means:\n\n- **Skewing your quotes** \u2014 if you're long and price is above the mean, you don't need symmetric quotes anymore. You can tighten/lower your ask (get out faster) and widen/lower your bid (be less eager to add to a position that's already working against reversion risk... or *more* eager, if you want to lean into the reversion). Either way, distance-from-mean becomes a signal for how to bias your book, not just a risk metric to hedge away.\n- **Sizing** \u2014 you mentioned this already in mem2: scale size with `|current price - mean|`. Bigger deviation = more confidence in the direction of the eventual correction = you can afford to run a larger position, because you have a probabilistic edge on which way it resolves, plus you know the hard bound (max deviation = 160 from the clip range) so worst-case risk is bounded even before the hedger does anything.\n- **Position limits as a function of deviation** \u2014 rather than a flat position cap, your effective risk tolerance can expand as deviation grows, since the \"wrong way\" scenario (further deviation) is bounded and increasingly less likely the further out you already are.\n\nSo the way I'd frame it: **fv tells you where to center your quotes, MR tells you how much inventory risk you're willing to carry and in which direction to lean.** The spread capture is still doing the actual profit-generation; MR is risk-adjusted position management layered on top, and it's also your foundation for the hedger's urgency logic later (deviation from mean \u2192 hedging urgency, not just raw position size).\n\nOne thing worth deciding before we write the loop: do you want MR skew to only affect *sizing/position limits*, or also *where you place the quotes themselves* (asymmetric offsets around `c`)? That changes what state the main loop needs to track per instrument.",

                "text": "You've basically got it, but there's a detail in the mechanics worth nailing down precisely, since it affects how you think about fills near the extremes.\n\n**What actually happens per move, looking at the mover code:**\n\nIt's not one order \u2014 it's a loop that fires every 0.2s while `abs(target - cur) >= 2`. Each tick it recomputes `need` fresh off the *live reconstructed book* (`sum of opposing-side volume at prices better than target`), then posts a marketable limit **priced exactly at target**, sized `need * 1.2 + 20`. So:\n\n1. It sweeps every resting order strictly better than the target price (eating through the book level by level).\n2. Since it's a *limit* order at `target`, not a market order, it can't cross past that price \u2014 so once it runs out of resting depth to eat, whatever's left of its own volume (the 20% + 20 buffer) **rests in the book at exactly the target price**. That's your \"wall.\"\n3. Next 0.2s tick checks again \u2014 if `cur` (now the new best bid/ask, which includes that resting wall) is within 2 of target, it stops. Otherwise it fires again with freshly recomputed `need`.\n\nSo in practice it's usually 1\u20132 ticks to get there, not a single order, but the end state matches your intuition: the mover leaves a chunk of its own size resting right at the new price, which functions as the new \"true\" best and effectively pins the mid there until something eats into it.\n\n**One thing worth flagging that isn't obvious from the description alone: the mover never cancels.** If a buy-side sweep leaves excess resting on the *bid*, that resting bid volume just sits there. If the next move is a reversal (target now below cur), the sell-side sweep's `need` calc will include that old leftover bid volume as depth it has to eat through. So residual walls from a prior move can get swept again later \u2014 the book isn't clean between moves, there's a bit of memory in it.\n\n**On the bound:** you're right that this is hard-capped, not just empirically likely \u2014 `target = clip(target + step, 440, 760)`, so max deviation from 600 is exactly 160, always. That's a real worst-case bound you can size against, not a tail estimate.\n\n**Ties back to your split (half-life = when, z-score = how far):** that's the right decomposition, and I'd add one implication from the mechanics above \u2014 right after a big move, the best price on that side isn't thin, it's got real size sitting behind it (the wall). So when your z-score signal says \"we're way out, time to lean into reversion,\" the fill you'd get trading toward the extreme isn't against a flickering top-of-book, it's against a deliberately-sized resting order. That's relevant for how confidently you can size a position at extension \u2014 there's usually real liquidity there, not just an ephemeral touch print.\n\nWant to move on to sketching what state the main loop needs to track per instrument to compute z-score/half-life live (rolling window, sample cadence, etc.), or dig further into the position/hedging risk model first?",

                "text": "Good instinct \u2014 the old metric (any large negative PnL = bug) doesn't work anymore because negative PnL is now an *expected phase* of the strategy, not a signal of malfunction. You need metrics that decompose PnL into \"is this working as designed\" vs \"is this broken,\" since a single scalar can't do that anymore.\n\nHere's how I'd split it:\n\n**1. Realized vs. mark-to-market PnL \u2014 track separately, always.**\nWhile a position is open and extended, unrealized PnL *should* be negative (you're leaning against the current move, before reversion has happened). That's expected and not a bug signal. What you actually care about is **realized PnL over completed cycles** \u2014 once a position from an extension event gets flattened, was that round-trip net positive? If realized PnL trends negative over many completed cycles, that's a real strategy or hedging problem. If only unrealized/mark-to-market dips while positions are open, that's just the strategy doing its job mid-cycle.\n\n**2. Per-cycle attribution: did positions taken at extension actually resolve via reversion?**\nFor each position opened when z-score crossed your threshold, tag it and track: did price actually revert toward the mean before you were forced to hedge out (dead-band, position limit, driver hit the bound and kept going the other way)? If a meaningful fraction of \"high-conviction\" extension trades never get to reap the reversion \u2014 you're getting hedged out before the payoff \u2014 that tells you your half-life/z-score thresholds are miscalibrated, separate from whether the sim itself is behaving.\n\n**3. Theoretical worst-case bound as a bug detector, not just a risk figure.**\nBecause deviation is hard-capped at 160 ticks from 600, for any given position size you can compute an exact worst-case loss (position \u00d7 max adverse move to the clip boundary). If realized drawdown on any single position *exceeds* that theoretical ceiling, that's not \"bad luck,\" that's a bug \u2014 sizing, pricing, or fill-side logic is wrong. This is a much sharper catch than \"PnL is very negative,\" because it's a hard deterministic ceiling, not a statistical judgment call.\n\n**4. Signed position vs. signed deviation correlation.**\nSince you're positioning *opposite* the current extension (leaning into reversion), signed position and signed z-score should be negatively correlated across the run. If that correlation flattens or flips sign, something's wrong in the positioning logic \u2014 sign flip, stale z-score read, wrong side of the trade, etc. This is a cheap sanity check you can compute continuously and alert on, rather than staring at a PnL chart.\n\n**5. Quote uptime / fill-symmetry, same as before.**\nKeep this \u2014 are both sides actually quoting when they should be, is one side getting starved, are quotes stuck paused. This catches mechanical/plumbing bugs independent of the MR logic entirely.\n\nSo the shape of it: instead of one number, you'd want **(realized cycle PnL) + (bound-violation count) + (position/deviation correlation) + (quote uptime)** as your four dials. Cycles of negative *unrealized* PnL are fine and expected; negative *realized* PnL over many cycles, bound violations, or correlation breakdown are your actual bug signals.\n\nWant to sketch what per-instrument state/logging you'd need to compute these live (e.g. tagging position-open events with entry z-score, tracking cycle completion)?",

                "text": "You're most of the way there, but there's a subtlety in the mover's mechanics that changes how you should think about \"almost surely\" \u2014 worth nailing down before you commit to a pricing rule.\n\n**The reversion isn't a per-step guarantee \u2014 it's a statistical property.** Look at the target selection: `direction = random.choice([-1, 1])` \u2014 that's a fair coin flip on *every* move, completely independent of where the current target sits (except right at the 440/760 boundaries, where clipping breaks the symmetry). So sitting at 620, the next move isn't \"more likely down than up\" in isolation \u2014 it's 50/50, same as it always is. What actually produces the reversion you're seeing in the data (that 16-36s half-life you measured) is an aggregate/boundary effect: because the walk is bounded and symmetric, it spends more *time* near 600 than near the edges, and large deviations statistically decay over many steps, not because any single next step is biased back toward the mean. This matters because it means you can't treat \"price will return to 600\" as a near-certainty on any given trade \u2014 it's a distribution of outcomes, and your half-life measurement already captures the real shape of that distribution (including clip-boundary effects), so lean on that empirical number rather than a \"coin flip toward the mean\" intuition.\n\n**So the actual tradeoff you're solving is fill-probability vs. profit-per-fill, not certainty vs. price.** Your example nails this: short at 620, bid at 610 fills almost certainly (small moves back toward 620 area get you there) but banks little. Bid at 605 might not fill at all if the mover reverses back up before ever printing that low. There's no free lunch here \u2014 moving your closing bid closer to 600 trades fill-probability for size of payout, and that's a real optimization, not just \"get as close to the target as you can.\"\n\n**Concretely, tying it to z-score like you proposed:** the entry z-score (how far you are from 600 when you open) tells you how much room there statistically is to profit from \u2014 bigger deviation, more room, and empirically (per your half-life data) a longer expected path back down, meaning more chances for price to pass through any given level on the way. That supports placing the closing bid further out toward the mean when entry deviation is large, since you're likely to get multiple opportunities to be crossed as the mover works back down in several jumps rather than one clean move.\n\n**One refinement worth considering: ladder it rather than a single price.** The mover moves in discrete jumps (steps of 20-60 normal, 40-120 on shock) rather than continuously, and it doesn't always fully round-trip back to 600 before reversing again. A single bid at one price is a bet on hitting that exact level; a ladder of resting bids between your entry and the mean captures partial profit at whatever depth the reversion actually reaches, and reduces the \"missed it entirely\" risk you flagged \u2014 if the mover only gets partway back before turning around again, you still got filled on the near levels even if the far ones never traded. This also lines up naturally with how the LP piggyback bots themselves quote (ladders), so it's consistent with the rest of your architecture.\n\nQuestion before we lock this down: are you thinking single order per entry, or a resting ladder across the reversion range? That decides whether the pricing rule is \"one number as a function of z-score\" or \"a spread of levels as a function of z-score and expected step size.\"",

                "text": "Good, and I think that \"half-life as a timing mechanism\" idea is actually sharper than it might sound at first \u2014 but there are two different things it could mean, and they lead to fairly different main-loop logic, so worth pinning down which one you're after.\n\n**Use case A: half-life as a \"give up and reprice\" timeout.**\nYou post your ladder at entry. Half-life tells you the *expected* time for deviation to decay by half \u2014 so if you're at z=3 with a 20s half-life, you'd expect roughly z=1.5 at t+20s. If you check back at, say, 1.5\u20132 half-lives and price *hasn't* meaningfully reverted, that's a signal your entry episode isn't tracking the average behavior \u2014 could be the mover's currently oscillating near an extreme, could be a fresh shock in the same direction extending things further. Either way, it's a trigger to reassess: pull the stale far-rungs of your ladder and reprice closer to current price (chase it in), or hand more urgency to the hedger rather than passively waiting for a fill that may not come on this cycle.\n\n**Use case B: half-life as a re-anchoring trigger when deviation *grows*.**\nIf the mover extends further away from mean after you've already laddered (new shock, bigger step), your half-life estimate itself changes \u2014 starting from a bigger deviation implies a longer expected reversion path. So you might want to add rungs further out (there's now more room to profit) or widen your existing ladder's range, rather than leaving it sized for the old, smaller deviation.\n\nThese aren't mutually exclusive, but they trigger off different things \u2014 (A) triggers off *elapsed time without reversion*, (B) triggers off *the driver hitting a new extreme*. Practically I think both matter, but they probably deserve separate handling in the loop rather than being one \"requote\" event: (B) is really just \"recompute z-score, recompute ladder\" on every driver update (which you're already doing structurally), while (A) needs its own clock \u2014 something like \"time since entry\" or \"time since last new extreme\" compared against the current half-life estimate, checked independently.\n\nOne thing worth flagging on the half-life estimate itself: is it a single global constant computed once from your captured EDA data, or something you're planning to estimate live/rolling as the sim runs? That matters a lot for (A) \u2014 if half-life is fixed, the timeout logic is simple (elapsed_time > k \u00d7 half_life). If it's live-estimated, you've got a two-way dependency where a \"position hasn't reverted yet\" episode could itself be dragging your half-life estimate up, which needs guarding against (e.g. computing half-life only from historical completed reversion episodes, not from currently-open ones).\n\nWhich of A/B (or both) did you mean by \"requote,\" and is half-life fixed-from-EDA or live-estimated in the current design?",

Either way, it's a trigger to reassess: pull the stale far-rungs of your ladder and reprice closer to current price (chase it in), or hand more urgency to the hedger rather than passively waiting for a fill that may not come on this cycle.\n\n**Use case B: half-life as a re-anchoring trigger when deviation *grows*.**\nIf the mover extends further away from mean after you've already laddered (new shock, bigger step), your half-life estimate itself changes \u2014 starting from a bigger deviation implies a longer expected reversion path. So you might want to add rungs further out (there's now more room to profit) or widen your existing ladder's range, rather than leaving it sized for the old, smaller deviation.\n\nThese aren't mutually exclusive, but they trigger off different things \u2014 (A) triggers off *elapsed time without reversion*, (B) triggers off *the driver hitting a new extreme*. Practically I think both matter, but they probably deserve separate handling in the loop rather than being one \"requote\" event: (B) is really just \"recompute z-score, recompute ladder\" on every driver update (which you're already doing structurally), while (A) needs its own clock \u2014 something like \"time since entry\" or \"time since last new extreme\" compared against the current half-life estimate, checked independently.\n\nOne thing worth flagging on the half-life estimate itself: is it a single global constant computed once from your captured EDA data, or something you're planning to estimate live/rolling as the sim runs? That matters a lot for (A) \u2014 if half-life is fixed, the timeout logic is simple (elapsed_time > k \u00d7 half_life). If it's live-estimated, you've got a two-way dependency where a \"position hasn't reverted yet\" episode could itself be dragging your half-life estimate up, which needs guarding against (e.g. computing half-life only from historical completed reversion episodes, not from currently-open ones).\n\nWhich of A/B (or both) did you mean by \"requote,\" and is half-life fixed-from-EDA or live-estimated in the current design?",

                            "description": "Creating the fresh mean-reversion quoter design doc, superseding the old crossing-based spec",
                            "path": "/mnt/user-data/outputs/mean_reversion_quoter_design.md",
                            "file_text": "# Cannon Capital Quoter \u2014 Mean Reversion Design (v1)\n\nStatus: current design. Supersedes the old rel-recovery and LP-crossing designs entirely\n(both abandoned \u2014 see mem2.md for history). This doc starts fresh from the mean-reversion\npivot.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Core Thesis\n\nWe are not trying to win a speed race against LPs, and we are not trying to predict where\nan LP will reprice to. We're market-making around a **known, exactly-computable fair value**\n(`fv(driver)`), and using the driver's **statistically bounded, mean-reverting behavior** to\ninform *positioning* \u2014 how much size to carry, in which direction, and where to place resting\norders to capture the reversion when it happens.\n\nMarket making still does the actual profit generation (two-sided quoting, spread capture).\nMean reversion is a risk-adjusted overlay on top of that: it tells us when deviation from\nfair value is large enough to be worth leaning into, and how confidently to size a position\nagainst it.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Ground-Truth Assumptions\n\n- **One driver, one piggyback per cluster.** No multi-piggyback clusters, no ambiguity in\n  driver/piggyback pairing.\n- **Bot behavior matches the sim source exactly** (confirmed by reading `market.py`, not\n  inferred from data):\n  - **Mover** (front-month only, e.g. AAH6): picks a new `target` every 2.5\u20134.5s, clipped to\n    `[440, 760]` around `START=600`. Direction is an independent fair coin flip each move\n    (`random.choice([-1, 1])`), step size 20\u201360 normal / 40\u2013120 on ~30% shock chance. Walks\n    toward target every 0.2s via marketable limit orders priced exactly at `target`, sized to\n    eat resting opposing depth (`need * 1.2 + 20`). Because it's a *limit* order at `target`,\n    once it exhausts resting depth better than `target`, its own leftover size **rests at\n    `target`** \u2014 this is the \"wall\" that pins price there until something eats through it.\n    The mover never cancels; leftover resting size from a prior move can persist and get\n    swept again on a later reversal.\n  - **Background piggyback LPs** (e.g. AAM6, AAU6): quote `c = round(fv(AAH6) + rel)`, `rel`\n    fixed per contract at bot startup. Full cancel/repost of a symmetric ladder\n    (`bid = c - offset - i`, `ask = c + offset + i`, `i in [0, levels)`) whenever rounded `c`\n    changes. Not something we trade against directly in this design \u2014 we quote on the\n    piggyback ourselves, independent of LP ladder mechanics.\n  - **Taker**: reads BBO off one random instrument, submits an aggressive/marketable order to\n    a different, independently-chosen instrument. Small size (`1 + int(20*random()**2)`).\n    Source of incidental crossing flow, not something we key logic off of.\n- **`fv(driver)` is exact, not estimated**: falls back to mid when spread \u2265 2 ticks or both\n  book-side volumes are zero, else microprice `(bid*askvol + ask*bidvol)/(bidvol+askvol)`.\n- **True mean is known exactly**: `E[price] = 600` for the driver (proven by the symmetric\n  bounded random walk structure, not empirically estimated), `E[c] = 600 + rel` for each\n  piggyback by the same symmetry argument.\n- **Hard deviation bound**: max deviation from 600 is exactly 160 (clip range), always. This\n  is a deterministic ceiling, not a statistical tail estimate \u2014 usable directly for worst-case\n  sizing.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Reversion Dynamics \u2014 Important Nuance\n\nThe reversion is **not** driven by a restoring force proportional to current deviation (i.e.\nthis is *not* an OU/AR(1) process, despite \"half-life\" language borrowed from that world).\nStep direction is an independent fair coin flip **everywhere**, with no bias toward the mean\nin the interior. Net reversion emerges only from the **clip boundary** at 440/760, which\nconcentrates future moves back toward center once you're near an edge.\n\nPractical implication: any given single step is not \"more likely\" to move back toward 600 \u2014\nit's still ~50/50 away from the boundary. Reversion is a property of the aggregate/long-run\ndistribution (time spent near center vs. edges), not a per-step guarantee. Treat half-life\nas a statistical expectation over many episodes, not a certainty on any individual trade.\n\n**Decision (v1, deliberately simplified):** treat half-life as a single constant, derived\nonce from a large captured sample of driver mid-price history, collected at startup /\noffline from EDA data. No rolling re-estimation (unlike the old debounce-window mechanism \u2014\nthere is no rolling mean here, the DGP is stationary for the life of the run).\n\n**Known open risk, deferred:** because reversion is boundary-driven rather than OU-style\ndecay, half-life may not actually be constant across different starting deviations (e.g. a\nshock near the boundary could revert at a different effective rate than a small drift near\ncenter). Flagged for a later bucketed check (segment historical deviation episodes by entry\nz-score bucket, compare realized decay time per bucket) once the single-constant version is\nworking end-to-end. Not blocking v1.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Signal Definitions\n\n- **`fv(driver)`**: computed live from driver BBO, per the formula above.\n- **`c` (piggyback fair center)**: `fv(driver) + rel`. `rel` is fixed per contract; needs to\n  be known/derivable per piggyback (open item \u2014 see \u00a78).\n- **`z-score`**: standardized deviation of current driver mid (or `c`, for piggybacks) from\n  its known true mean (600, or `600+rel`), scaled by a fixed empirical stdev estimate from\n  the same offline sample used for half-life.\n- **`half-life`**: fixed constant, estimated offline from captured historical driver mid data\n  before the strategy goes live (large sample, collected while sitting idle at startup or\n  from pre-captured EDA CSVs).\n\n---\n\n## 5. Positioning & Pricing Logic\n\n### 5.1 Entry trigger\nEnter (lean into reversion) when `|z-score|` crosses a fixed threshold. Direction is opposite\nthe current deviation: price above mean \u2192 go short (post asks); price below mean \u2192 go long\n(post bids).\n\n### 5.2 Order structure: ladder, not single order\nA single order at one price is all-or-nothing \u2014 statistically profitable in expectation but\nwith real risk of being caught on the wrong side of realized PnL for a while, which is\nunacceptable given the sim may end mid-cycle (grading is wall-clock, no guarantee we're\nflat/positive at cutoff).\n\n**Decision:** resting **ladder** of orders between entry price and the mean, rather than one\norder at one level.\n- Captures partial profit if reversion only gets partway before reversing again (matches\n  observed mover behavior \u2014 it doesn't always fully round-trip through 600 before turning).\n- Reduces \"missed it entirely\" risk from a single mis-placed price.\n- Consistent with how the sim's own LP bots quote (ladders), and reuses structural patterns\n  already built for LP ladder handling.\n\n### 5.3 Ladder pricing\n- Rungs span from just past entry price back toward the mean.\n- Larger entry deviation (higher z-score) \u2192 statistically more room and (per current fixed\n  half-life assumption) a longer expected reversion path with more opportunities for price to\n  pass through intermediate levels \u2192 supports placing the far/closing rung(s) further out\n  toward the mean, and potentially more rungs.\n- Rung closest to entry trades higher fill-probability for smaller profit-per-fill; rung\n  closest to the mean trades lower fill-probability for larger profit-per-fill. This tradeoff\n  is real and tunable, not something to \"solve\" \u2014 pick a reasonable spacing and revisit with\n  data.\n\n### 5.4 Sizing\n- Position size per entry should be **small relative to what the hedger can absorb** \u2014 the\n  whole point of small positioning is minimizing the work (and the risk) handed to the\n  hedger, not relying on the hedger to bail out oversized entries.\n- Scale size with `|current price - mean|` (larger deviation \u2192 more confidence in eventual\n  direction \u2192 can size up modestly), bounded by the known hard cap (max deviation = 160) for\n  a hard worst-case loss ceiling per position.\n- Old heuristic (\"LP's per-level volume minus 1\") is a candidate additional per-level cap,\n  not load-bearing in this design (we're not keying off LP ladders anymore).\n\n### 5.5 Requote / re-anchor triggers\nTwo distinct triggers, handled separately rather than merged into one \"requote\" event:\n\n- **(A) Re-anchor on new extreme** \u2014 every driver update, recompute `fv`, z-score, and\n  ladder. If deviation has grown past the existing ladder's range (new shock), extend/widen\n  the ladder rather than leaving it sized for the old, smaller deviation. This is naturally\n  continuous, not timer-based.\n- **(B) Give-up/reprice timeout** \u2014 if elapsed time since entry exceeds some multiple of the\n  fixed half-life (e.g. `k \u00d7 half_life`) without meaningful reversion, treat this episode as\n  not tracking the average behavior (could be an extended run near an extreme, could be a\n  fresh shock in the same direction). Trigger: pull stale far rungs and reprice closer to\n  current price, and/or escalate urgency to the hedger rather than passively waiting.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Risk Model\n\n- **Hard bound**: 160 ticks max deviation from true mean, deterministic. For any position\n  size, worst-case loss to the clip boundary is exactly computable \u2014 this is a bug detector,\n  not just a risk number (see \u00a77).\n- **Clean separation from hedger** (carried over from the old design, still holds): quoter\n  only defends its own position (pauses/pulls quotes when threatened), never self-flattens by\n  crossing the spread. All active flattening is the hedger's job. Small positioning here is\n  specifically so the hedger's job stays small and boring.\n- **Circuit breaker**: per-instrument pause on detected jump/gap events, same rationale as\n  before \u2014 quoter is the only place that can cancel a still-resting stale order, so gap\n  protection has to live here, not in the hedger.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Performance Metrics (bug-catching, not just PnL)\n\nOld metric (\"any large negative PnL = bug\") doesn't work anymore \u2014 negative *unrealized* PnL\nmid-cycle is now expected behavior, not a fault signal. Decompose into:\n\n1. **Realized (per-completed-cycle) PnL** vs. **mark-to-market PnL**, tracked separately.\n   Unrealized dips while a position is open and extended are expected. Realized PnL trending\n   negative over many completed cycles is the real signal.\n2. **Per-cycle attribution**: tag positions with entry z-score; track whether they resolved\n   via reversion before being forced out (dead-band / position limit / hedger intervention).\n   A high rate of \"never got to reap the reversion\" indicates miscalibrated thresholds, not\n   necessarily a broken sim.\n3. **Bound-violation check**: for any position, worst-case loss is exactly computable from the\n   160-tick hard bound. Realized drawdown exceeding that theoretical ceiling on any single\n   position is a hard bug signal (sizing, pricing, or fill logic), not statistical noise.\n4. **Signed position vs. signed deviation correlation**: should be negatively correlated\n   throughout the run (we position opposite the current extension). Flattening/flipping\n   correlation = sign error, stale read, or wrong-side logic somewhere.\n5. **Quote uptime / fill-symmetry**: both sides quoting when expected, no one-sided\n   starvation, no stuck-paused instruments. Catches mechanical/plumbing bugs independent of\n   MR logic.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Open Items\n\n- **`rel` per piggyback**: how is this known/derived in the new design? (Old design recovered\n  it from LP requote bursts \u2014 abandoned. New design may not need LP-ladder recovery at all if\n  `rel` can be treated as a fixed per-contract constant discoverable another way \u2014 needs a\n  decision.)\n- **Half-life bucketing by entry z-score** \u2014 deferred per \u00a73, revisit once v1 is working.\n- **`InstrumentState` struct** \u2014 needs a full MR-oriented redesign (old version was\n  ladder/burst-tracking-oriented for the abandoned crossing design). Needs to carry at\n  minimum: rolling driver mid history (or reference to offline-computed mean/stdev/half-life),\n  current z-score, active ladder state, entry timestamp(s) for the (B) timeout check, position\n  state per instrument.\n- **Main loop structure** \u2014 not yet designed under this direction. Next step.\n- **Hedger** \u2014 not yet designed under this direction (previously deferred, still deferred).\n- **`DESK_STATE` shape** \u2014 still unresolved, still the original pre-LP-ID topic, still\n  outstanding.\n- **Ladder spacing rule** \u2014 \"reasonable spacing, revisit with data\" is a placeholder, not a\n  formula yet.\n- **z-score stdev estimate** \u2014 needs to come from the same offline sample as half-life;\n  method not yet specified (simple rolling stdev vs. something else).\n\n---\n\n## 9. Next Step\n\nDesign the main loop: per-instrument state, event handling (driver update \u2192 recompute z-score\n\u2192 re-anchor check per \u00a75.5(A); timer/tick \u2192 timeout check per \u00a75.5(B)), and how offline\nhalf-life/mean/stdev estimation feeds into live state at startup.\n"
