Core Thesis\\n\\nWe are not trying to win a speed race against LPs, and we are not trying to predict where\\nan LP will reprice to. We're market-making around a **known, exactly-computable fair value**\\n(`fv(driver)`), and using the driver's **statistically bounded, mean-reverting behavior** to\\ninform *positioning* \\u2014 how much size to carry, in which direction, and where to place resting\\norders to capture the reversion when it happens.\\n\\nMarket making still does the actual profit generation (two-sided quoting, spread capture).\\nMean reversion is a risk-adjusted overlay on top of that: it tells us when deviation from\\nfair value is large enough to be worth leaning into, and how confidently to size a position\\nagainst it.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2. Ground-Truth Assumptions\\n\\n- **One driver, one piggyback per cluster.** No multi-piggyback clusters, no ambiguity in\\n  driver/piggyback pairing.\\n- **Bot behavior matches the sim source exactly** (confirmed by reading `market.py`, not\\n  inferred from data):\\n  - **Mover** (front-month only, e.g. AAH6): picks a new `target` every 2.5\\u20134.5s, clipped to\\n    `[440, 760]` around `START=600`. Direction is an independent fair coin flip each move\\n    (`random.choice([-1, 1])`), step size 20\\u201360 normal / 40\\u2013120 on ~30% shock chance. Walks\\n    toward target every 0.2s via marketable limit orders priced exactly at `target`, sized to\\n    eat resting opposing depth (`need * 1.2 + 20`). Because it's a *limit* order at `target`,\\n    once it exhausts resting depth better than `target`, its own leftover size **rests at\\n    `target`** \\u2014 this is the \\\"wall\\\" that pins price there until something eats through it.\\n    The mover never cancels; leftover resting size from a prior move can persist and get\\n    swept again on a later reversal.\\n  - **Background piggyback LPs** (e.g. AAM6, AAU6): quote `c = round(fv(AAH6) + rel)`, `rel`\\n    fixed per contract at bot startup. Full cancel/repost of a symmetric ladder\\n    (`bid = c - offset - i`, `ask = c + offset + i`, `i in [0, levels)`) whenever rounded `c`\\n    changes. Not something we trade against directly in this design \\u2014 we quote on the\\n    piggyback ourselves, independent of LP ladder mechanics.\\n  - **Taker**: reads BBO off one random instrument, submits an aggressive/marketable order to\\n    a different, independently-chosen instrument. Small size (`1 + int(20*random()**2)`).\\n    Source of incidental crossing flow, not something we key logic off of.\\n- **`fv(driver)` is exact, not estimated**: falls back to mid when spread \\u2265 2 ticks or both\\n  book-side volumes are zero, else microprice `(bid*askvol + ask*bidvol)/(bidvol+askvol)`.\\n- **True mean is known exactly**: `E[price] = 600` for the driver (proven by the symmetric\\n  bounded random walk structure, not empirically estimated), `E[c] = 600 + rel` for each\\n  piggyback by the same symmetry argument.\\n- **Hard deviation bound**: max deviation from 600 is exactly 160 (clip range), always. Quote asymmetrically / pull proactively instead of reactively racing.**\nSince you can predict roughly when the LP's center will cross a rounding boundary (you already track fv(driver) and rel), you could pull your quote *before* the boundary crossing rather than trying to win the race to requote after. You need the two to work as a system.\n\n**4. If `c` changes while you're halfway through laying down your ladder, the right move is to abort the remaining adds and restart the whole cycle (cancel what you just posted, recompute, repost) rather than finish posting a ladder that's half stale. Otherwise you've built a subtler version of the same \"acted on outdated state\" bug from before, just moved into the posting phase instead of the repricing phase.\n\n**Observing `c`, not raw `fv(driver)`**\n\nThis is correct and it's a real tightening, not just a rename \u2014 worth being clear on why in your own head so it's not lost when you write the spec. The LP's actual code only cancels/reposts when `c` itself crosses a rounding boundary; it doesn't act on every sub-tick move in `fv(driver)`. We'd already landed on this rule earlier (trigger = `round(fv(driver)+rel)` changing), but \"observe `c`\" is the cleaner way to state it for docs, and it removes any temptation to accidentally wire the trigger to raw `fv` changes again later.\n\nOne thing to make explicit in the spec since it's easy to lose: `c` is **per-piggyback**, not a single shared driver-level value \u2014 because `rel` differs per piggyback, AAM6's `c` and AAU6's `c` cross their rounding boundaries at different moments even though they're driven by the same `fv(driver)`. So \"observe `c`\" needs to mean \"observe each piggyback's own `c`, independently,\" with independent cancel/repost cycles per instrument \u2014 consistent with the per-instrument independence you locked in earlier for the discovery pipeline, just make sure the trigger logic mirrors that same independence.\n\nWant to draft the MD instructions/spec now with this tightened sequencing, or keep working through position control first like you said earlier?",

A hedger taking an opposing position after seeing those fills come in is fundamentally a cleanup mechanism: it can offset the position you already took, but it cannot stop your *still-resting* stale order from getting hit again by the next wave of the same burst, because the resting order is still sitting there live on the exchange until something explicitly cancels it. Only the quoter can do that \u2014 the hedger has no authority over the quoter's orders and no faster path to the exchange for that specific action.\n\nSo if you route \"drop everything on jump\" through the hedger, what actually happens on a big jump is: quoter's stale orders sit exposed and keep eating fills \u2192 hedger sees position moving and starts flattening those fills after the fact.                 "uuid": "01a05b9c-8499-7c78-97a5-5366b7a1ab6f",
                "text": "The arithmetic itself checks out \u2014 `randint(20,60)` gives a non-shock floor of 20/600 \u2248 3.33%, and `E[uniform(40,120)] = 80`, so 80/600 \u2248 13.3% for the expected shock. No issue there. But two things worth working through before you lock in 40 as the threshold.\n\n**1. A threshold of 40 doesn't cleanly separate \"shock\" from \"normal.\"**\n\nSince shock range is [40,120] and non-shock range is [20,60], a 40-unit cutoff catches *every* shock (good, min shock is exactly 40) but also catches roughly the top half of ordinary non-shock moves (anything in [40,60], which is half the non-shock uniform range). Rough math: 30% chance shock \u00d7 100% caught, plus 70% chance non-shock \u00d7 ~50% caught (the [40,60] slice of [20,60]) \u2248 65% of *all* moves would trigger pause-and-sit, not just the sharp ones. That might be exactly the trade-off you want (bias hard toward safety, accept a lot of idle time), but it's worth naming explicitly rather than calling it \"conservative\" \u2014 conservative undersells that you'd be pausing on most ordinary moves too, not just the dangerous tail.\n\nIf you want the threshold to actually discriminate shock from non-shock rather than just be a low bar that shocks always clear, you'd want it above 60 (out of non-shock's reach entirely) \u2014 but then you're deliberately *not* pausing on the top of the non-shock range, which per the CSV data might still be enough to run you over depending on your buffer width.                 "text": "Almost certainly not guaranteed to be simultaneous, and this is worth being precise about because it's actually the crux of the whole problem, not a side detail.\n\nNATS pub/sub doesn't give you delivery-order or delivery-time guarantees across different subscribers by default. When the exchange publishes a BBO update on `ex.bbo.<FRONT>`, it's one publish, but it fans out to every subscriber (you, the LP, and however many other processes are subscribed) independently. Each subscriber's client library, network path, and processing queue are separate \u2014 so \"the LP received and processed this message\" and \"you received and processed this message\" are two different events that can happen at different wall-clock times, even though they originated from the same publish. Under normal conditions the gap is probably small (sub-millisecond to a few ms, depending on load), but \"probably small\" is exactly the kind of assumption that produces intermittent scatter rather than a clean signal, which is exactly what you're seeing.\n\nThis matters more than it might seem because of how the LP's trigger actually works \u2014 recall:\n\n```python\nasync def on_bbo(_m):\n    fv = fair_value(bbo.get(FRONT))\n    ...\n    c = int(round(fv + rel))\n    if c != center[0]:\n        await requote(c)\n```\n\nThe LP only acts when the *rounded* `c` changes. That means the LP isn't reacting to every driver tick \u2014 only to the ticks that happen to push it across a rounding boundary. If you're sampling your own `fv(driver)` at the moment you observe the LP's *resulting requote*, but the driver has ticked again (even slightly) between the LP's `on_bbo` firing and your own read of `bbo`/`fv`, you can land in a different rounding bucket than the LP actually used \u2014 even though both of you are looking at \"the same\" BBO subscription in principle.\n\nSo this reframes the diagnosis from last message: it's not necessarily that your `fairValue()` formula is wrong (though still worth diffing against the reference), it's that **\"observe c, then read your own live fv(driver) right now\" implicitly assumes simultaneity that NATS doesn't give you.** That's exactly why the causal-anchor approach existed in the first place \u2014 not as unnecessary complexity, but because this ordering gap is real. The part that was actually likely wrong wasn't the *idea* of anchoring, it was possibly the specific implementation (which timestamp it anchored to, e.g. cancel vs add).\n\nGiven that, worth reconsidering: rather than trying to eliminate the anchoring entirely (which reintroduces the exact race this was solving), the fix might be to anchor to something tighter and more directly tied to the LP's actual moment of decision \u2014 e.g., anchor to the timestamp of the LP's **cancel** message specifically (the earliest visible sign the LP decided to requote), not the add, and make sure `midHistory` has fine enough granularity that `valueAtOrBefore` isn't skipping past a real intervening driver move.\n\nWant to check what `burstTs` is actually anchored to right now in your code, since that's the concrete thing to verify before deciding whether to keep or rework the anchoring?",

                "text": "`valueAtOrBefore` does exactly what its name says: given a timestamp `ts`, it finds the most recent history entry whose timestamp is `<= ts`, and returns that entry's value. Walking through it:\n\n- `hist` is a deque of `(timestamp, fv)` pairs, and it's implicitly assumed to be sorted ascending by timestamp (since it's built by `push_back` as new market data arrives \u2014 append-only, so it's naturally in time order).\n- `hist.front().first > ts` \u2014 if even the *earliest* recorded point is already after `ts`, there's no valid \"at or before\" point to return, so it bails out with `false`. This handles the cold-start case (asking about a time before you'd started recording anything).\n- `std::upper_bound(..., ts, comparator)` \u2014 this is doing a binary search for the first element whose timestamp is **strictly greater than** `ts`. The comparator `[](long long t, const pair& p) { return t < p.first; }` is the custom \"is `t` less than this element\" predicate that `upper_bound` uses to walk the search \u2014 so it returns an iterator `it` pointing to the first entry with `timestamp > ts`.\n- `if (it == hist.begin()) return false;` \u2014 if *every* entry has `timestamp > ts`, there's nothing at-or-before `ts` either (shouldn't really happen given the front-check above, but it's a defensive guard).\n- `--it;` \u2014 step back one, from \"first entry strictly after ts\" to \"last entry at-or-before ts\". That's the entry you actually want.\n- `out = it->second; return true;` \u2014 returns that entry's fv value.\n\nSo mechanically, this function is correct for what it claims to do: it finds the most recent fv sample recorded at or before a given timestamp. No bug in the binary search logic itself.\n\nBut here's the thing you just said that matters more than the function's mechanics \u2014 **you jumped straight to blaming `fairValue()`'s mid/microprice branching without us actually checking whether that's the problem.** That's worth slowing down on, because there are now three live hypotheses in play (anchor timestamp choice, `midHistory` granularity, and the fv formula itself) and you're about to debug the third one without having ruled out the first two \u2014 which is exactly the kind of thing that wastes a debugging session chasing the wrong layer.\n\nSpecifically: even if `valueAtOrBefore`'s binary search is perfectly correct, it can only return what's actually **in** `midHistory` \u2014 and `midHistory` only gets a new entry every time your own `onBBO` fires for the driver. If the driver's BBO doesn't update between two LP repricing events (or updates less often than the LP's internal reprice cadence), `valueAtOrBefore` will correctly return the \"at or before\" point \u2014 but that point could still be stale relative to what the LP actually saw, simply because nothing newer existed yet to record.                 "text": "Kind of, yeah \u2014 and it's worth naming exactly where the complexity crept in, because I think you had the right instinct several messages ago and then talked yourself past it.\n\nHere's the actual shape of the problem: `rel` is a fixed constant. You have a deterministic formula relating it to two things you can both observe. The only real obstacle is that your `fv(driver)` and the LP's `fv(driver)` might not be looking at the exact same driver state at the exact same instant, because of NATS delivery timing.\n\nEverything since then \u2014 burst-timestamp anchoring, `valueAtOrBefore`, debating the mid/microprice formula, transition-matching schemes \u2014 is all different ways of trying to solve *that one specific problem* (make sure you're comparing against the fv the LP actually used). That's not wrong to worry about, but it's a lot of machinery for what might be a small effect. Given the driver ticks fast and `rel` is exact, the ordering gap between \"LP saw this fv\" and \"you see this fv\" is probably milliseconds at most \u2014 small relative to how much the driver typically moves in that window, *except* during exactly the volatile moments (mover walks/shocks) you've been fighting the whole task.\n\nSo here's the actually simple version, no anchoring, no reconstruction: **just take the median (or mode) of your raw `rel_candidate = c - fv(driver)` samples, and let the noise wash out on its own, but reject outliers instead of trusting a mean/stdev gate.**\n\nWhy this is different from what you tried a few messages ago and got scattered results: a plain mean/stdev trust gate treats every sample as equally valid and gets dragged around by the mismatched-bucket samples (which is why your `sdTicks` was *growing*, not shrinking). Ladder is symmetric: bid=`c-offset-i`, ask=`c+offset+i` for i in [0,levels); `offset`, `levels`, `volume` also fixed per contract at startup, not re-randomized per burst (volume ~ randint(2,6))\n- `fair_value()` reference formula: falls back to mid when spread >= 2 ticks or both book-side volumes are zero, else microprice `(bid*ask_vol + ask*bid_vol)/(bid_vol+ask_vol)`\n- Taker bot: reads BBO from one randomly chosen instrument, submits to an independently/separately chosen instrument (mismatched book pricing), aggressive/marketable pricing, size skewed small (`1 + int(20*random()**2)`)\n- EDA on captured data: all three instruments show significant individual mean-reversion (half-lives ~16-36s) once given enough samples (~13-14 min cold start needed for reliable significance); cross-instrument cointegration approach was abandoned as unnecessary given strong individual mean-reversion \u2014 hedger does independent per-instrument flattening, not cross-instrument netting\n- Grading sim confirmed by organizers to run at real wall-clock speed; instrument scope/count deliberately unspecified \u2014 quoter discovers instruments at runtime via EX_META, no hardcoding\n\n## Strategy evolution (superseded designs, compacted)\n- Early quoter iterations (rolling-mean fair value, then own-book microprice, then regression/cointegration pricing for piggybacks) were all superseded. Root findings that drove the pivots: AAH6 (front) losses were caused by the mover's walk mechanism itself (not stale pricing) \u2014 decided to stop quoting AAH6 directly and use it only as a latent signal; AAM6/AAU6 own-book pricing was confirmed noisy/disconnected from the LP's true price (piggyback book is thin), which is what motivated recovering the LP's exact deterministic `rel` constant instead of statistical estimation\n- Settled quoter approach (current): treat driver (AAH6) as unquoted signal-only; discover driver/piggyback clusters at runtime (lagged correlation + stability debounce); recover each piggyback's `rel` from the LP's own requote-burst ladder (algebraically cancels offset via inner-level midpoint); quote symmetrically around `c = fv(driver)+rel`, fixed +/-N ticks outside the LP's max ladder reach (not ratcheted to historical min spread); own order volume = LP's observed per-level volume minus 1\n- Settled hedger approach (current): separate Python process, subscribes to all instruments' fill streams to reconstruct desk-wide (quoter+hedger+taker) position, converts piggyback positions to driver-equivalent terms via published rel/offset (DESK_STATE KV), nets into one combined exposure number; small dead-band near zero; urgency scales continuously with |net exposure|/position_limit; reacts per-fill, not on a timer. Not yet built \u2014 deliberately deferred so quoter-only runs isolate whether unmanaged position growth is the sole remaining problem\n- Clean separation of responsibilities settled: quoter only defends (pulls/pauses its own quotes when threatened), never self-flattens by crossing the spread; all position flattening is the hedger's job exclusively\n- Open, unresolved hedger design questions: concrete numeric position cap (task only says \"low\", undefined); whether hedger ever trades the driver (AAH6) directly via IOC orders vs. only through piggybacks; exact hedger-to-quoter coordination signal (proposed: hedger publishes urgency/action state to DESK_STATE so quoter can suppress the side being actively flattened); whether the taker (unmodified legacy code) needs to react to hedger state or is just background noise in the exposure calc\n\n## Quoter rewrite (quoter.cpp, built off quoter_build_spec.md) \u2014 concurrency issues found and fixed\n- Rewrote quoter per a consolidated build spec: debounced cluster/driver locking (permanent once locked, removed from discovery churn), burst-triggered rel recovery (off raw A/C messages, not BBO-both-sides-moved), contamination guard with a mover-camping escape hatch (falls back to best non-mover level, trust requires 3 clean samples AND stddev-in-ticks gate), continuous per-event driver fv tracking triggering immediate per-piggyback reprice, fixed +/-N tick quoting clamped to meta.band, full print checklist for stdout diagnosability\n- Found and fixed (independently, before presenting to Claude) a causal-mismatch bug: burst-processing used live fv(driver) instead of the fv the LP actually saw when it decided to reprice, since ex.md.<driver>.* and ex.md.<piggyback>.* have no cross-subject ordering guarantee. Fix: `valueAtOrBefore()` does an at-or-before-timestamp lookup into the driver's `midHistory` deque, anchored to `burstTs` (the timestamp of the LP's first cancel in the burst, i.e. when it definitely recomputed c)\n- Identified and fixed three computing hazards independently before presenting to Claude:\n  1. Concurrent `requoteInstrument()` calls on the same instrument (multiple callback paths racing, `requoteVersion` guard only protects struct write-back not actual resting exchange orders \u2014 a leaked order at a price neither thread's bookkeeping remembers was possible). Fix applied: queued requote requests (`gPendingRequotes` dedup set + single `requoteWorkerLoop` consumer thread) instead of calling `requoteInstrument` directly from every callback\n  2. `publishPairing`/`kvStore_PutString` blocking call was made while gMutex held, unlike the already-fixed `requoteInstrument` pattern \u2014 fixed by copying needed locals out, unlocking, doing the blocking KV call unlocked, relocking (Claude reviewed this fix: correct, matches the requoteInstrument pattern, no stale-writeback risk since nothing destructive is written after relock)\n  3. `runDiscoveryPass` holds gMutex for the full O(instruments\u00b2\u00d7lag) correlation sweep every 2s \u2014 explicitly deferred by user as low-priority since discovery is a one-time cold-start phase, not revisited in steady state (needs confirming that discovery pass actually stops firing once locked, not just becomes less consequential)\n- Claude's code review of the queue fix found it only PARTIALLY closes the race: the queue correctly serializes `onBBO`/`onMD` fill path/`checkDriverFvUpdate`, but the safety-net loop in `main()` (100ms tick) still calls `requoteInstrument` directly with its own separate lock, bypassing the queue entirely \u2014 so the original race (worker thread vs. safety-net thread both mid-flight on the same instrument) is still possible, not rare. Fix identified: route the safety-net loop through `requestRequote()` too, making the worker thread the sole caller of `requoteInstrument`. Side effect once fixed: all instruments' actual order-entry round trips serialize through one worker thread (does not block market-data ingestion, only order placement) \u2014 acceptable given likely only 2-3 piggybacks\n\n## Major finding: quoting-too-tight losses, and the pivot to wide/defensive quoting\n- Diagnosed root cause of persistent quoter losses via reasoning first, then confirmed against PnL data: quoting inside/near the LP's ladder meant getting crossed immediately on LP reprice, refilling at a worse price than the position just taken, guaranteeing a loss each cycle; the resting-order cancel wasn't landing before the LP's reprice crossed it\n- Corrected finding from reviewing actual PnL CSV (user initially misread column 10 as fair value; it's avg entry price \u2014 column 11 is mid): a single mid-price gap of ~161 units (790.667 \u2192 629, roughly 20% of price level) in the same ~1.3ms window explained a run of 11+ consecutive losing fills on a stale resting bid at ~784-785 while true mid sat at 629 \u2014 not a routine ladder-overlap cross, a genuine large gap event\n- Settled fix direction (multi-part), replacing the earlier ratchet-to-historical-min-spread idea:\n  1. Width: quote one tick beyond the LP's farthest ladder reach (`c \u00b1 (offset+levels-1) \u00b1 1`), aiming to land top-of-book once the LP's ladder clears; explicitly a starting point for iteration, not a final number\n  2. Sizing: match LP's own observed per-level volume (recovered from trade fills against the LP, not the burst) minus 1, so any single bad fill stays small \u2014 reduces both direct PnL hit and what the hedger has to absorb later\n  3. Cancel/recalc/post sequence: bulk-cancel \u2192 lock-free recalc \u2192 re-check trigger before posting \u2192 post ladder one-at-a-time (protocol constraint) \u2192 re-check trigger between EACH individual add, abort-and-restart the whole cycle if `c` moves mid-post rather than finishing a partially-stale ladder\n  4. Reprice trigger: observe `c` itself (the LP's exact rounding-boundary rule), independently per-piggyback (rel differs per piggyback so boundary-crossing moments differ) \u2014 not raw fv(driver) changes\n  5. Jump/gap circuit breaker (in response to the 161-unit gap finding): user proposed folding this into the hedger (immediate opposing position = flattening); Claude pushed back \u2014 hedger can only clean up after a fill already happened, it has no authority to cancel the quoter's still-resting stale order, so routing jump-defense through the hedger turns a preventable problem into a pure-absorption one. Settled instead on keeping this in the quoter: a per-instrument `paused` flag checked at the same site `checkDriverFvUpdate` already computes `c`, set when a jump is detected, checked by all existing call sites before requoting \u2014 reuses existing locked-struct infrastructure, not a redesign\n  6. Detection metric settled: NOT delta-between-consecutive-c-polls (rejected \u2014 a shock's total move can arrive across several smaller updates rather than one big jump, so a fixed delta threshold could miss a genuinely dangerous drift that's spread across ticks); settled instead on tracking the live gap `|resting_px - c|` continuously, pulling/sitting out when it exceeds a threshold (reuses the buffer-width concept as a baseline) \u2014 directly measures the actual risk quantity regardless of how many ticks the underlying move took\n\n## Current live debugging thread: rel recovery not converging (unresolved)\n- Symptom: rel samples scattered wildly (121.5, 105.0, 15.5, -77.5 across consecutive samples) with sdTicks *increasing* as more samples accumulate (46\u219251+) rather than shrinking \u2014 this is the signature of a bias/mixture problem (samples drawn from different true buckets), not insufficient sample count\n- Diagnostic path so far: ruled out burst-detection not firing (sample count is climbing fine, #886+) and ruled out `valueAtOrBefore`'s binary-search logic itself (mechanically correct \u2014 confirmed by walking through it line by line)\n- Key insight surfaced (Claude): NATS gives no cross-subscriber delivery-order/timing guarantee, so \"the LP's fv(driver) at decision time\" and \"your fv(driver) read live\" are NOT guaranteed to agree, even off the same subscription \u2014 this is the real reason `valueAtOrBefore`/causal anchoring exists at all, not unnecessary complexity as the user suspected partway through\n- User's counter-proposal (dropping anchoring entirely, just sample live fv(driver) whenever a new `c` is observed and expect convergence \"with enough samples\") was pushed back on by Claude: this only converges if samples reliably land in the same LP rounding-bucket, which the ordering-gap finding says isn't guaranteed \u2014 averaging a mixture of different true values doesn't converge to the right one, consistent with the observed rising sdTicks\n- Claude's suggested next diagnostic step (not yet done, user found it too jargon-heavy/needed hand-holding on how to add a debug printf; walked through concretely): log `burstTs` (LP's cancel timestamp, current anchor point), the resolved `midHistory` timestamp `valueAtOrBefore` actually picked, and the gap between them, to determine whether the problem is (a) anchor granularity/staleness or (b) the fv formula itself \u2014 user had jumped to blaming the mid/microprice branching in `fairValue()` without this check\n- Claude's proposed simpler alternative to try (pending): keep raw `rel_candidate = c - fv(driver)` sampling (user's original instinct, no timestamp reconstruction), but replace the mean+stddev trust gate with a MEDIAN-based estimator \u2014 robust to a minority of wrong-bucket samples where mean+stddev is not (matches the observed rising-not-shrinking sdTicks pattern); trust once the median stabilizes across recent samples. hypotheses: fair-value lag during the mover's price walks causing adverse selection, or the 250ms requote cadence being too slow relative to sweep events)\n- Initial EDA findings (small-subset sample, later superseded by a longer run): identified that the \"mover\" bot trades AAH6 very frequently (thousands of mover trades vs. single digits/low teens on AAM6/AAU6) and its trading is likely what drives price shifts in the other two instruments as well\n- Re-ran the full EDA (order posting, trade analysis, half-life, ACF, cointegration) after letting the sim run longer (~1157 return obs vs. ~467 originally, still under a full day): all three instruments now show statistically significant individual mean-reversion (half-lives ~16-36s, p-values 0.0005-0.026, versus insignificant p-values 0.17-0.28 in the small-sample run); Johansen test now shows full rank 3 (cointegrating relations at 95%) rather than rank 2 from the small-sample run, consistent with each individual series being near-stationary rather than needing cross-instrument combination to achieve stationarity; pairwise Engle-Granger cointegration still holds for all three pairs; ADF on the current (rank-3) Johansen first eigenvector confirms strong stationarity (statistic -8.0, p\u22480.0000); order-arrival ACF remains significant across nearly all lags 1-40 for all three instruments, treated as characteristic bursty/clustered order flow rather than a tradeable signal\n- Conclusion drawn from the updated EDA: cross-instrument hedging (via cointegration/Johansen weights) is not worth the added complexity given individual mean-reversion is now the dominant, well-supported finding; sticking with the original plan of independent per-instrument flattening in the hedger, and planning to note in NOTES.md that this choice is supported by the individual mean-reversion results reducing the marginal benefit of cross-instrument hedging\n- Next planned step for the hedger: use the mean-reversion half-lives (~16-36s) as justification for a more patient/passive hedging trigger and sizing approach (letting small residual positions ride briefly since they're statistically likely to shrink on their own) rather than aggressively crossing the spread immediately whenever off-flat\n- Found and read the actual \"mover\" bot simulation code: it only trades FRONT (AAH6), never AAM6/AAU6 directly; every 2.5-4.5s picks a new random target price (coin-flip direction, step size 20-60, or 40-120 on a ~30% \"shock\" chance) and every 0.2s walks price toward that target via a single marketable limit order sized to eat exactly the resting depth between current price and target plus a 20% buffer \u2014 so \"sweeps\" are not a separate behavior from \"walking,\" just the large-magnitude tail of the same mechanism; decided this should be built into the quoter (detecting in-progress mover walks / reacting to them) rather than treated as a separate task\n- Found a fair_value() reference implementation (likely the exchange's own fair-value/reference-price definition) using a microprice formula: falls back to simple mid when spread >= 2 ticks or when both book-side volumes are zero, otherwise computes (bid*ask_vol + ask*bid_vol)/(bid_vol+ask_vol) \u2014 decided to switch the quoter's fair value calc to this microprice approach (confirmed this snippet is from the actual simulation/exchange source, not just inspiration)\n- Found and read the taker's action logic: every 0.05-0.5s it reads BBO from one randomly chosen instrument but submits its order to an independently, separately randomly chosen instrument (two separate random.choice(ALL) calls, not tied together) \u2014 meaning taker orders are frequently priced using a different instrument's book than the one they're actually submitted to, a likely source of noisy/mispriced fills distinct from the mover's behavior; taker order price is aggressive/marketable (ask+0-6 ticks or bid-0-6 ticks) and size is skewed toward small values (1 + int(20*random()**2), squared-uniform distribution concentrates near small sizes)\n- Ran own-book microprice change and compared against previous rolling-mean baseline: AAH6 results are similar (fair-value estimation was never the dominant AAH6 problem \u2014 confirms the mover's walk mechanism, not stale pricing, is the main AAH6 loss driver); AAM6 results got worse than the rolling-mean baseline (confirms the piggyback hypothesis \u2014 AAM6/AAU6's own book is thin/noisy and disconnected from the price the dominant background quoters actually use, so an accurate own-book estimate is a confident estimate of the wrong thing)\n- Decided on the AAM6/AAU6 fix: regress each piggyback instrument on the driving instrument (AAM6 = intercept + hedge_ratio*AAH6 + residual, same direction as the true generative relationship AAM6 = AAH6 + rel found in the quoter source) and price off that regression instead of own-book microprice; will compute this as an incremental/rolling OLS in C++ (running sums n, \u03a3x, \u03a3y, \u03a3xy, \u03a3x\u00b2 updated per sample, O(1) per update) rather than in a separate Python process, both because strategy/ must not be Python per the task spec and because the incremental OLS is computationally trivial (cheaper than the existing rolling-mean/z-score logic already in C++)\n- Decided to keep own-book microprice as a cold-start fallback for the regression-based estimate, mirroring the existing rolling-mean \u2192 EX_META ref_price fallback pattern already in the quoter\n- Measured how long it takes to get enough samples for a statistically significant Engle-Granger p-value: captured ~816s (~13.6 min) of live session data, resampled to a 500ms cadence, yielding 1632 samples \u2014 this was the point p-values first became reliably significant (consistent with the earlier finding that small/underpowered samples gave misleadingly insignificant results); concluded the 500ms-spaced sampling cadence (not raw tick data, which is highly autocorrelated and would inflate sample count without adding independent information) is what makes the p-value trustworthy, so decided to sample into the regression's rolling buffer at a fixed ~500ms cadence rather than feeding every raw BBO tick, and to treat ~13-14 minutes as the expected cold-start duration before trusting the regression, falling back to own-book microprice until then\n- Plan to generalize driver detection beyond the known AAH6 case: regress instruments against each other to find which instrument (Y) reliably explains multiple others (X1, X2...); flagged that contemporaneous-only regression can't distinguish a true driver from a fellow piggybacker (since two piggybackers of the same driver will also correlate with each other), so lead-lag structure (checking whether Y_{t-1} predicts X_t about as well as Y_t does) may be needed to confirm direction if generalizing beyond the AAH6-known-driver case\n- Root cause for AAH6 losses identified as being run over by the mover repeatedly: loss-triggered recalibration was making this worse, not better, because recalibrating after a bad fill resets fair value toward the price the mover just imposed, then requoting there puts the quoter right back in the mover's path \u2014 decided this needs a dedicated walk-detection/defense mechanism rather than adjusting the recalibration loss threshold\n- Decided on a mover walk-detector for AAH6 based on consecutive same-side adverse fills in a short window (e.g. 2+ fills on the same side within one requote cycle) as the primary signal, since it directly mirrors the confirmed mechanism (mover eats resting depth on one side via rapid marketable orders); response on trigger is to cancel/pull the resting order on that side and pause repricing on that side for a cooldown period, rather than immediately recalibrating and requoting into the same path; considered book-imbalance-via-microprice-divergence and rate-of-BBO-change as secondary/refinement signals if time allows\n- Decided on a clean separation of responsibilities: the quoter only defends (pulls/pauses quotes when it detects it's being run over), and actual position flattening stays entirely the hedger's job \u2014 the quoter will not self-flatten by crossing the spread\n- Found and read the actual background quoter bot source for AAM6/AAU6: it computes `center = round(fair_value(AAH6) + rel)` each time fair_value(AAH6) changes, then requotes symmetrically around center (bid at center-offset-i, ask at center+offset+i per level) \u2014 rel is a fixed constant chosen once per contract at bot startup and never changes during the session\n- Decided to abandon the regression/cointegration approach for AAM6/AAU6 pricing in favor of directly recovering rel, since it's an exact deterministic constant (not a statistical relationship): rel = mid(AAM6_BBO) - fair_value(AAH6), observable almost immediately (a short robust sample, e.g. median over a small window, rather than the ~14min cointegration cold-start) rather than needing sustained data collection; plan to verify this against already-captured BBO CSV data before implementing\n- Settled offset-detection method for identifying driver vs piggyback instruments and recovering AAM6/AAU6 fair value: piggyback instruments should reliably regress onto the true driver instrument (used to ID which instrument is the driver when the number/identity of instruments in play isn't known in advance); once driver is identified, recover the background quoter bot's center per requote by taking (max_bid + min_ask)/2 across its innermost order levels immediately after detecting a requote burst \u2014 this cancels the bot's offset out algebraically regardless of its value, since orders sit symmetrically at center\u00b1offset\u00b1i; then rel = fair_value(driver) - center, and the quoter quotes a tick or two inside rel\u00b1offset to sit tighter than the background bots\n- Known risks/caveats on the offset-detection method, explicitly accepted: (1) requires being first to sample right after a requote burst \u2014 asymmetric fills on one side (e.g. from the mover hitting one side only) before sampling will bias the center estimate, though symmetric fills still cancel correctly; (2) works fine even if the market data feed is anonymized/lacks sender attribution, since it only needs aggregate BBO read right after a detected requote-burst event, not per-order attribution \u2014 but requires PROTOCOL.md to confirm individual order messages (A/C/E/T) arrive in a way that lets a requote burst be detected as a discrete event, not just a fully pre-aggregated BBO snapshot; (3) the whole approach assumes background quoters use this same fixed-rel deterministic quoting logic in the actual grading market, which is unverified and could be wrong, with no fast statistical fallback available if it is wrong (statistical/cointegration-based estimation takes too long, ~14min cold start, to be a reliable backup)\n- Decided to gate trust in the rel estimate on its own stability: track variance/spread of recovered rel estimates over time \u2014 tight/stable readings mean the deterministic-quoting assumption holds and the quoter trusts rel and quotes tight; noisy/drifting readings signal the assumption is broken, triggering fallback to the existing own-book microprice/rolling-mean approach (accepting worse edge) rather than trusting a wrong deterministic assumption\n- Current status: microprice (own-book) implemented and tested; rel-based direct pricing for AAM6/AAU6 (settled design above, replacing the earlier regression plan) and the AAH6 walk-detector are both designed but not yet implemented; hedger has a design (per-instrument independent A driver and every\n//           piggyback that tracks it will all show high pairwise R^2\n//           against EACH OTHER, not just against the driver -- so R^2\n//           alone can only find the cluster, never which member is the\n//           driver.\n//        c. Within a cluster, the member whose trade flow is dominated by\n//           one sender (a \"mover\" shape) is the driver; everyone else in\n//           the cluster is a piggyback of it. This is a structural signal\n//           (who trades what), not a statistical one, and it's what\n//           actually breaks the symmetry OLS can't.\n//   3. Once a piggyback's driver is known, watch its own best bid/ask for a\n//      \"requote burst\" (both sides move together -- the live signature of\n//      the background bot repricing). Sample rel = driverFairValue -\n//      (bid+ask)/2 from that snapshot. Trust the recovered rel once enough\n//      samples exist and their spread is tight.\n//   4. IMPORTANT contamination guard: never trust a sample, and never quote\n//      against, a level currently owned by the cluster's identified mover.\n//      The mover has been observed to occasionally rest real two-sided\n//      orders directly on piggybacks (not just sweep the driver) -- if you\n//      sample rel while the mover, not the LP, is sitting at the top of\n//      book, you recover garbage that looks statistically clean. This is\n//      tracked live from add/cancel messages, not inferred after the fact.\n//   5. Once trusted, publish {driver, rel} for that piggyback to a\n//      \"DESK_STATE\" JetStream KV bucket, so the (separate, Python) hedger\n//      process can independently reconstruct desk-wide driver-equivalent\n//      exposure without any direct coupling to this process.\n//\n// DISCOVERY-GATE note: rather than one global \"everything about the market\n// is now known\" flag, each piggyback goes live independently the moment\n// ITS OWN driver+rel is confirmed AND its book is currently clean of the\n// mover. This is a deliberate, pragmatic choice: with unknown N, waiting\n// for a global \"fully discovered\" signal that may never fire (there could\n// always be one more cluster you haven't seen enough trades for yet) isn't\n// implementable. The practical effect is still that nothing trades until\n// SOMETHING is confirmed -- there is no order-placement code path anywhere\n// in this file that doesn't first check relTrusted -- but it is not a\n// literal single global gate across the whole instrument universe.                 "text": "Good catch bringing this up before building more on top of it, because I don't think the language switch actually fixes what's making it inconsistent, and there's a real redundancy in the plan as you've described it.\n\n**The architectural point first:** your hedger design already independently subscribes to `ex.md.<FEED>.*` for all instruments. So \"use the quoter to pass market info to the hedger\" is routing data through a process that already has it. What you actually want is simpler: keep the hedger's existing direct market data subscription, move the discovery logic (steps 2-4 in your comment block) into the hedger, have the hedger publish `{driver, rel}` to DESK_STATE, and have the quoter subscribe to DESK_STATE instead of writing to it. That's a straight role-swap on the KV, not a new data pipe through the quoter. Adding the quoter as a relay just adds a hop and a reason for staleness, for zero benefit since the hedger doesn't need it.\n\n**The bigger issue: rewriting in Python doesn't fix noisy discovery, it just makes the noisy discovery easier to write.** \"Bit shit and inconsistent, works well when it works\" points at specific failure modes in the algorithm itself, not the language:\n\n- **Union-find contamination.** One noisy pairwise R\u00b2 above your floor merges two real clusters permanently for that discovery pass. With thin piggyback books (which you already found in your EDA), spurious high-R\u00b2 pairs across unrelated clusters aren't rare, they're expected. This alone could cause the \"some runs it's great, some runs it bleeds\" pattern, since it's a single bad edge away from misclassifying an entire cluster.\n- **Early trust on the mover-dominance signal.** With low trade counts early on, \"dominated by one sender\" is noisy. A cluster can form, a false driver can get picked by chance, and once `relTrusted` flips true you're confidently quoting off garbage. Your discovery-gate note already flags this class of risk but the mover-dominance check itself has no minimum-sample floor mentioned.\n- **Periodic re-clustering causes discontinuities.** Re-running discovery every few seconds means a piggyback's driver assignment can flip mid-session. Every flip means a rel reset and a burst of requoting on a brand new anchor, exactly when you're least sure it's right.\n\nNone of these get better by moving to `numpy`/`scipy`/`statsmodels`. What Python buys you is easier access to *better estimators* than what you likely have now: hierarchical clustering with a real distance metric instead of threshold-and-union-find (avoids the transitivity problem), a minimum-sample gate before trusting the dominance signal, robust (median/MAD-based) rel trust checks instead of naive tight-spread, and reuse of your existing Johansen/cointegration code from the EDA phase for cluster validation instead of raw pairwise R\u00b2.\n\nSo: keep the plan to move discovery to the Python hedger, drop the quoter-as-relay step, and before you write any of it, decide which of those three failure modes is actually causing your PnL bleed. be Python per the task spec and because the incremental OLS is computationally trivial (cheaper than the existing rolling-mean/z-score logic already in C++)\n- Decided to keep own-book microprice as a samples for a statistically significant Engle-Granger p-value: captured ~816s (~13.6 min) of live session data, resampled to a 500ms cadence, yielding 1632 samples \u2014 this was the point p-values first became reliably significant (consistent with the earlier finding that small/underpowered samples gave misleadingly insignificant results); concluded the 500ms-spaced sampling cadence (not raw tick data, which is highly autocorrelated and would inflate sample count without adding independent information) is what makes the p-value trustworthy, so decided to sample into the regression's rolling buffer at a fixed ~500ms cadence rather than feeding every raw BBO tick, and to treat ~13-14 minutes as the expected cold-start duration before trusting the regression, falling back to own-book microprice until then\n- Plan to generalize driver detection beyond the known AAH6 case: regress instruments against each other to find which instrument (Y) reliably explains multiple others (X1, X2...); flagged that contemporaneous-only regression can't distinguish a true driver from a fellow piggybacker (since two piggybackers of the same driver will also correlate with each other), so lead-lag structure (checking whether Y_{t-1} predicts X_t about as well as Y_t does) may be needed to confirm direction if generalizing beyond the AAH6-known-driver case\n- Root cause for AAH6 losses identified as being run over by the mover repeatedly: loss-triggered recalibration was making this worse, not better, because recalibrating after a bad fill resets fair value toward the price the mover just imposed, then requoting there puts the quoter right back in the mover's path \u2014 decided this needs a dedicated walk-detection/defense mechanism rather than adjusting the recalibration loss threshold\n- Decided on a mover walk-detector for AAH6 based on consecutive same-side adverse fills in a short window (e.g. 2+ fills on the same side within one requote cycle) as the primary signal, since it directly mirrors the confirmed mechanism (mover eats resting depth on one side via rapid marketable orders); response on trigger is to cancel/pull the resting order on that side and pause repricing on that side for a cooldown period, rather than immediately recalibrating and requoting into the same path; considered book-imbalance-via-microprice-divergence and rate-of-BBO-change as secondary/refinement signals if time allows\n- Decided on a clean separation of responsibilities: the quoter only defends (pulls/pauses quotes when it detects it's being run over), and actual position flattening stays entirely the hedger's job \u2014 the quoter will not self-flatten by crossing the spread\n- Found and read the actual background quoter bot source for AAM6/AAU6: it computes `center = round(fair_value(AAH6) + rel)` each time fair_value(AAH6) changes, then requotes symmetrically around center (bid at center-offset-i, ask at center+offset+i per level) \u2014 rel is a fixed constant chosen once per contract at bot startup and never changes during the session\n- Decided to abandon the regression/cointegration approach for AAM6/AAU6 pricing in favor of directly recovering rel, since it's an exact deterministic constant (not a statistical relationship): rel = mid(AAM6_BBO) - fair_value(AAH6), observable almost immediately (a short robust sample, e.g. median over a small window, rather than the ~14min cointegration cold-start) rather than needing sustained data collection; plan to verify this against already-captured BBO CSV data before implementing\n- Settled offset-detection method for identifying driver vs piggyback instruments and recovering AAM6/AAU6 fair value: piggyback instruments should reliably regress onto the true driver instrument (used to ID which instrument is the driver when the number/identity of instruments in play isn't known in advance); once driver is identified, recover the background quoter bot's center per requote by taking (max_bid + min_ask)/2 across its innermost order levels immediately after detecting a requote burst \u2014 this cancels the bot's offset out algebraically regardless of its value, since orders sit symmetrically at center\u00b1offset\u00b1i; then rel = fair_value(driver) - center, and the quoter quotes a tick or two inside rel\u00b1offset to sit tighter than the background bots\n- Known risks/caveats on the offset-detection method, explicitly accepted: (1) requires being first to sample right after a requote burst \u2014 asymmetric fills on one side (e.g. from the mover hitting one side only) before sampling will bias the center estimate, though symmetric fills still cancel correctly; (2) works fine even if the market data feed is anonymized/lacks sender attribution, since it only needs aggregate BBO read right after a detected requote-burst event, not per-order attribution \u2014 but requires PROTOCOL.md to confirm individual order messages (A/C/E/T) arrive in a way that lets a requote burst be detected as a discrete event, not just a fully pre-aggregated BBO snapshot; (3) the whole approach assumes background quoters use this same fixed-rel deterministic quoting logic in the actual grading market, which is unverified and could be wrong, with no fast statistical fallback available if it is wrong (statistical/cointegration-based estimation takes too long, ~14min cold start, to be a reliable backup)\n- Decided to gate trust in the rel estimate on its own stability: track variance/spread of recovered rel estimates over time \u2014 tight/stable readings mean the deterministic-quoting assumption holds and the quoter trusts rel and quotes tight; noisy/drifting readings signal the assumption is broken, triggering fallback to the existing own-book microprice/rolling-mean approach (accepting worse edge) rather than trusting a wrong deterministic assumption\n- Current status: microprice (own-book) implemented and tested; rel-based direct pricing for AAM6/AAU6 (settled design above, replacing the earlier regression plan) and the AAH6 walk-detector are both designed but not yet implemented; hedger has a design (per-instrument independent flattening, patient/passive triggering informed by mean-reversion half-lives) but no code written yet\n- Update: generalized the strategy design to assume N mover bots, M liquidity-provider bots, and K casual-trader bots in the grading market, rather than hardcoding the sample sim's specific bot roster \u2014 explicit key assumption being made is that grading-sim bot *behavior* (mechanisms) will match the sample sim's, even if counts/params differ\n- Update: decided to stop trading the front-month (AAH6) directly, since it was the main source of loss; now using AAH6 purely as a latent signal (via the deterministic rel/offset formula) to price and trade the back-end contracts (AAM6/AAU6) instead\n- Update: designed a new hedger in Python (separate process, runs in the live phase) with a more aggressive design than the earlier per-instrument/patient plan: independently subscribes to ex.md.<FEED>.* for all instruments and reconstructs desk-wide (quoter+taker+hedger) position per instrument from the raw fill stream, keyed by known desk sender tags; watches a DESK_STATE KV for pairing/offsets and converts piggyback positions into driver-equivalent terms, netting into one combined exposure number; small dead-band around zero to avoid churning on tiny residuals; urgency scales continuously with |net exposure|/driver position_limit \u2014 passive near zero, progressively more aggressive/marketable as exposure grows; reacts on every fill rather than on a timer; deliberately drops the earlier mean-reversion-based patience logic in favor of pure magnitude-driven risk control (rationale: small position held a long time = low risk, large position even briefly held = high risk)\n- Current status update: all three seats (quoter, hedger, taker) now have designs reflecting the above changes; still may revise the quoter and/or hedger design depending on results from the new quoter's trial run, and may separately revise the hedger design depending on what role the taker ends up playing\n- Design decision: rather than defensively pulling the quoter's resting order when a piggyback's background-quoter (LP) reprice/walk is detected, considering leading it instead \u2014 since rel is known and driver fair value is tracked live, aiming to compute the LP's next center ahead of/as fast as the LP itself and cross into its stale resting orders (become the sweeper instead of the swept), contingent on confirming whether the LP recomputes its center continuously per driver tick or on a periodic/triggered basis\n- Confirmed priority: ship the hedger first (currently only a design, not yet built) before further work on the quoter's LP-walk response, since unbounded inventory (no hedger running) was identified as the actual cause of the PnL loss in the logic in the actual grading market, which is unverified and could be wrong, with no fast statistical fallback available if it is wrong (statistical/cointegration-based estimation takes too long, mean the deterministic-quoting assumption holds and the quoter trusts rel and quotes tight; noisy/drifting readings signal the assumption is broken, triggering fallback to the existing own-book microprice/rolling-mean approach (accepting worse edge) rather than trusting a wrong deterministic assumption\n- Current status: microprice (own-book) implemented and tested; rel-based direct pricing for AAM6/AAU6 (settled design above, replacing the earlier regression plan) and the AAH6 walk-detector are both designed but not yet implemented; hedger has a design (per-instrument independent flattening, patient/passive triggering informed by mean-reversion half-lives) but no code written yet\n- Update: generalized the strategy design to assume N mover bots, M liquidity-provider bots, and more aggressive design than the earlier per-instrument/patient plan: independently subscribes to ex.md.<FEED>.* for all instruments and reconstructs desk-wide (quoter+taker+hedger) position per combined exposure number; small dead-band around zero to avoid churning on tiny residuals; urgency scales continuously with |net exposure|/driver position_limit \u2014 passive near zero, progressively more aggressive/marketable as exposure grows; reacts on every fill rather than on a timer; deliberately drops the earlier mean-reversion-based patience logic in favor of pure magnitude-driven risk control (rationale: small position held a long time = low risk, large position even briefly held = high risk)\n- Current status update: all three seats (quoter, hedger, taker) now have designs reflecting the above changes; still may revise the quoter and/or hedger design depending on results from the new quoter's trial run, and may separately revise the hedger design depending on what role The way to ground it: you have $100k margin and you've already seen a real worst-case gap size (the 137-point AAM6 jump that cost you -3300 on a ~730 lot position). Work backward: pick a max tolerable loss as a fraction of margin (say a number you're comfortable defending, 10-20%), divide by the worst observed gap size times contract multiplier, and that's your hard position cap per instrument. That turns \"low\" from a vibe into a number you chose for a stated reason, which is exactly what a grader is going to want to see you do given the instrument scope was deliberately left unspecified.\n\n**2. The urgency-scaling design you already have is the right shape, but it needs that cap to calibrate against.** Continuous scaling with |net exposure|/limit only works once `limit` is a real number, not a placeholder. That part of the design doesn't change.\n\n**3. \"Avoid the influence of the mover\" while hedging is a distinct problem from getting caught by it, and worth being precise about which one you mean.** I'd read it as: don't cross the spread into a piggyback's book at the exact moment it's mid-reprice or freshly gapped from a burst, because you'll either pay a distorted price or hit a thin/stale side. That argues for the hedger reusing the same burst-detection signal the quoter uses (or, once you settle the timer-vs-threshold question from before, actively timing hedges to just after a burst resolves rather than blindly IOC-ing mid-event). This is a case where the quoter's market-microstructure awareness and the hedger's risk logic actually need to share information, not just position numbers.\n\n**4. One decision you haven't stated yet and need to: does the hedger ever hedge by trading AAH6 directly, or does it only trade the piggybacks?** Driver-equivalent exposure is most precisely and cheaply flattened by trading the driver itself. But you deliberately pulled the quoter off AAH6 because resting there gets swept. A hedger crossing the spread with marketable orders isn't exposed the same way a resting quote is (it takes liquidity instantly, it doesn't sit in the mover's path), so trading AAH6 defensively via the hedger might be fine even though quoting it passively wasn't. If you avoid AAH6 entirely and only hedge through the piggybacks, you're hedging through thinner books with the `rel` uncertainty baked in, which is slower and less precise. This is a real fork, not a detail, pick one and say why in NOTES.md.\n\n**5. \"Hedger needs to talk to the quoter\" is currently vague enough to build wrong. What's the actual coordination problem?** Concretely: if the hedger crosses the spread to sell down an AAM6 long, and the quoter's resting bid on AAM6 is still sitting there, the quoter may just buy it straight back. You'd pay the spread twice and net exposure barely moves. The fix isn't a chat channel, it's the hedger publishing its current urgency/action state to DESK_STATE (which you already planned as the shared KV), and the quoter reading that state to suppress or skew its own quote on the side the hedger is actively flattening. That's a specific, buildable mechanism. Same question applies to the taker: is it silently contributing to net exposure with no signal back to it at all (in which case the hedger just has to absorb whatever noise it adds), or do you want the taker to actually throttle when the desk is near its cap? Given taker is legacy code you own but haven't modified, I'd default to treating it as read-only noise the hedger accounts for, and only touch it if you find it's actively working against the hedger rather than just adding harmless randomness. Going through it in order, most of it matches what we already validated, but there are three places I'd push back before writing any code, because they're predictable failure points given what we've already found in your own logs.\n\n**1. Discovery (leading-variable regression + trade concentration) \u2014 matches, but don't rebuild it without the fix from last turn.** Your reasoning here is sound and matches the existing code exactly. But we already found the bug in this exact step: a cluster can lock in a driver call before all its real members have joined (AAM6/AAU6 correlating with each other and getting mistakenly resolved before AAH6 joins the cluster). If you rebuild discovery from this description without carrying that fix over, you'll likely reproduce the \"kept re-discovering, couldn't settle\" symptom again. Make sure the cluster-membership debounce is in the rebuild, not just the dominance debounce.\n\n**2. Offset reliability \u2014 \"aggregate of at least 3 repricing runs\" needs to say what happens when one of those 3 is bad.** Your plan drops two things the current code has: the contamination guard (skip a sample if the mover currently owns the level you'd sample from) and the tightness check (only trust the aggregate once its spread is tight, not just once you have enough of them). Without those, one contaminated or noisy sample out of 3 pollutes your entire average, and 3 is a small enough window that a single bad sample dominates the mean. I'd keep both: filter out mover-contaminated snapshots before they enter the aggregate, and require the samples you do keep to be tight before trusting the mean, not just numerous. This is the exact mechanism that got AAU6 to `relTrusted` correctly and is worth not throwing away just because you're rewriting the surrounding code.\n\n**3. Repost trigger \u2014 \"watch mover trades on the driver\" is narrower than it needs to be, and that narrowness can bite you.** The thing that actually determines whether your price is stale is whether `fv(driver)` changed, full stop, not specifically whether the mover caused it. If any other participant trades on the driver and moves its BBO, or if the book depth shifts the microprice without a trade at all, your quotes go stale under your rule but you wouldn't reprice, because you're filtering for \"mover trades\" specifically. The simpler and more correct trigger: reprice the piggyback on *any* market data event for its driver, not conditionally on the sender. You're already subscribed to the driver's feed for other reasons, this is strictly less code and strictly more correct.\n\n**4. Quote tightness \u2014 this is the one I'd flag hardest.** Tracking the LP's all-time minimum observed spread and ratcheting to just inside it is a real risk given something we already know: the mover sometimes rests directly on piggybacks at prices that don't reflect the LP's normal quoting behavior at all. If the mover's resting order happens to produce an unusually tight spread reading even once, your floor permanently locks onto that artifact, since a running minimum only ever shrinks, and you'd be stuck quoting inside a spread that was never actually the LP's real behavior. A minimum is an extreme-value statistic, one bad data point breaks it forever. I'd use something robust instead: a rolling percentile of recent spreads (say the 10th percentile of the last N clean observations, same contamination filter as the offset), or keep the current EMA approach and just bias it tighter. Either gives you competitiveness without a single outlier locking you in permanently.\n\n**On the rampant-positioning test itself:** to actually isolate \"the hedger is the only remaining problem,\" keep sizing at flat minimum-volume for this run, don't also let size scale with anything yet. If you change sizing at the same time you're testing whether the hedger alone fixes things, you won't be able to tell whether position growth came from fill frequency (what you're trying to isolate) or from bigger clips (a second, separate variable). Flat size now, scale it later once the hedger's confirmed working.\n\nTwo things I need an answer on before building: do you want the contamination guard and tightness check kept in the offset aggregation as described above, or genuinely simplified to just \"mean of 3+\"? Those are different filters applied to different data, they're not interchangeable, and using the discovery-phase history for offset recovery would silently readmit contaminated samples you already agreed to exclude. On top of that, `bestPriceOwnedBy` only reflects current live-order ownership, there's no historical record of who owned what at a past timestamp, so retroactively mining old samples for validity isn't even mechanically possible with the current state you're keeping. If you wait for a \"mass cancel then mass add\" event before starting to collect this, you'll needlessly delay cluster/driver discovery, which doesn't need that pattern at all.\n- **Burst-triggered rel/offset samples** \u2014 this is what step 7 actually needs, and it's the one that legitimately waits for the cancel-then-add pattern, because that pattern *is* the LP recentering, which is the only moment `c` is a fresh, meaningful reading.\n\nSo rewrite step 3 as two parallel things starting at the same time, not one gated thing: raw market data collection for discovery begins immediately at connection, and separately, burst-detection for offset recovery begins watching from the same moment but won't produce a usable sample until it actually sees a burst.\n\n**Step 7 has a real bug in it: \"the samples should still be valid for recovery\" is not true, and reusing them reintroduces the exact problem we just fixed.** The continuous discovery-phase samples (midHistory) are raw, unfiltered fair-value ticks, taken with zero regard for whether the mover was resting on the book at that instant. The offset samples need to specifically exclude moments the mover owned the level, per the contamination guard you just re-derived yourself two turns ago in point 2. Those are different filters applied to different data, they're not interchangeable, and using the discovery-phase history for offset recovery would silently readmit contaminated samples you already agreed to exclude. On top of that, `bestPriceOwnedBy` only reflects current live-order ownership, there's no historical record of who owned what at a past timestamp, so retroactively mining old samples for validity isn't even mechanically possible with the current state you're keeping. Simplify instead of trying to reuse anything: once driver+cluster lock, start rel sample collection fresh, live, forward from that point. Given bursts showed up roughly every ~2ms in the log we looked at earlier when the market was active, you'll hit your minimum sample count in seconds, there's no real cost to not reusing old data.\n\n**Print checkpoints, updated for the corrected sequence:**\n1. `CONNECTED` (strategy, hedger \u2014 two lines)\n2. `DISCOVERY: absorbing market data` (heartbeat, once, at start)\n3. `CLUSTER LOCKED: {members}` (new, needs the membership-debounce from before)\n4. `DRIVER LOCKED: {feed}, mover={sender}` (distinguish from the old `DRIVER_IDENTIFIED`, since locking is now a separate, later confirmation step per your point 1 earlier)\n5.                             "file_text": "# Quoter Build Spec (strategy/ seat)\n\n## 0. Core assumptions (explicit, stated up front)\n- The grading market's participant *behaviors* (movers, LPs, takers) mirror the sample sim's mechanisms, even if instrument count/underlyings differ. Nothing about symbol names, sender names, or instrument counts is hardcoded anywhere.\n- LPs quote piggyback instruments symmetrically around `c = fv(driver) + offset`, where `offset` is a fixed constant set once at LP startup.\n- Takers act randomly and are not modeled.\n- The driver instrument is never quoted by us. Its fair value is set by an adversarial random process (the mover) we don't try to predict.\n- No self-flattening in the quoter. Position resulting from providing liquidity is normal and expected; keeping desk-wide position low is the (separate, Python) hedger's job.\n- For this build/test cycle specifically: sizing stays flat at `meta.min_volume` for every quote, no scaling with position or headroom yet. This is deliberate \u2014 the hedger does not exist yet, and unmanaged position growth is being used as a **control variable** to confirm the hedger is the only remaining gap. Don't conflate this test by also varying size.\n\n## 1. Process roles\n- `strategy/` (this file, C++): discovers driver/piggyback structure, recovers offsets, quotes piggybacks, publishes `{driver, rel}` to DESK_STATE.\n- `hedger` (separate Python process, not part of this spec): reads DESK_STATE + raw fills, manages combined desk position. Out of scope here.\n- `taker` (legacy Python, untouched): random noise generator, treated as read-only in this system.\n\n## 2. Discovery pipeline\n\n### 2.1 Data collection (starts immediately, unconditional)\nFrom the moment market data subscriptions are live, for every instrument:\n- Append `(timestamp, fair_value)` to a rolling history buffer.\n- Increment per-sender trade counts from execution messages.\n\nThis does **not** wait for any burst pattern or any other gating condition. It is the raw substrate discovery runs on.\n\n### 2.2 Clustering (periodic pass, e.g. every ~2s)\nFor every pair of instruments with enough overlapping history:\n- Search a small lag grid in both directions, take the best-fit `(direction, lag, R\u00b2)` via correlation.\n- Pair is \"related\" if `R\u00b2 >= floor`.\n- Union-find related pairs into clusters. Note: a driver and every piggyback tracking it will show high pairwise R\u00b2 against **each other**, not just against the driver \u2014 R\u00b2 alone only finds cluster membership, never which member is the driver.\n\n### 2.3 Cluster lock (debounced on membership stability, not completeness)\n**This is a correction to the original design and must not be skipped:** a cluster's member set must be **stable across several consecutive discovery passes** before anything downstream is allowed to run. Do not lock a cluster just because it currently has \u22652 members \u2014 with unknown N, \"all members present\" can never be verified, only \"membership hasn't changed in a while.\"\n\nReasoning: two piggybacks of the same driver will correlate with each other and can form a 2-member cluster before the actual driver has accumulated enough history to join. If a driver call is allowed to lock in against an incomplete cluster, it can permanently mislabel a piggyback as a driver. This must be prevented at the cluster level, not just the dominance level.\n\nPrint: `CLUSTER LOCKED: {members}`\n\n### 2.4 Driver identification (once, per locked cluster)\nWithin a locked cluster: the member whose trade flow is dominated by one sender (fraction \u2265 dominance floor) is the driver \u2014 a structural signal (who trades what), not a statistical one. Require several consecutive passes of dominance above floor before locking this in (debounce against small-sample flukes), same spirit as the cluster lock above.\n\nIf more than one member looks driver-shaped, or zero do: do not guess. Log and wait for more data.\n\nOnce locked: **no further changes.** Freeze cluster membership and driver assignment permanently. Simpler than a reopenable state machine, and an accepted, explicit scope cut \u2014 document it as such.\n\nPrint: `DRIVER LOCKED: {feed}, mover={sender}`\n\n## 3. Offset (rel) recovery \u2014 per piggyback, fully independent\n\nOnce a cluster + driver are locked, **each piggyback in that cluster runs its own independent recovery loop.** One piggyback finishing (or stalling) must have zero effect on any other piggyback's progress. This must not become a single global \"cluster is ready\" gate \u2014 that was a real bug we hit (one piggyback silently blocked while its sibling traded fine).\n\n### 3.1 Burst detection (the sampling trigger)\nWatch the piggyback's own book for a \"requote burst\" \u2014 the live signature of the LP repricing: a batch of cancellations immediately followed by a batch of additions (both sides of the book move together). This is the moment `c` is a fresh, meaningful reading. Do **not** reuse raw discovery-phase history (\u00a72.1) for this \u2014 that data was never filtered for mover contamination and there's no way to retroactively determine who owned a book level at a past timestamp. Start sample collection fresh, live, once the driver+cluster lock, forward only.\n\n### 3.2 Contamination guard (keep this, it's load-bearing)\nBefore taking a sample: if the mover currently owns the best bid or best ask on this piggyback, **skip the sample entirely.** The mover has been observed resting real two-sided orders directly on piggybacks, not just sweeping the driver \u2014 sampling `c` while the mover, not the LP, sits at top of book produces a statistically-clean-looking but wrong offset.\n\n### 3.3 Escape hatch (new requirement \u2014 prevents permanent stalls)\nThe contamination guard above has no timeout in the original design, and that's a real bug: if the mover camps on a level indefinitely (never gets crossed by taker flow), the guard blocks forever and that piggyback never accumulates a single sample. Fix: track how long the current owner has held that price level. Past a threshold with no change, either (a) sample from the next book level in instead of top-of-book, or (b) allow the sample through anyway, since an order that's been stable that long isn't behaving like an active contamination event anymore.\n\n### 3.4 Aggregation and trust\n- Require a minimum of 3 clean (non-contaminated) samples before considering trust at all.\n- Trust is **not** just a sample count. Compute the mean and require the spread (std dev, in driver ticks) of recent samples to be tight before trusting the mean. A small sample count with no tightness check lets one noisy sample dominate the aggregate \u2014 keep the tightness gate.\n- Once trusted: publish `{driver, rel}` to DESK_STATE KV for this piggyback. Go live for **this piggyback only.**\n\nPrint: `REL SAMPLE #n = <value>` (while still building trust) \u2192 `REL TRUSTED: driver=X rel=Y sdTicks=Z` \u2192 `LIVE \u2014 quoting {piggyback}`\n\n## 4. Ongoing driver fair-value tracking (separate from \u00a73, easy to conflate)\n\nThis was the root cause of getting picked off historically: requoting was on a fixed timer, unrelated to when the driver's price actually moved, so quotes went stale and sat in the LP's path.\n\nFix: **continuously recompute `fv(driver)` on every market data event for the driver instrument** (not gated to \"mover trades\" specifically \u2014 any trade or book change on the driver can move its fair value, and tying the trigger to sender identity misses non-mover-caused moves). Whenever the newly computed `fv(driver)` differs from the previously used value, immediately reprice and repost quotes for every **live** piggyback tied to that driver.\n\nThis is distinct from \u00a73's burst detection: \u00a73 is about recovering the offset in the first place; this section is about staying priced correctly against a known-good offset, on an ongoing basis, for as long as the piggyback is live.\n\nPrint (new, requested): `DRIVER FV UPDATED: {driver} old={x} new={y} -> repricing {list of dependent piggybacks}`\n\n## 5. Note: a driver and every piggyback tracking it will show high pairwise R\\u00b2 against **each other**, not just against the driver \\u2014 R\\u00b2 alone only finds cluster membership, never which member is the driver.\\n\\n### 2.3 Cluster lock (debounced on membership stability, not completeness)\\n**This is a correction to the original design and must not be skipped:** a cluster's member set must be **stable across several consecutive discovery passes** before anything downstream is allowed to run. Do not lock a cluster just because it currently has \\u22652 members \\u2014 with unknown N, \\\"all members present\\\" can never be verified, only \\\"membership hasn't changed in a while.\\\"\\n\\nReasoning: two piggybacks of the same driver will correlate with each other and can form a 2-member cluster before the actual driver has accumulated enough history to join. If a driver call is allowed to lock in against an incomplete cluster, it can permanently mislabel a piggyback as a driver. This must be prevented at the cluster level, not just the dominance level.\\n\\nPrint: `CLUSTER LOCKED: {members}`\\n\\n### 2.4 Driver identification (once, per locked cluster)\\nWithin a locked cluster: the member whose trade flow is dominated by one sender (fraction \\u2265 dominance floor) is the driver \\u2014 a structural signal (who trades what), not a statistical one. Fix: track how long the current owner has held that price level. Past a threshold with no change, either (a) sample from the next book level in instead of top-of-book, or (b) allow the sample through anyway, since an order that's been stable that long isn't behaving like an active contamination event anymore.\\n\\n### 3.4 Aggregation and trust\\n- Require a minimum of 3 clean (non-contaminated) samples before considering trust at all.\\n- Trust is **not** just a sample count. Compute the mean and require the spread (std dev, in driver ticks) of recent samples to be tight before trusting the mean. A small sample count with no tightness check lets one noisy sample dominate the aggregate \\u2014 keep the tightness gate.\\n- Once trusted: publish `{driver, rel}` to DESK_STATE KV for this piggyback.
