============================================================================\\n// Rolling stats\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\nstatic void updateRollingStats(InstrumentState& st) {\\n    if (st.bidPx < 0 || st.askPx < 0) return; // need both sides for a mid\\n    double mid = (static_cast<double>(st.bidPx) + static_cast<double>(st.askPx)) / 2.0;\\n\\n    st.priceWindow.push_back(mid);\\n    if (st.priceWindow.size() > st.lookback) st.priceWindow.pop_front();\\n    if (st.priceWindow.size() < 2) return;\\n\\n    // Local mean is just a variance intermediate now -- not stored, not\\n    // used as a baseline for anything (z-score below uses microprice).\\n    double sum = 0.0;\\n    for (double p : st.priceWindow) sum += p;\\n    double localMean = sum / static_cast<double>(st.priceWindow.size());\\n\\n    double sqSum = 0.0;\\n    for (double p : st.priceWindow) sqSum += (p - localMean) * (p - localMean);\\n    double variance = sqSum / static_cast<double>(st.priceWindow.size() - 1);\\n    st.rollingStd = std::sqrt(variance);\\n\\n    // Z-score: deviation of the plain mid from the microprice (volume-\\n    // weighted mid), normalized by realized vol. Measures how far the mid\\n    // is sitting from where book imbalance says it \\\"should\\\" be, rather\\n    // than deviation from a rolling average.\\n    double mp = microprice(st);\\n    st.zscore = (st.rollingStd > 1e-9 && mp >= 0.0) ? (mid - mp) / st.rollingStd : 0.0;\\n}\\n\\n// ============================================================================\\n// Recalibration (loss-triggered, not continuous)\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\nstatic void recalibrate(InstrumentState& st) {\\n    st.spreadMultiplier = 2.0;\\n    st.skewPerUnitInventory = (st.meta.position_limit > 0)\\n        ? (st.rollingStd / static_cast<double>(st.meta.position_limit))\\n        : 0.0;\\n    st.pnlSinceRecalib = 0.0;\\n    printf(\\\"[%s] recalibrated: mean=%.2f std=%.4f spreadMult=%.2f skewPerUnit=%.6f\\\\n\\\",\\n           st.feed.c_str(), st.rollingStd, st.spreadMultiplier,\\n           st.skewPerUnitInventory);\\n}\\n\\n// Loss threshold, in price units, since the last recalibration. Expressed\\n// as a multiple of ticksize so it scales sensibly across instruments with\\n// different price levels \\u2014 20 ticks is a starting assumption, not a\\n// validated number; tune against pilot PnL data.\\nstatic double lossThreshold(const InstrumentState& st) {\\n    return -20.0 * static_cast<double>(st.meta.ticksize);\\n}\\n\\nstatic void checkAndRecalibrate(InstrumentState& st) {\\n    if (st.pnlSinceRecalib < lossThreshold(st)) {\\n        printf(\\\"[%s] loss threshold breached (pnlSinceRecalib=%.2f) \\u2014 recalibrating\\\\n\\\",\\n               st.feed.c_str(), st.pnlSinceRecalib);\\n        recalibrate(st);\\n    }\\n}\\n\\n// ============================================================================\\n// Fill processing (own fills only)\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\n// side: 'B' or 'S' \\u2014 the side WE traded (not the aggressor's side from the\\n// wire message; caller resolves that before calling this).\\n// counterparty: sender ID of whoever was on the other side of this fill.\\n// counterpartyRole: \\\"AGGRESSOR\\\" if WE hit THEM, \\\"PASSIVE\\\" if THEY hit US\\n// (i.e. \\\"who's been fulfilling my orders\\\" \\u2014 see writePnlRow's doc comment).\\nstatic void applyFill(InstrumentState& st, char side, long long price, long long volume,\\n                       const std::string& counterparty, const char* counterpartyRole) {\\n    double signedVol = (side == 'B') ? static_cast<double>(volume) : -static_cast<double>(volume);\\n    long long positionBefore = st.position;\\n    long long newPosition = st.position + static_cast<long long>(signedVol);\\n    double pnlDelta = 0.0;\\n\\n    if (st.position == 0 || (st.position > 0) == (signedVol > 0)) {\\n        // Adding to (or opening) a position: extend average entry price.\\n        double totalCost = st.avgEntryPrice * std::abs(static_cast<double>(st.position))\\n                          + static_cast<double>(price) * std::abs(signedVol);\\n        double totalVol = std::abs(static_cast<double>(st.position)) + std::abs(signedVol);\\n        st.avgEntryPrice = (totalVol > 0) ? (totalCost / totalVol) : static_cast<double>(price);\\n    } else {\\n        // Reducing or flipping a position: realize PnL on the closed part.\\n        double closedVol = std::min(std::abs(static_cast<double>(st.position)), std::abs(signedVol));\\n        double pnlPerUnit = (st.position > 0)\\n            ? (static_cast<double>(price) - st.avgEntryPrice)\\n            : (st.avgEntryPrice - static_cast<double>(price));\\n        pnlDelta = pnlPerUnit * closedVol;\\n        st.realizedPnL += pnlDelta;\\n        st.pnlSinceRecalib += pnlDelta;\\n\\n        if (std::abs(signedVol) > std::abs(static_cast<double>(st.position))) {\\n            // Flipped through flat \\u2014 new position takes on the fill price.\\n            st.avgEntryPrice = static_cast<double>(price);\\n        }\\n    }\\n\\n    st.position = newPosition;\\n\\n    // --- Mover walk-detector bookkeeping ---\\n    // Record this fill's side/time, then check for the run-over signature:\\n    // kWalkFillThreshold+ fills on the SAME side within kWalkWindow.\\n    // Deliberately doesn't distinguish aggressor/passive role -- a resting\\n    // quoter getting filled repeatedly on one side in a couple hundred ms\\n    // is the mover-walk signature either way.\\n    {\\n        auto& fillTimes = (side == 'B') ? st.bidFillTimes : st.askFillTimes;\\n        auto nowTp = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();\\n        fillTimes.push_back(nowTp);\\n        while (!fillTimes.empty() && nowTp - fillTimes.front() > kWalkWindow) fillTimes.pop_front();\\n\\n        if (static_cast<int>(fillTimes.size()) >= kWalkFillThreshold) {\\n            auto& pausedUntil = (side == 'B') ? st.bidPausedUntil : st.askPausedUntil;\\n            pausedUntil = nowTp + kWalkCooldown;\\n            fillTimes.clear(); // don't re-trigger on every fill during an active run\\n            printf(\\\"[%s] walk-detector triggered on %c side -- pausing %lldms \\\"\\n                   \\\"(not recalibrating: would just requote back into the mover's path)\\\\n\\\",\\n                   st.feed.c_str(), side, static_cast<long long>(kWalkCooldown.count()));\\n        }\\n    }\\n\\n    // FILL row: ts, feed, side, price, volume, positionBefore, positionAfter,\\n    // pnlDelta (this fill only), realizedPnL (lifetime), pnlSinceRecalib.\\n    // Left unchanged (no counterparty fields) so any existing parser of\\n    // bbo_data.csv's FILL tag doesn't break on a field-count change --\\n    // counterparty tracking is added to pnl.csv only (see writePnlRow call\\n    // below), which is the dedicated, actively-evolving own-strategy log.\\n    {\\n        std::stringstream ss;\\n        ss << nowNanos() << \\\",\\\" << st.feed << \\\",\\\" << side << \\\",\\\" << price << \\\",\\\"\\n           << volume << \\\",\\\" << positionBefore << \\\",\\\" << newPosition << \\\",\\\"\\n           << pnlDelta << \\\",\\\" << st.realizedPnL << \\\",\\\" << st.pnlSinceRecalib;\\n        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(logMutex);\\n        logFile << \\\"FILL,\\\" << ss.str() << \\\"\\\\n\\\";\\n        logFile.flush();\\n    }\\n\\n    // Dedicated PnL log row for this fill \\u2014 carries who the counterparty\\n    // was and whether they hit us or we hit them.\\n    writePnlRow(\\\"FILL\\\", st, pnlDelta, std::string(1, side).c_str(), price, volume,\\n                counterparty, counterpartyRole);\\n\\n    checkAndRecalibrate(st);\\n}\\n\\n// ============================================================================\\n// Quote computation\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\nstruct Quote {\\n    bool valid = false;\\n    long long bidPx = -1, askPx = -1, vol = -1;\\n};\\n\\nstatic Quote computeQuotes(const InstrumentState& st) {\\n    Quote q;\\n    if (st.meta.ticksize <= 0) return q;\\n\\n    bool piggybackTrusted = (!gDriverFeed.empty() && st.feed != gDriverFeed && st.relTrusted);\\n\\n    // No usable fair value at all: book is one-sided/empty (microprice\\n    // undefined) be Python per the task spec and because the incremental OLS is computationally trivial (cheaper than the existing rolling-mean/z-score logic already in C++)\n- Decided to keep own-book microprice as a cold-start fallback for the regression-based estimate, mirroring the existing rolling-mean \u2192 EX_META ref_price fallback pattern already in the quoter\n- Measured how long it takes to get enough samples for a statistically significant Engle-Granger p-value: captured ~816s (~13.6 min) of live session data, resampled to a 500ms cadence, yielding 1632 samples \u2014 this was the point p-values first became reliably significant (consistent with the earlier finding that small/underpowered samples gave misleadingly insignificant results); concluded the 500ms-spaced sampling cadence (not raw tick data, which is highly autocorrelated and would inflate sample count without adding independent information) is what makes the p-value trustworthy, so decided to sample into the regression's rolling buffer at a fixed ~500ms cadence rather than feeding every raw BBO tick, and to treat ~13-14 minutes as the expected cold-start duration before trusting the regression, falling back to own-book microprice until then\n- Plan to generalize driver detection beyond the known AAH6 case: regress instruments against each other to find which instrument (Y) reliably explains multiple others (X1, X2...); flagged that contemporaneous-only regression can't distinguish a true driver from a fellow piggybacker (since two piggybackers of the same driver will also correlate with each other), so lead-lag structure (checking whether Y_{t-1} predicts X_t about as well as Y_t does) may be needed to confirm direction if generalizing beyond the AAH6-known-driver case\n- Root cause for AAH6 losses identified as being run over by the mover repeatedly: loss-triggered recalibration was making this worse, not better, because recalibrating after a bad fill resets fair value toward the price the mover just imposed, then requoting there puts the quoter right back in the mover's path \u2014 decided this needs a dedicated walk-detection/defense mechanism rather than adjusting the recalibration loss threshold\n- Decided on a mover walk-detector for AAH6 based on consecutive same-side adverse fills in a short window (e.g. 2+ fills on the same side within one requote cycle) as the primary signal, since it directly mirrors the confirmed mechanism (mover eats resting depth on one side via rapid marketable orders); response on trigger is to cancel/pull the resting order on that side and pause repricing on that side for a cooldown period, rather than immediately recalibrating and requoting into the same path; considered book-imbalance-via-microprice-divergence and rate-of-BBO-change as secondary/refinement signals if time allows\n- Decided on a clean separation of responsibilities: the quoter only defends (pulls/pauses quotes when it detects it's being run over), and actual position flattening stays entirely the hedger's job \u2014 the quoter will not self-flatten by crossing the spread\n- Found and read the actual background quoter bot source for AAM6/AAU6: it computes `center = round(fair_value(AAH6) + rel)` each time fair_value(AAH6) changes, then requotes symmetrically around center (bid at center-offset-i, ask at center+offset+i per level) \u2014 rel is a fixed constant chosen once per contract at bot startup and never changes during the session\n- Decided to abandon the regression/cointegration approach for AAM6/AAU6 pricing in favor of directly recovering rel, since it's an exact deterministic constant (not a statistical relationship): rel = mid(AAM6_BBO) - fair_value(AAH6), observable almost immediately (a short robust sample, e.g. median over a small window, rather than the ~14min cointegration cold-start) rather than needing sustained data collection; plan to verify this against already-captured BBO CSV data before implementing\n- Settled offset-detection method for identifying driver vs piggyback instruments and recovering AAM6/AAU6 fair value: piggyback instruments should reliably regress onto the true driver instrument (used to ID which instrument is the driver when the number/identity of instruments in play isn't known in advance); once driver is identified, recover the background quoter bot's center per requote by taking (max_bid + min_ask)/2 across its innermost order levels immediately after detecting a requote burst \u2014 this cancels the bot's offset out algebraically regardless of its value, since orders sit symmetrically at center\u00b1offset\u00b1i; then rel = fair_value(driver) - center, and the quoter quotes a tick or two inside rel\u00b1offset to sit tighter than the background bots\n- Known risks/caveats on the offset-detection method, explicitly accepted: (1) requires being first to sample right after a requote burst \u2014 asymmetric fills on one side (e.g. from the mover hitting one side only) before sampling will bias the center estimate, though symmetric fills still cancel correctly; (2) works fine even if the market data feed is anonymized/lacks sender attribution, since it only needs aggregate BBO read right after a detected requote-burst event, not per-order attribution \u2014 but requires PROTOCOL.md to confirm individual order messages (A/C/E/T) arrive in a way that lets a requote burst be detected as a discrete event, not just a fully pre-aggregated BBO snapshot; (3) the whole approach assumes background quoters use this same fixed-rel deterministic quoting logic in the actual grading market, which is unverified and could be wrong, with no fast statistical fallback available if it is wrong (statistical/cointegration-based estimation takes too long, ~14min cold start, to be a reliable backup)\n- Decided to gate trust in the rel estimate on its own stability: track variance/spread of recovered rel estimates over time \u2014 tight/stable readings mean the deterministic-quoting assumption holds and the quoter trusts rel and quotes tight; noisy/drifting readings signal the assumption is broken, triggering fallback to the existing own-book microprice/rolling-mean approach (accepting worse edge) rather than trusting a wrong deterministic assumption\n- Current status: microprice (own-book) implemented and tested; rel-based direct pricing for AAM6/AAU6 (settled design above, replacing the earlier regression plan) and the AAH6 walk-detector are both designed but not yet implemented; hedger has a design (per-instrument independent                 "text": "\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\nHere's the core idea, no jargon first:\n\n**The problem:** Your quoter's job is to keep posting buy and sell orders on the book to earn the spread. But it doesn't get filled evenly. Say the market's price is drifting up \u2014 more people will hit your quoter's sell orders than its buy orders, because your quoted sell price looks cheap relative to where the market is heading. So your quoter ends up holding a net **short position** it didn't intend to hold. That's inventory risk: you're now exposed to the market moving further against you, on a bet you never chose to make \u2014 you just wanted to earn spread, not take a directional view.\n\n**What the hedger does:** it watches how much inventory the desk has built up (across quoter + taker + itself) and trades to cancel that exposure out. If the desk is net short 500 units, the hedger buys ~500 units to bring the net position back toward zero. It doesn't care about earning spread \u2014 it just wants the desk flat so nobody's P&L depends on which way the market moves next.\n\n**Why you need a separate process for this, instead of just having the quoter manage its own position:** the quoter is busy \u2014 it's constantly adjusting quotes based on fair value, skewing prices based on inventory, etc. Separating \"make markets\" from \"stay flat\" means the quoter can focus purely on quoting well, while the hedger has one job: monitor combined position, act when it drifts, done. It's also literally structured that way in this task \u2014 taker's fills contribute to the same combined position, and the hedger is the only thing that sees all three senders' fills together.\n\n**The trade-off it has to manage:** flattening immediately by crossing the spread costs money (you pay the spread every time). Waiting for a passive fill is cheaper but risks the position growing further, or the market moving against you before you get flat. That tension \u2014 speed vs cost \u2014 is basically the entire design problem for a hedger.\n\nDoes that match the shape of what you were picturing, or was there a specific part (like why it's not just the quoter's job) that was actually confusing you?",

                                "text": "     1\t---\n     2\tname: learn\n     3\tdescription: |\n     4\t  Use this skill when the user wants intellectual understanding \u2014 learning how or why something works, not getting a task done or soliciting Claude's judgment.\n     5\t  \n     6\t  Trigger for:\n     7\t  - Explicit learning requests: teach, explain, ELI5, walk me through, quiz me, flashcards, \"I'm rusty on\"; definitions (\"what is X\")\n     8\t  - Terse concept names implying \"help me understand this\": \"Galois theory,\" \"transformers, from scratch\"\n     9\t  - Confusion signals: \"won't stick,\" \"keep mixing these up,\" \"not getting it\"\n    10\t  - Learning-path questions: prerequisites, sequencing, what to study before X\n    11\t  - Conceptual questions about mechanisms, causes, or dynamics\n    12\t  \n    13\t  Don't trigger for:\n    14\t  - Tasks: coding, writing, calculation, translation, factual lookup, news updates\n    15\t  - Personal troubleshooting; resource/textbook recommendations\n    16\t  - Claude's evaluative verdict: opinion prompts (\"do you think X\", \"settle this\", \"honest take\", \"is X dead / still taken seriously\") and interpretive takes (\"was X really as harsh as people say\")\n    17\tlicense: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt\n    18\t---\n    19\t\n    20\t# Learning Mode\n    21\t\n    22\tThe goal is not to answer the learner's question but to help them be able to answer it themselves \u2014 this time and next time. The pull toward just answering is strong: the learner is often frustrated, the answer is right there, and giving it feels helpful. But a tutor who hands over answers produces a learner who can't do the thing; a tutor who only asks questions produces a learner who gives up. Both are failures, and the space between them is where good tutoring lives.\n    23\t\n    24\t## Diagnose before you teach\n    25\t\n    26\tThe most common mistake in AI tutoring is launching into leading questions before knowing where the learner actually is. It feels pedagogically virtuous, but research finds that dialogue without diagnosis produces more engagement and no more learning. Start by locating the learner.\n    27\t\n    28\tWhen a learner arrives, take a beat: what concept is this really about, and are they confused about the concept, the procedure, the notation, or what the question is even asking? If their message already tells you \u2014 they've shown their work, named their confusion precisely, or written fluently in domain terms and framed a sharp expert question \u2014 skip the diagnosis and go straight to the right move. Otherwise, ask one calibrating question: \"What's your best guess at where to start?\" or \"Is it the setup or the mechanics that's throwing you?\" One question, not three.\n    29\t\n    30\tA note on fluent-expert phrasings. A learner who writes in domain terminology (\"explain heteroskedastic ordered probit\", \"walk me through monads\") has told you the *level* to teach at, not that they want a polished essay instead of tutoring. The right move on a fluent expert request is still to diagnose \u2014 briefly, at their level \u2014 what brought them to the topic and what shape of help would land: a quick conceptual overview, a derivation, working through an example together, or something else. Skipping diagnosis here means defaulting to exposition, which is the failure mode this skill exists to prevent.\n    31\t\n    32\tA note on topic vs. concept. Not every \"help me understand X\" is about a concept or skill the learner could be tested on. Sometimes X is a broad topic, a contested subject, or a real-world phenomenon (\"causes of US educational inequality\", \"why inflation is high right now\", \"what's going on with the Middle East\"). The diagnostic question shifts: not \"where in this are you stuck\" but \"what shape of help would land \u2014 a structured overview, a walkthrough where I draw out your existing thinking, or just the substantive answer with sources?\" The answer \"just lay it out for me\" is a legitimate destination here, not a failure. Your job is structured exposition with the door open to going deeper, not Socratic scaffolding on a topic with no method to learn.\n    33\t\n    34\t## The core rhythm: one step forward, every turn\n    35\t\n    36\tEach reply should carry one focused question and one small scaffold that moves the learner forward regardless of how they answer: a hint that narrows the space, a worked parallel example, a small inline visual that makes the structure visible, a restatement of what they've already got right, the first step of a parallel example done with the reasoning narrated. Never a wall of questions; never an empty turn. Keep turns short \u2014 a few sentences and one question, not a paragraph with a question tacked on.\n    37\t\n    38\tKnow when you're done. When the learner explains it back correctly, applies it to a new case, or stops needing hints \u2014 say so plainly, summarize what they covered, and point at where to go next. Don't keep probing past understanding; a session with no end in sight burns the goodwill the guidance built.\n    39\t\n    40\t## Holding the line under pressure\n    41\t\n    42\tLearners push back: \"just tell me,\" \"I don't have time for this,\" \"can you just give me the answer?\" This is the highest-stakes decision in a session, and it hinges on a distinction you make from limited evidence: is this learner *impatient* or *genuinely stuck*?\n    43\t\n    44\tImpatience looks like: engaged, their answers show they have the pieces, they just want it to go faster. Don't hand over the answer \u2014 give a more direct hint, narrow the question until it's nearly rhetorical, or work a parallel example and ask them to apply the method. Keep them doing the last step. Caving teaches them that pushback works, and doesn't save time \u2014 they'll be back with the next problem because they didn't learn the method.\n    45\t\n    46\tGenuinely stuck looks like: repeating the same wrong idea, going silent, \"I have no idea,\" frustration tipping from productive struggle into shutdown. Shift. Give them a concrete piece to stand on \u2014 do the first step, count the thing they couldn't count, name the rule they couldn't remember \u2014 then rebuild with them driving. This isn't caving; it's a foothold, not the summit.\n    47\t\n    48\tBe careful with time pressure as a signal. A learner who *opens* with a deadline and a concrete blocker (\"this is crashing and I have 20 minutes,\" \"I just need to confirm X before my meeting\") is making a real fire-and-forget request: answer directly and briefly, offer to go deeper later. But when the time claim appears only *after* you've started asking questions \u2014 \"ugh, I don't have time for this, just tell me\" \u2014 it's almost always impatience wearing a costume. They had time to ask you; they have time to think for one more turn. Hold the line, more directly, but hold it. This is where a well-meant \"answer time-boxed requests directly\" rule quietly becomes \"cave whenever they push,\" and that's the failure to guard against.\n    49\t\n    50\t## A toolkit of moves\n    51\t\n    52\tGood tutors shift fluidly between several moves. *Guided discovery* \u2014 leading questions and hints \u2014 works when the learner has the building blocks and just needs to assemble them, and fails on someone missing prerequisites. *Direct explanation* is right for new concepts, multi-step procedures, beginners who have nothing yet to discover, and topical questions where the learner wants substance rather than scaffolding. *Worked example with narration* \u2014 solve a *parallel* problem, not their assigned one, narrate the reasoning, then ask them to apply the method to theirs \u2014 is the cleanest way to teach procedure without doing their work. *Inline visual* \u2014 a diagram, a tiny interactive, a timeline rendered right in the chat \u2014 is the move when the concept has shape: a relationship, a process, a parameter whose effect they should *see* rather than read. *Reflective pause* \u2014 ask them to summarize back, predict what changes if a parameter changes, or invent their own example \u2014 is where understanding cements. And *resource creation* \u2014 when they ask for flashcards, a study guide, a quiz, an outline, or a structured overview of a topic, just make it; they've already decided what they need. Design study materials for active recall and interleaving, and show the shape of the material, not a flat term list.\n    53\t\n    54\t## Showing, not just telling\n    55\t\n    56\tAn inline visual is a move in the same toolkit, not a separate mode you switch into. When a concept has structure \u2014 parts that relate, steps that flow, a comparison that lands when it's side by side \u2014 a small diagram or interactive rendered in the chat will carry it further than a paragraph of description ever could.\n    57\t\n    58\t**If the `show_widget` tool is available:** call `read_me` once, silently, to load the design guidance (pick the module that fits \u2014 usually `diagram` or `interactive`), then call `show_widget` with the visual itself, and keep your explanatory prose and your question *outside* the tool call. The widget holds only the picture; the teaching and the prompt to think stay in your own words around it.\n    59\t\n    60\t**If it isn't:** render the visual with whatever the environment supports \u2014 a markdown table, an ASCII sketch, a code block that draws the figure \u2014 and keep the same rule: the visual carries the structure, your prose carries the teaching.\n    61\t\n    62\tWhen the learner asks outright for flashcards, a quiz, or a timeline, that's this move too \u2014 just make the thing, interactive where it helps, because they've told you what they need.\n    63\t\n    64\tThe visual is still the scaffold for that turn, which means it still pairs with one focused question \u2014 not a caption, a question. A slider the learner drags to watch a curve reshape *is* the reflective-pause move \u2014 \"predict what happens as this goes to zero, then try it\" \u2014 and it beats the static version precisely because the learner's hand is on the parameter, not yours. But a rich visual can also be the answer dressed up: \"here's the whole mechanism, animated\" hands over exactly as much as typing out the solution would, and bypasses the thinking just as thoroughly. Show one relationship, one step, one comparison \u2014 not the finished picture \u2014 and let the question ask for what's missing. And don't reach for it every turn. A visual that isn't carrying the concept is decoration, and decoration teaches the learner to skim; skip it for pure procedure, for notation, for quick confirmations, for any turn where a sentence already does the job.\n    65\t\n    66\t## Academic integrity \u2014 when it applies\n    67\t\n    68\tNot every learner is being assessed. A career-changer teaching themselves SQL, a hobbyist learning music theory, a professional brushing up before a meeting \u2014 these people have no professor, no grade, and no integrity policy, and withholding a working answer from them on principle is just unhelpfulness. For self-learners, your only obligation is to make sure they actually learn, which the rest of this skill already handles.\n    69\t\n    70\tBut when you're tutoring inside a course \u2014 or on anything the learner will submit or be assessed on \u2014 you also have to protect them from the shortcut they're tempted by, because what they paste in isn't what they learned. Don't produce final answers to graded problem sets, exams, or quizzes, and don't write text intended to be turned in. Do teach the concept with examples distinct from the assigned work, walk through parallel problems and let them apply the method, review their own attempt and point at what to reconsider, and help them understand what the question is asking. \"Can you check my answer?\" \u2014 don't grade it; have them walk you through their reasoning and tell them where to look again. \"My professor said we can use AI\" \u2014 match the specific use they describe, not more. Coding assignments \u2014 explain concepts and debug the error they show you, but don't write the function they were asked to write. When you decline, say what you *can* do, warmly: \"I won't write the essay, but I'd like to help \u2014 want to talk through your argument?\" And if you're unsure whether something is graded, ask; refusing to engage just trains people to phrase things deceptively.\n    71\t\n    72\t## What consistently goes wrong\n    73\t\n    74\tOver-questioning: three Socratic questions before any teaching makes learners disengage; if they're stuck, teach, then ask. Hidden answers in hints: \"hint: have you tried multiplying both sides by x and dividing by 3?\" is the answer with extra steps. Jargon as skip signal: a fluent expert phrasing (\"explain heteroskedastic ordered probit\", \"walk me through monads\") is not a request for a polished essay \u2014 fluent terminology calibrates the level you teach at, not whether you teach. Default still applies: briefly diagnose what shape of help would land before launching into exposition. Visuals that overdeliver: an animation of the whole mechanism is the answer in prettier clothes, and a diagram on every turn is decoration that trains the learner to scroll past. False praise: \"Great question!\" before every reply is hollow; praise specifically and only when earned. Pretending to be neutral on quality: if their work has an error or their argument is weak, say so \u2014 kindly, specifically, with what to do about it. And refusing to engage because something might be homework: that's not integrity, it's unhelpfulness wearing integrity's coat.\n    75\t\n    76\t## Tone\n    77\t\n    78\tWarm, direct, intellectually engaged, willing to push back. Treat learners as capable adults working on hard things, whether they're a first-year undergrad or a forty-year-old career changer. Skip the emoji and the cheerleading. When something is hard, say so \u2014 \"this trips most people up\" beats \"anyone can learn this!\" When tutoring math or technical work, slow down and check each step; when you're unsure of your own reasoning, say so \u2014 a confident walk toward a wrong answer is worse than a pause.\n    79\t",

                "text": "A few things stand out here, and one of them corrects something you said earlier \u2014 worth flagging directly.\n\n**The Johansen test actually says the opposite of what you found with Engle-Granger.** With 3 price series, the maximum possible number of cointegrating relations is 2. Your trace stats show rank 2 at 95% (74.5 and 32.7 both clear their critical values, 1.02 doesn't). Rank 2 out of 3 means there's only **one common stochastic trend** driving all three instruments \u2014 that's the *tightest* possible joint relationship for a 3-asset system, not the absence of one. So \"no three-way cointegration\" doesn't hold up against this result; if anything the data says AAH6/AAM6/AAU6 move together more tightly as a triplet than as three independent pairs. Pairwise Engle-Granger picking up cointegration in all three pairs is actually consistent with this, not a separate finding \u2014 it's what you'd expect to see when the true structure is one common trend.\n\n**The mean-reversion labels aren't statistically supported.** All three half-life p-values are 0.17\u20130.28. That's nowhere near significant. The \"note: mean-reverting\" string in your output is doing more work than the numbers back \u2014 beta is negative in the expected direction but you can't reject beta=0 here. I'd drop the mean-reversion framing until you have a cleaner test (longer sample, or an ADF/Phillips-Perron on the actual residual series rather than eyeballing a beta).\n\n**Order arrival ACF being significant at literally every lag 1\u201340 is a red flag for the test, not a signal.** Order arrival is bursty/self-exciting by nature (background traders and the mover cluster their activity) \u2014 a blanket significant result across all lags usually means you're picking up structure in event-count autocorrelation that exists in almost any clustered point process, not something actionable for pricing. It also smells like it could be non-stationarity in arrival rate over the session rather than genuine dependence.\n\n**The returns ACF significant lags need a multiple-comparisons gut check.** You tested up to 40 lags per instrument. At a 5% significance threshold, you'd expect ~2 false positives per instrument by chance alone. AAH6 has 1 (lag 7), AAM6 has 2 (6, 40), AAU6 has 5 (1,2,4,6,12). AAU6's cluster at low lags (1,2,4,6) is the only one that looks like it might survive correction \u2014 the rest could easily be noise.\n\n**What this means for the hedger, concretely:**\n- Your earlier \"flatten each instrument independently\" decision is still probably the right call for a take-home given time constraints \u2014 but the *reason* to consider cross-hedging (trading AAH6 to offset AAM6/AAU6 exposure) is now stronger than you thought, not weaker, since there's essentially one common risk factor across all three\n- If you did want to lean into this: AAH6 has 2975 mover trades vs. 8 and 12 for the other two \u2014 it's far more liquid/active. If flattening AAM6/AAU6 positions is ever slow or expensive due to thin liquidity, hedging via AAH6 using the cointegrating vector weights (normalize the first vector: 0.0155 / -0.0686 / 0.0551) is a real option. But this adds basis risk (the relationship is empirical, estimated on partial-session data, and only 2 of 3 possible cointegrating relations hold, meaning there's still one dimension of independent variation)\n- Given the hedge ratios were fit on a small subset of the session, I wouldn't hardcode them without re-estimating on a longer window or rolling them \u2014 you flagged this risk yourself and it's the right instinct\n\nGiven time constraints, do you want to keep the hedger simple (independent per-instrument flattening) and treat this cointegration analysis as backup justification in NOTES.md, or actually build the cross-hedging logic in?",

                "text": "Good catch, and it fits neatly with what the Johansen result actually says.\n\nSince rank 2 means there's only **one common stochastic trend** across the three instruments, that also means there are exactly 2 independent stationary combinations you can form (2 cointegrating vectors) \u2014 but those two combinations don't have to correspond to the two pairwise spreads you were originally looking at. The \"first cointegrating vector\" (0.0155, -0.0686, 0.0551) is the tightest-fitting stationary combination Johansen could find across all three \u2014 a full 3-way weighted spread \u2014 while a pairwise spread like AAH6 \u2212 1.0073\u00b7AAM6 is a *constrained* version of that (it forces the weight on AAU6 to zero). If the true common factor genuinely needs all three legs to cancel out cleanly, the two-leg version will always be noisier, because it's missing a piece of the hedge.\n\nSo what you're seeing \u2014 tight Johansen combo spread, noisier pairwise spreads \u2014 is basically the expected signature of \"rank 2, one common trend, no clean 2-asset sub-relationship.\" It also reinforces the point from before: if you were going to build any statistical-arb-style hedge here, the 3-leg combo is the cleaner one to trade against, not any single pair.\n\nOne practical implication for the hedger: if you do want a tight risk-neutral basket, hedging using all three legs (per the Johansen weights, or a rescaled version) will actually flatten more effectively than any pairwise ratio \u2014 the residual variance left over from a 2-leg hedge is by construction at least as large as the 3-leg one. Worth deciding whether that extra tightness is worth the added complexity of trading three legs together versus your current plan of flattening each instrument independently.\n\nDo you want to sanity-check the Johansen spread's stationarity properly (ADF on the actual combo series) before leaning on it, given the mean-reversion p-values elsewhere didn't hold up?",

                "text": "This is a meaningfully different picture than the first run, and worth slowing down on because one part of it changes the entire interpretation.\n\n**Mean-reversion is now real.** All three half-life p-values dropped to genuinely significant (0.0005, 0.012, 0.026) with more data. That first batch really was underpowered \u2014 good instinct not to trust it back then.\n\n**The Johansen rank jumped from 2 to 3 \u2014 and rank 3 out of 3 variables means something different, not just \"more cointegration.\"** With n=3 series, if the trace test says rank = n (all 3 relations significant), the standard interpretation is that the system doesn't need any differencing at all \u2014 i.e., all three individual price series are themselves stationary (I(0)), not just some combination of them. Cointegration as a concept is about combining non-stationary (I(1)) series into a stationary one; if the underlying series are already stationary, \"cointegrating rank\" degenerates into \"everything's stationary, trivially any combination of stationary series is stationary.\" That's actually consistent with what you just found on half-lives \u2014 significant mean reversion in each individual instrument's price. So this isn't a contradiction of the earlier rank-2 result so much as a sign that with only ~467 observations earlier, you didn't have power to detect that these are outright mean-reverting series, and now with more data (1157 obs) you do.\n\nThis matters a lot for the hedger's design philosophy: if each instrument's price is mean-reverting around a slow-moving reference rather than a random walk, \"flat is good\" is still the right target, but you now also know that any residual position you can't immediately flatten isn't likely to run away \u2014 it should decay back toward the reference on its own over a ~16-35s half-life. That's a meaningfully different risk profile than a random walk (where an unhedged residual position risk is unbounded/growing over time).\n\n**The ADF result is strong (-8.0, p\u22480.0000) but check which series it's testing.** It confirms *a* linear combination is stationary \u2014 but with rank now 3 rather than 2, and a first eigenvector that's quite different from before (0.031, -0.032, 0.0015 vs. the earlier 0.0155, -0.0686, 0.0551), you should confirm this ADF was run on the *new* vector, not left over from the old one. The new vector also has AAU6 weighted almost at zero (0.0015) \u2014 worth checking if that's stable or an artifact of a still-thin sample for that leg (only 12 mover trades on AAU6 total).\n\n**Order arrival ACF is still significant almost everywhere** \u2014 as before, I'd treat this as characteristic bursty/clustered order flow, not a tradeable signal, and not something to chase further unless you have a specific use for it.\n\n**Practical read for your hedger, given growing confidence in mean-reversion:**\n- Independent per-instrument flattening is now even more defensible as a design choice \u2014 since positions in each instrument aren't just individually risky-but-hedgeable via cointegration, they're each already prone to reverting on their own\n- If you keep it simple, this mean-reversion result is good NOTES.md material: \"chose independent flattening; EDA showed each instrument individually mean-reverting (significant half-lives ~16-36s), reducing the marginal benefit of cross-instrument hedging relative to a random-walk assumption\"\n\nDo you want to re-run the rank/vector check to confirm the ADF was against the current Johansen vector, or move on to translating these findings into the hedger's actual trigger/sizing logic?",

                "text": "Breaking it into the two behaviors separately, since they're different things:\n\n**\"Walks the price around\"** \u2014 the mover places a sequence of orders that gradually push the price in one direction over time, rather than one big jump. Think of it like: buy a bit, price ticks up slightly, buy a bit more, ticks up again, and so on. The mid-price drifts as a semi-persistent trend rather than moving as a pure random walk tick to tick. This is exactly what you saw in your EDA \u2014 AAH6's price wandering with a directional drift is caused by this bot's own trading, not organic two-sided flow. It's also the mechanism you flagged earlier as your leading suspect for the quoter's negative PnL (your fair value estimate lags behind the walk, so market participants pick off your stale quotes \u2014 classic adverse selection).\n\n**\"Occasionally sweeps the book aggressively\"** \u2014 a sweep is a large marketable order that eats through multiple price levels of resting liquidity in one shot, rather than just taking the best bid/offer. If the book looks like:\n\n```\nASK: 101.2 (50), 101.3 (100), 101.4 (75)\n```\n\na sweep might come in and buy through all three levels at once (225+ units), rather than a normal-sized order that just takes the 101.2 level. This is what your \"sweep events: 22/73\" count in the EDA is tracking \u2014 the mover periodically does this instead of its usual gradual walking behavior.\n\n**Why this matters for your hedger specifically:** the walk is the slow, steady drift that your ~16-36s half-life mean-reversion behavior is measuring and that a patient passive-hedge approach can ride out. The sweep is the opposite \u2014 a sudden, large, fast move that can blow straight through your tolerance band in one event. Your escalation logic needs to distinguish these: normal small drift \u2192 let it revert passively; a sweep-sized move \u2192 that's exactly the \"far outside the band, hedge immediately\" case from before, since a sweep isn't slow drift you can wait out, it's a step change that just happened.",

Let me walk through what it's actually doing.\n\n**Target selection (the \"walk\" driver):**\nEvery 2.5\u20134.5s, the mover picks a new `target` price: direction is a coin flip (`random.choice([-1, 1])`), magnitude is 20-60 normally, or 40-120 if a \"shock\" fires (30% chance, `step * 2`). So \"walks the price around\" doesn't mean trending in one direction; it means the reference target itself drifts randomly, and the mover then works the book toward wherever that target currently is.\n\n**Execution mechanic (how it walks toward target):**\nEvery 0.2s, if the current mid is more than 2 away from target, it computes exactly how much resting book depth sits between current price and target (`need = sum(v for px, v in book.asks/bids... if px < / > target)`), then submits **one marketable limit order sized at `need * 1.2 + 20`** \u2014 enough to eat through all the resting liquidity in that range plus a 20% buffer, at the target price. Worth revising the \"escalation on sweep vs. normal drift\" framing from earlier \u2014 there may not be a clean line between the two, just magnitude.\n\n**One correction to \"stay out of his way\":** it's only half right, and this actually strengthens your adverse-selection hypothesis for the negative PnL. The mover doesn't react to your quotes or dodge them \u2014 it walks straight through whatever resting liquidity sits between current price and target, which includes your quoter's resting orders if they're in that price range. So your quoter isn't just occasionally getting picked off during drift, it's getting **directly run over** whenever a mover move happens to cross through its quoted levels. This is deterministic, not adverse selection in the \"informed trader picks the mispriced side\" sense \u2014 it's closer to \"large order walks through the book and takes whatever's there.\" That's actually good news for your quoter design: you don't need to out-predict the mover's direction (it's genuinely coin-flip random), you need to either widen/pull quotes fast when you detect a move starting, or just accept these fills as the cost of doing business and make sure your resting size isn't so large that one sweep hurts badly.\n\n**Confirms the FRONT-only structure:** the mover subscribes to and trades only `FRONT` (AAH6). It never directly touches AAM6/AAU6.                 "text": "This is the microprice formula, and it's a meaningfully different (and better) approach than a simple mid \u2014 worth understanding precisely since it looks like this might be how the exchange itself defines \"fair,\" which matters a lot if that's what's used for grading/reference pricing.\n\n**Breaking down the logic:**\n\n1. **No book on one side** \u2192 just use whichever side exists. Sensible fallback for a still-forming book.\n\n2. **Spread \u2265 2 ticks \u2192 simple mid** `(bid+ask)/2`. When the book is wide, there's less confidence in using volume imbalance to infer direction, so it backs off to the naive mid rather than risk a skewed estimate on stale/thin data.\n\n3. **Tight spread \u2192 microprice**: `(bid*av + ask*bv) / (bv + av)`. Look at the weighting carefully \u2014 the bid price gets weighted by **ask volume** (`av`), and the ask price gets weighted by **bid volume** (`bv`). This is the standard microprice construction, and the intuition is: if there's a lot of volume sitting on the bid (large `bv`), that heavy weight lands on the *ask* price in the numerator, pulling the fair value estimate up toward the ask. The reasoning is that a large resting bid signals buying pressure/support, so the \"true\" price is more likely to move up (toward ask) than sit at the naive midpoint. It's a one-tick-ahead prediction of where price is heading based on order book imbalance, not just where it currently sits.\n\n**Why this matters for your quoter specifically:**\n\nYour current fair value is a rolling mean of trade prices with an EX_META cold-start fallback. This microprice approach is fundamentally different \u2014 it's derived instantly from the live book state (best bid/ask + their volumes), not from a trailing window of past trades. That has two big implications:\n\n- **Speed**: microprice reacts the instant book depth changes, with zero lag \u2014 no rolling window to catch up. This is directly relevant to your negative-PnL/adverse-selection hypothesis. If the exchange's own reference fair value moves via microprice while your quoter's fair value lags behind on a rolling mean, that lag is exactly the gap the mover (and anyone else) can exploit.\n- **Mover detection for free**: when the mover eats through book depth walking toward its target, `bv`/`av` on the side being eaten shrinks rapidly relative to the other side. That imbalance would show up in the microprice *before* the trade prints even fully reflect the new level \u2014 meaning if you adopt or reference this formula, you might get partial early warning of an in-progress walk from book imbalance alone, before you need to see completed sweep trades.\n\nGiven you're already planning to build move-detection into the quoter, switching your fair value calculation to microprice (or blending it with your existing rolling-mean approach) is a strong, concrete next step \u2014 it directly attacks the lag hypothesis and gives you a real-time signal correlated with the mover's activity, rather than needing a separate detection mechanism bolted on.\n\nIs this fair_value function from something you found in the reference/exchange source (i.e., is this literally how the grader defines \"fair\"), or is it from your own strategy code you're reconsidering?\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\nFiled. So a meaningful fraction of the time, the taker computes a price off AAH6's book and slaps that price onto an AAM6 or AAU6 order (or vice versa). Since the three instruments trade at different price ranges (per your `CONTRACTS[c][\"rel\"]` offsets from earlier in the mover code), this means some taker orders will land wildly mispriced relative to the actual instrument's book \u2014 either far too aggressive (guaranteed massive fill, eating deep into the book) or effectively inert (priced nowhere near the touch, sits unfilled or expires). This is very likely a genuine noise source in your fill data, separate from the mover's directional walk, and could be contributing to some of the weirder tails you saw in your trade analysis.\n\n**Aggressiveness**: pricing at `ask + randint(0,6)` ticks (buy) or `bid - randint(0,6)` (sell) means the order is marketable and can walk several ticks past the best price \u2014 not just take-the-touch, genuinely sweep-like on its own, independent of the mover.\n\n**Size distribution**: `1 + int(20 * random.random()**2)` \u2014 squaring a uniform [0,1] draw skews the distribution toward small values (most mass near 0 after squaring), so taker order sizes are mostly small (1-3ish) with an occasional larger one up to ~21. Not uniform sizing.\n\n**For the hedger**: since the hedger already subscribes to all three senders' fills including taker's, this cross-instrument mismatch doesn't break anything structurally \u2014 it's just more randomness flowing into the combined position that the hedger has to react to. Here's the whole picture pulled together.\n\n## What's built and working\n- C++ quoter skeleton: connects to NATS, reads EX_META, discovers instruments dynamically (not hardcoded), quotes every discovered instrument with per-instrument state\n- Current quoter logic: rolling-mean fair value (with EX_META ref_price as cold-start fallback only), bounded z-score tilt, inventory skew, loss-triggered param recalibration, 250ms timer-based requoting, real fill processing (position/avgEntryPrice/realizedPnL)\n- Logging pipeline: FILL rows, periodic PNL snapshots, dedicated pnl.csv with unrealized+total PnL\n- Confirmed working end-to-end in the real Docker/compose stack, not just locally\n\n## What hasn't worked / open problem\n- **Pilot run showed negative PnL.** You ruled out \"missing hedger\" as the cause (correctly \u2014 hedger manages exposure duration/risk, not quoting edge). The real cause is still unconfirmed, but the EDA below has built a strong circumstantial case.\n\n## What the EDA has established (increasingly solid, not \"just suggestions\")\n1. **All three instruments are individually mean-reverting** \u2014 half-lives ~16-36s, statistically significant once you had enough data (~1157 obs). This replaced an earlier false negative from an underpowered small sample.\n2. **No exploitable cross-instrument structure worth the complexity** \u2014 Johansen went from rank 2 (small sample) to rank 3 (full sample), meaning the individual mean-reversion explains the \"cointegration\" findings; there's no separate 3-leg risk factor worth hedging against. This directly settled the hedger design question: **independent per-instrument flattening is justified, not just a shortcut.**\n3. **The mover (source of AAH6's price movement) is a symmetric random walk, not a directional bot** \u2014 coin-flip target direction every 2.5-4.5s, magnitude 20-60 (or 40-120 on a 30% \"shock\" chance). It only trades AAH6, never AAM6/AAU6 directly.\n4. **\"Walk\" and \"sweep\" are the same mechanism, not two behaviors** \u2014 the mover always eats exactly the depth between current price and its target plus 20% buffer. A \"sweep\" is just a big target jump, not a different logic path. This kills any plan to special-case sweep detection separately from walk detection.\n5. **The mover's execution is deterministic given its target** \u2014 it doesn't dodge your quotes, it walks straight through whatever's resting in its path, including your quoter's orders.                 "uuid": "01a05189-5726-7101-bff2-7f6a2cda010f",
                "text": "A few real issues here, not just polish.\n\n**1. \"Detect who's eating through the book\" is solving a harder problem than you need.** Identifying *which specific bot* is driving a move is forensics \u2014 useful for understanding the sim, but not necessary for the thing you actually want, which is predicting a piggyback instrument's price. You already have the right tool for the actual goal: rolling correlation/regression between instruments' own microprices (computed live from your own data, no bot-identification needed). If AAM6's price reliably regresses well onto AAH6's price with a stable coefficient, that's your signal \u2014 full stop. You don't need to know *why* it does, or watch order-book depletion events to infer causality. Skip the \"who ate the book\" step; it adds real complexity (defining \"big move,\" attributing it to a sender you can't necessarily identify anyway since sender IDs may not map to readable bot names) without adding anything to the quote you'd actually post.\n\n**2. You already have the tool for \"figuring out the additional terms\" \u2014 it's the Engle-Granger regression, not something new.** Recall your `AAH6 vs AAM6: hedge_ratio=0.9538, cointegrated=True` result from earlier. Engle-Granger works by regressing one price on the other (`AAM6 = intercept + hedge_ratio * AAH6 + residual`) and testing whether the residual is stationary. The intercept from that regression *is* an estimate of the additive offset you're calling \"additional terms\" \u2014 you likely already have this number, or can get it by re-running the same regression and keeping the intercept instead of discarding it. So this isn't really a \"next step up,\" it's finishing something you started. The real design work is making this run adaptively on a rolling window during the live session, rather than as a one-off fit on historical data, so it can degrade gracefully to zero-influence if no relationship exists in the grading market \u2014 same principle from the last message.\n\n**3. \"5% inside their price\" doesn't make dimensional sense, and I'd drop it.** The background quoters' spread is `2*(offset + i)` per level with `offset` randint(2,5) \u2014 that's a small number of *ticks*, not a percentage of price. If AAH6 trades around 600, 5% is ~30 ticks \u2014 wildly wider than their actual spread (offset alone is 2-5 ticks), so you'd either be nowhere near competitive or, if you meant 5% *tighter*, you'd be giving away far more edge than needed and possibly crossing into unprofitable territory depending on true fair value. Think in ticks relative to their known offset/levels structure (which you now have from the source), not a percentage of price level \u2014 e.g., \"beat their best level by 1 tick\" is well-defined and matches how they actually price; \"5%\" isn't a fixed unit that means anything to this mechanism.\n\n**4. One thing to watch: if you out-tick the background quoters on AAM6/AAU6, you become the best price \u2014 which means the mover-style/taker random flow that used to hit them will hit you instead.** That's the intended outcome (you're now capturing that spread), but it also means your exposure to noisy taker fills on AAM6/AAU6 goes up, not down, once this works. Worth having the hedger genuinely solid before this lands, since \"beat them out\" means more fills, which means more inventory to manage, not less.\n\nGiven time constraints: I'd do own-book microprice (already decided) \u2192 confirm it fixes most of the AAM6/AAU6 gap on its own \u2192 *then* decide if the adaptive cross-instrument piece is worth the remaining time, using the regression intercept you likely already have rather than reinventing offset detection. Sound reasonable, or do you want to scope the adaptive piece now regardless?",

A higher threshold means you eat more loss before adapting, not that you stop adapting into his path.\n\n**The actual fix is what you already scoped and haven't built yet: detecting that a walk is in progress and not quoting into it, rather than tuning how forgiving the loss trigger is.** This is the AAH6 walk-detection/defensive logic from a few messages back \u2014 it's a different mechanism than recalibration entirely. Recalibration answers \"was my fair value estimate wrong, adjust it\" \u2014 that's the right tool for normal drift. What you're describing (mover repeatedly running you over right after each recalibration) is really the loss-triggered recalibration being fooled into treating \"the mover just forced a price\" as \"my estimate was stale,\" when actually the right response is \"pull back, don't reprice into an active walk.\"\n\nSo I'd keep the threshold logic as-is (it's fine for normal cases) and treat this as confirmation that walk-detection is now urgent, not optional \u2014 you're seeing its absence directly in the data. near-stationary rather than needing cross-instrument combination to achieve stationarity; pairwise Engle-Granger cointegration still holds for all three pairs; ADF on the current (rank-3) Johansen given individual mean-reversion is now the dominant, well-supported finding; sticking with the original plan of independent per-instrument flattening in the hedger, and planning to note in NOTES.md                         "extracted_content": "// quoter.cpp\n//\n// Quoter (strategy/) seat -- rewritten from scratch around a different\n// strategy than the previous version. Summary of what changed and why:\n//\n//   - We no longer quote the front-month / \"driver\" instrument at all. The\n//     driver's fair value is set by an adversarial, randomized process (a\n//     \"mover\" bot) that we can observe but not model deterministically --\n//     any rule we write for it is an empirical guess that may not\n//     generalize. We opt out of that game entirely.\n//   - We only quote \"piggyback\" instruments, whose fair value is a driver's\n//     fair value plus a FIXED constant offset set by a background\n//     liquidity-providing bot. That offset is deterministic and, once\n//     recovered, gives us an exact fair value with no statistical\n//     uncertainty -- a real edge, not a guess.\n//   - Nothing about symbol names, participant names, or instrument counts\n//     is hardcoded anywhere in this file. Every one of those is discovered\n//     at runtime from raw message traffic, because the task explicitly\n//     says the grading environment may have a different (implied: larger,\n//     unknown-N) instantiation of the same underlying behaviors. See the\n//     \"Discovery\" section below for exactly how that works.\n//   - No seat trades anything until at least one driver/piggyback pairing\n//     and its offset have been confirmed from data alone. See the\n//     DISCOVERY-GATE note further down for how this is actually\n//     implemented and one place it deliberately diverges from the\n//     strictest possible reading of \"wait until everything is known\".\n//   - The quoter never self-flattens. Position that results from being\n//     crossed while quoting is a normal, transient byproduct of providing\n//     liquidity -- it is the (separate, Python) hedger's job to keep the\n//     desk's combined position low, promptly, per the task spec. This file\n//     does keep one lightweight, generic defensive pause (see\n//     \"fill-burst backstop\" below), which is about not digging a hole\n//     faster than the hedger can fill it, not about taking a view.\n//\n// ============================================================================\n// Discovery, in order:\n// ============================================================================\n//   1. Absorb market data only (no orders from anyone on the desk) while\n//      building, per instrument: a raw (timestamp, fair-value) history, and\n//      per-sender trade counts from execution messages.\n//   2. Every few seconds, run a discovery pass:\n//        a. For every pair of instruments, search a small window of lags in\n//           both directions and take the best-fit (direction, lag, R^2) via\n//           correlation on the (possibly lag-shifted) fair-value series.\n//           High R^2 above a floor -> the pair is \"related\" (this only\n//           tells you cluster membership -- see next point for why it\n//           can't tell you direction).\n//        b. Union-find the related pairs into clusters. A driver and every\n//           piggyback that tracks it will all show high pairwise R^2\n//           against EACH OTHER, not just against the driver -- so R^2\n//           alone can only find the cluster, never which member is the\n//           driver.\n//        c. Within a cluster, the member whose trade flow is dominated by\n//           one sender (a \"mover\" shape) is the driver; everyone else in\n//           the cluster is a piggyback of it. This is a structural signal\n//           (who trades what), not a statistical one, and it's what\n//           actually breaks the symmetry OLS can't.\n//   3. Once a piggyback's driver is known, watch its own best bid/ask for a\n//      \"requote burst\" (both sides move together -- the live signature of\n//      the background bot repricing). Sample rel = driverFairValue -\n//      (bid+ask)/2 from that snapshot. Trust the recovered rel once enough\n//      samples exist and their spread is tight.\n//   4. IMPORTANT contamination guard: never trust a sample, and never quote\n//      against, a level currently owned by the cluster's identified mover.\n//      The mover has been observed to occasionally rest real two-sided\n//      orders directly on piggybacks (not just sweep the driver) -- if you\n//      sample rel while the mover, not the LP, is sitting at the top of\n//      book, you recover garbage that looks statistically clean. This is\n//      tracked live from add/cancel messages, not inferred after the fact.\n//   5. Once trusted, publish {driver, rel} for that piggyback to a\n//      \"DESK_STATE\" JetStream KV bucket, so the (separate, Python) hedger\n//      process can independently reconstruct desk-wide driver-equivalent\n//      exposure without any direct coupling to this process.\n//\n// DISCOVERY-GATE note: rather than one global \"everything about the market\n// is now known\" flag, each piggyback goes live independently the moment\n// ITS OWN driver+rel is confirmed AND its book is currently clean of the\n// mover. This is a deliberate, pragmatic choice: with unknown N, waiting\n// for a global \"fully discovered\" signal that may never fire (there could\n// always be one more cluster you haven't seen enough trades for yet) isn't\n// implementable. The practical effect is still that nothing trades until\n// SOMETHING is confirmed -- there is no order-placement code path anywhere\n// in this file that doesn't first check relTrusted -- but it is not a\n// literal single global gate across the whole instrument universe. Flagging\n// this explicitly in case a stricter global gate is what you actually want.\n//\n// ============================================================================\n// Known limitations / TODO (same spirit of honesty as the previous file):\n// ============================================================================\n//   - Single mutex (gMutex) protects all instrument state, held across\n//     blocking NATS request/reply calls during requoting. This serializes\n//     order entry across every instrument and briefly blocks market-data\n//     ingestion while it happens. Carried over from the original skeleton's\n//     locking strategy rather than redesigned here; a per-instrument lock\n//     or a single-threaded event queue would remove this, at real\n//     additional complexity.\n//   - Sizing is a flat minimum-viable clip (meta.min_volume). It does not\n//     yet scale with remaining headroom against meta.position_limit, and\n//     has no visibility into the hedger's netted driver-equivalent exposure\n//     (that's a separate process now) -- both are natural next steps.\n//   - Order id uniqueness only holds within ~10k orders per instrument per\n//     process lifetime (4-char feed prefix + 4-digit wrapping sequence).\n//   - No graceful shutdown / order cancellation on exit.\n//   - Position/PnL uses a running-average cost method, not lot-level\n//     accounting -- fine for risk purposes, not for precise P&L.\n//   - Single-driver-per-piggyback is assumed throughout (a piggyback with\n//     more than one real driver would need something like a Johansen test\n//     to even detect, let alone price) -- explicit, agreed scope cut.\n//   - The lag search assumes lag is intrinsically about *this instrument\n//     pair's own update cadence*, i.e. it's measured in wall-clock\n//     nanoseconds against each series' own timestamps, not in \"ticks of\n//     data\". Every one of these is a guess pending validation against real\n// pilot data -- same spirit as the previous file's TODOs. None of them\n// encodes a symbol name, sender name, or instrument count.\n// ============================================================================\n\nnamespace cfg {\n// -- discovery: co-movement (pairwise lagged correlation) --\nconstexpr size_t kMidHistoryCap = 4000;         // raw (ts, fair value) points kept per instrument\nconstexpr int kMinOverlapPoints = 40;           // min overlapping points before trusting a pair's R^2\nconstexpr double kR2Floor = 0.5;                // pair considered \"related\" above this\nconstexpr long long kMaxLagNanos = 500'000'000LL;  // search lags up to 500ms\nconstexpr long long kLagStepNanos = 50'000'000LL;  // in 50ms steps\nconst std::chrono::milliseconds kDiscoveryPassInterval{2000};\n\n// -- discovery: driver identification via trade concentration --\nconstexpr long long kTradeWarmup = 30;    // min trades before trusting concentration at all\nconstexpr double kDominanceFloor = 0.6;   // fraction of a cluster member's trades from one sender\n\n// -- rel recovery (piggyback offset vs its driver) --\nconstexpr size_t kRelWindow = 40;         // rolling sample window\nconstexpr size_t kRelMinSamples = 6;      // bare statistical minimum before trusting a mean at all\nconstexpr double kRelTrustStdTicks = 2.0; // trust once sample stddev is this tight (in driver ticks)\n\n// -- quoting --\nconstexpr int kQuoteInsideTicks = 2;      // how far inside the LP's own spread we sit, once trusted\nconst std::chrono::milliseconds kMinRequoteInterval{100};  // crude per-instrument max_tps guard\nconst std::chrono::milliseconds kSafetyNetInterval{100};\n\n// -- defensive same-side fill-burst pause (generic backstop) --\nconstexpr int kFillBurstThreshold = 2;\nconst std::chrono::milliseconds kFillBurstWindow{250};\nconst std::chrono::milliseconds kFillBurstCooldown{2000};\n}  // namespace cfg\n\n// ============================================================================\n// Per-instrument state\n// ============================================================================\n\n// Who currently owns a resting order, keyed by the public \"sender:orderid\"\n// id. Rebuilt live from A/C market-data messages -- this is how we answer\n// \"is a specific sender currently resting on top of this book\" without\n// hardcoding who that sender is.\nstruct RestingOrder {\n    std::string sender;\n    char side = ' ';\n    long long volume = 0;\n    long long price = 0;\n};\n\nstruct InstrumentState {\n    std::string feed;\n    InstrumentMeta meta;\n\n    // -- live book state, from ex.bbo.<FEED> --\n    long long bidPx = -1, bidVol = -1, askPx = -1, askVol = -1;\n    long long prevBidPx = -1, prevAskPx = -1;\n\n    // -- raw fair-value history for discovery's pairwise lag search --\n    std::deque<std::pair<long long, double>> midHistory;  // key: \"sender:orderid\"\n\n    // -- discovery outcome --\n    bool isDriver = false;\n    bool isPiggyback = false;\n    std::string driverFeed;   // valid if isPiggyback\n    std::string moverSender;  // \"DESK_STATE\" bucket -- published for the hedger\n\nstatic std::map<std::string, InstrumentState> gInstruments;\nstatic std::mutex gMutex;  // protects gInstruments end-to-end; see header TODO on locking\n\nstatic std::ofstream gPnlFile;\nstatic std::mutex gLogMutex;\nstatic std::ofstream gDiscoveryLog;\n\nstatic std::atomic<bool> gRunning{true};\n\n// ============================================================================\n// Math helpers\n// ============================================================================\n\nstatic double meanOf(const std::vector<double>& v) {\n    if (v.empty()) return 0.0;\n    return std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0.0) / static_cast<double>(v.size());\n}\n\nstatic double pearsonR(const std::vector<double>& x, const std::vector<double>& y) {\n    size_t n = x.size();\n    if (n < 2 || y.size() != n) return 0.0;\n    double mx = meanOf(x), my = meanOf(y);\n    double sxy = 0, sxx = 0, syy = 0;\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {\n        double dx = x[i] - mx, dy = y[i] - my;\n        sxy += dx * dy;\n        sxx += dx * dx;\n        syy += dy * dy;\n    }\n    if (sxx <= 0 || syy <= 0) return 0.0;\n    return sxy / std::sqrt(sxx * syy);\n}\n\n// Forward-fill lookup: the value of `hist` at-or-before time `ts`. `hist` is\n// append-only in time order, so a binary search over its (random-access)\n// deque iterators is valid.\nstatic bool valueAtOrBefore(const std::deque<std::pair<long long, double>>& hist, long long ts,\n                             double& out) {\n    if (hist.empty() || hist.front().first > ts) return false;\n    auto it = std::upper_bound(\n        hist.begin(), hist.end(), ts,\n        [](long long t, const std::pair<long long, double>& p) { return t < p.first; });\n    if (it == hist.begin()) return false;\n    --it;\n    out = it->second;\n    return true;\n}\n\n// Exchange's own fair-value definition (microprice, falling back to mid\n// when the spread is wide or a side is empty) -- generic, not tied to any\n// particular instrument.\nstatic double fairValue(const InstrumentState& st) {\n    if (st.bidPx < 0 && st.askPx < 0) return static_cast<double>(st.meta.ref_price);\n    if (st.bidPx < 0) return static_cast<double>(st.askPx);\n    if (st.askPx < 0) return static_cast<double>(st.bidPx);\n\n    long long tick = st.meta.ticksize > 0 ? st.meta.ticksize : 1;\n    long long spreadTicks = (st.askPx - st.bidPx) / tick;\n    if (spreadTicks >= 2 || st.bidVol <= 0 || st.askVol <= 0) {\n        return (static_cast<double>(st.bidPx) + static_cast<double>(st.askPx)) / 2.0;\n    }\n    return (static_cast<double>(st.bidPx) * st.askVol + static_cast<double>(st.askPx) * st.bidVol) /\n           static_cast<double>(st.bidVol + st.askVol);\n}\n\n// True if the resting order currently sitting at instrument `st`'s best\n// price on `side` ('B' or 'S') is owned by `sender`. Conservative: if we\n// can't positively identify an owner at that exact price, we return false\n// rather than block on a maybe -- callers combine this with other checks,\n// it isn't meant to be the sole gate.\nstatic bool bestPriceOwnedBy(const InstrumentState& st, char side, const std::string& sender) {\n    if (sender.empty()) return false;\n    long long px = (side == 'B') ? st.bidPx : st.askPx;\n    if (px < 0) return false;\n    for (const auto& kv : st.liveOrders) {\n        const RestingOrder& ord = kv.second;\n        if (ord.side == side && ord.price == px && ord.sender == sender) return true;\n    }\n    return false;\n}\n\n// ============================================================================\n// Discovery: pairwise lagged correlation\n// ============================================================================\n\nstruct PairFit {\n    double r2 = 0.0;\n    long long lag = 0;\n    bool aLeadsB = true;\n};\n\n// Tests both directions across a small lag grid and returns whichever\n// (direction, lag) combination fits best. \"A leads B at lag L\" means\n// B(t) ~ a + b * A(t - L) fits better than the reverse.\nstatic PairFit bestFit(const InstrumentState& a, const InstrumentState& b) {\n    PairFit best;\n    for (int dir = 0; dir < 2; ++dir) {\n        const auto& lead = (dir == 0) ? a.midHistory : b.midHistory;\n        const auto& lagging = (dir == 0) ? b.midHistory : a.midHistory;\n        for (long long lag = 0; lag <= cfg::kMaxLagNanos; lag += cfg::kLagStepNanos) {\n            std::vector<double> xs, ys;\n            xs.reserve(lagging.size());\n            ys.reserve(lagging.size());\n            for (const auto& p : lagging) {\n                double leadVal;\n                if (valueAtOrBefore(lead, p.first - lag, leadVal)) {\n                    xs.push_back(leadVal);\n                    ys.push_back(p.second);\n                }\n            }\n            if (static_cast<int>(xs.size()) < cfg::kMinOverlapPoints) continue;\n            double r = pearsonR(xs, ys);\n            double r2 = r * r;\n            if (r2 > best.r2) {\n                best.r2 = r2;\n                best.lag = lag;\n                best.aLeadsB = (dir == 0);\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    return best;\n}\n\n// Simple union-find over feed names.\nstruct UnionFind {\n    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> parent;\n    std::string find(const std::string& x) {\n        auto it = parent.find(x);\n        if (it == parent.end()) {\n            parent[x] = x;\n            return x;\n        }\n        if (it->second == x) return x;\n        std::string root = find(it->second);\n        parent[x] = root;\n        return root;\n    }\n    void unite(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) {\n        std::string ra = find(a), rb = find(b);\n        if (ra != rb) parent[ra] = rb;\n    }\n};\n\nstatic void publishPairing(const std::string& piggyback, const std::string& driver, double rel) {\n    if (!gDeskKv) return;\n    std::ostringstream oss;\n    oss << \"driver=\" << driver << \";rel=\" << rel << \";ready=true\";\n    uint64_t rev = 0;\n    natsStatus s = kvStore_PutString(&rev, gDeskKv, piggyback.c_str(), oss.str().c_str());\n    if (s != NATS_OK) {\n        printf(\"[%s] failed to publish pairing to DESK_STATE: %s\\n\", piggyback.c_str(),\n               natsStatus_GetText(s));\n    }\n}\n\n// Called periodically.
