{\\n    return (v < lo) ? lo : (v > hi) ? hi : v;\\n}\\n\\nstatic long long nowNanos() {\\n    auto now = std::chrono::system_clock::now().time_since_epoch();\\n    return std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(now).count();\\n}\\n\\n// ============================================================================\\n// Fair value\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\n// Fair value source: rolling mean once the lookback window has enough\\n// samples; EX_META's ref_price as a fallback before that. Without this,\\n// the quoter would sit out entirely at startup even though EX_META hands\\n// us a usable reference price immediately. Resolves the earlier open\\n// design question (\\\"fair value source: BBO mid vs. ref_price/\\n// last_traded_price with fallback\\\") as: rolling mean is primary, ref_price\\n// is the cold-start fallback only, not a permanent blend.\\nstatic double fairValue(const InstrumentState& st) {\\n    if (st.priceWindow.size() >= st.lookback / 4) {\\n        return st.rollingMean;\\n    }\\n    return static_cast<double>(st.meta.ref_price);\\n}\\n\\n// Current mid from the latest BBO, if both sides are present; falls back to\\n// fairValue() (rolling mean, or EX_META's ref_price during cold start) if\\n// one side is currently empty, so PnL marks don't go stale/undefined just\\n// because the book is one-sided for a tick.\\nstatic double currentMid(const InstrumentState& st) {\\n    if (st.bidPx >= 0 && st.askPx >= 0) {\\n        return (static_cast<double>(st.bidPx) + static_cast<double>(st.askPx)) / 2.0;\\n    }\\n    return fairValue(st);\\n}\\n\\n// Unrealized PnL: mark our open position at the current mid vs. our average\\n// entry price. (mid - st.avgEntryPrice) : (st.avgEntryPrice - mid);\\n    return pnlPerUnit * std::abs(static_cast<double>(st.position));\\n}\\n\\n// Writes one row to the dedicated PnL/loss csv (data/pnl.csv), writing the\\n// header once on first use. event_type is \\\"FILL\\\" (one row per fill) or\\n// \\\"SNAPSHOT\\\" (one row per periodic tick, so you can see PnL drift even with\\n// no fills, e.g. an open position bleeding against you).\\nstatic bool pnlHeaderWritten = false;\\nstatic void writePnlRow(const char* eventType, const InstrumentState& st,\\n                         double pnlDelta, const char* side, long long price,\\n                         long long volume) {\\n    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(pnlMutex);\\n    if (!pnlHeaderWritten) {\\n        pnlFile << \\\"ts,event_type,feed,side,fill_price,fill_volume,position,\\\"\\n                    \\\"avg_entry_price,mid,realized_pnl,unrealized_pnl,total_pnl,\\\"\\n                    \\\"pnl_since_recalib\\\\n\\\";\\n        pnlHeaderWritten = true;\\n    }\\n    double unreal = unrealizedPnL(st);\\n    pnlFile << nowNanos() << \\\",\\\" << eventType << \\\",\\\" << st.feed << \\\",\\\"\\n             << side << \\\",\\\" << price << \\\",\\\" << volume << \\\",\\\" << st.position << \\\",\\\"\\n             << st.avgEntryPrice << \\\",\\\" << currentMid(st) << \\\",\\\" << st.realizedPnL << \\\",\\\"\\n             << unreal << \\\",\\\" << (st.realizedPnL + unreal) << \\\",\\\" << st.pnlSinceRecalib\\n             << \\\"\\\\n\\\";\\n    pnlFile.flush();\\n    (void)pnlDelta; // kept as a param for FILL rows if you want to log it separately later\\n}\\n\\n// ============================================================================\\n// Rolling stats\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\nstatic void updateRollingStats(InstrumentState& st) {\\n    if (st.bidPx < 0 || st.askPx < 0) return; // need both sides for a mid\\n    double mid = (static_cast<double>(st.bidPx) + static_cast<double>(st.askPx)) / 2.0;\\n\\n    st.priceWindow.push_back(mid);\\n    if (st.priceWindow.size() > st.lookback) st.priceWindow.pop_front();\\n    if (st.priceWindow.size() < 2) return;\\n\\n    double sum = 0.0;\\n    for (double p : st.priceWindow) sum += p;\\n    double mean = sum / static_cast<double>(st.priceWindow.size());\\n\\n    double sqSum = 0.0;\\n    for (double p : st.priceWindow) sqSum += (p - mean) * (p - mean);\\n    double variance = sqSum / static_cast<double>(st.priceWindow.size() - 1);\\n    double stddev = std::sqrt(variance);\\n\\n    st.rollingMean = mean;\\n    st.rollingStd = stddev;\\n    st.zscore = (stddev > 1e-9) ? (mid - mean) / stddev : 0.0;\\n}\\n\\n// ============================================================================\\n// Recalibration (loss-triggered, not continuous)\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\nstatic void recalibrate(InstrumentState& st) {\\n    st.spreadMultiplier = 2.0;\\n    st.skewPerUnitInventory = (st.meta.position_limit > 0)\\n        ? (st.rollingStd / static_cast<double>(st.meta.position_limit))\\n        : 0.0;\\n    st.pnlSinceRecalib = 0.0;\\n    printf(\\\"[%s] recalibrated: mean=%.2f std=%.4f spreadMult=%.2f skewPerUnit=%.6f\\\\n\\\",\\n           st.feed.c_str(), st.rollingMean, st.rollingStd, st.spreadMultiplier,\\n           st.skewPerUnitInventory);\\n}\\n\\n// Loss threshold, in price units, since the last recalibration. (totalCost / totalVol) : static_cast<double>(price);\\n    } else {\\n        // Reducing or flipping a position: realize PnL on the closed part.\\n        double closedVol = std::min(std::abs(static_cast<double>(st.position)), std::abs(signedVol));\\n        double pnlPerUnit = (st.position > 0)\\n            ? (static_cast<double>(price) - st.avgEntryPrice)\\n            : (st.avgEntryPrice - static_cast<double>(price));\\n        pnlDelta = pnlPerUnit * closedVol;\\n        st.realizedPnL += pnlDelta;\\n        st.pnlSinceRecalib += pnlDelta;\\n\\n        if (std::abs(signedVol) > std::abs(static_cast<double>(st.position))) {\\n            // Flipped through flat \\u2014 new position takes on the fill price.\\n            st.avgEntryPrice = static_cast<double>(price);\\n        }\\n    }\\n\\n    st.position = newPosition;\\n\\n    // FILL row: ts, feed, side, price, volume, positionBefore, positionAfter,\\n    // pnlDelta (this fill only), realizedPnL (lifetime), pnlSinceRecalib.\\n    {\\n        std::stringstream ss;\\n        ss << nowNanos() << \\\",\\\" << st.feed << \\\",\\\" << side << \\\",\\\" << price << \\\",\\\"\\n           << volume << \\\",\\\" << positionBefore << \\\",\\\" << newPosition << \\\",\\\"\\n           << pnlDelta << \\\",\\\" << st.realizedPnL << \\\",\\\" << st.pnlSinceRecalib;\\n        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(logMutex);\\n        logFile << \\\"FILL,\\\" << ss.str() << \\\"\\\\n\\\";\\n        logFile.flush();\\n    }\\n\\n    // Dedicated PnL log row for this fill \\u2014 this is the one to watch for\\n    // losses, since it carries realized + unrealized + total in one place.\\n    writePnlRow(\\\"FILL\\\", st, pnlDelta, std::string(1, side).c_str(), price, volume);\\n\\n    checkAndRecalibrate(st);\\n}\\n\\n// ============================================================================\\n// Quote computation\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\nstruct Quote {\\n    bool valid = false;\\n    long long bidPx = -1, askPx = -1, vol = -1;\\n};\\n\\nstatic Quote computeQuotes(const InstrumentState& st) {\\n    Quote q;\\n    if (st.meta.ticksize <= 0) return q;\\n    // No usable price at all \\u2014 no rolling data AND no ref_price from\\n    // EX_META (would be 0 if the key were missing/malformed). Stay out.\\n    if (st.priceWindow.empty() && st.meta.ref_price <= 0) return q;\\n\\n    double fv = fairValue(st);\\n\\n    // rollingStd is 0 until the window has >= 2 samples, so before that,\\n    // half-spread is entirely the tick-based floor below \\u2014 this is the\\n    // cold-start case where we're quoting off ref_price, not realized vol.\\n    double halfSpread = std::max(\\n        st.spreadMultiplier * st.rollingStd / 2.0,\\n        static_cast<double>(st.minSpreadTicks * st.meta.ticksize) / 2.0);\\n\\n    // Inventory skew: lean the fair value away from our current position so\\n    // resting quotes naturally bias toward flattening.\\n    double inventorySkew = -st.skewPerUnitInventory * static_cast<double>(st.position);\\n\\n    // Z-score tilt: bounded to a quarter of the half-spread and clamped to\\n    // +/-2 std, so it nudges quoting rather than becoming a directional\\n    // signal. This is a mean-reversion bias on a market-making quote, not\\n    // a \\\"take a position because z-score says so\\\" trigger.\\n    double clampedZ = clampValue(st.zscore, -2.0, 2.0);\\n    double zscoreTilt = -clampedZ * (halfSpread * 0.25);\\n\\n    double adjustedFV = fv + inventorySkew + zscoreTilt;\\n\\n    long long bidPx = static_cast<long long>(std::round((adjustedFV - halfSpread) / st.meta.ticksize))\\n                       * st.meta.ticksize;\\n    long long askPx = static_cast<long long>(std::round((adjustedFV + halfSpread) / st.meta.ticksize))\\n                       * st.meta.ticksize;\\n\\n    long long lo = st.meta.ref_price - st.meta.band;\\n    long long hi = st.meta.ref_price + st.meta.band;\\n    bidPx = clampValue(bidPx, lo, hi);\\n    askPx = clampValue(askPx, lo, hi);\\n    if (askPx <= bidPx) askPx = bidPx + st.meta.ticksize;\\n\\n    // Base size: placeholder fixed size within instrument limits. Sizing\\n    // strategy (e.g. scaling down as position approaches position_limit)\\n    // is a further refinement, not yet implemented.\\n    long long baseSize = 10;\\n    long long vol = std::max(st.meta.min_volume, std::min(st.meta.max_volume, baseSize));\\n\\n    q.valid = true;\\n    q.bidPx = bidPx;\\n    q.askPx = askPx;\\n    q.vol = vol;\\n    return q;\\n}\\n\\n// ============================================================================\\n// Order entry (ex.req.<SENDER> request/reply)\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\nstatic std::string nextOrderId(InstrumentState& st) {\\n    // 4-char feed (feeds are always 4 chars per PROTOCOL.md) + 4-digit\\n    // wrapping sequence = 8 chars, unique per feed for ~10k live orders.\\n    char buf[9];\\n    long long seq = (st.orderSeq++) % 10000;\\n    snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), \\\"%.4s%04lld\\\", st.feed.c_str(), seq);\\n    return std::string(buf);\\n}\\n\\n// Sends \\\"<SENDER> A <FEED> <id> <B|S> <volume> <price> <L>\\\" and returns\\n// true if the exchange accepted it (reply starts with \\\"Y\\\").\\nstatic bool addOrder(const std::string& feed, const std::string& orderId,\\n                      char side, long long volume, long long price) {\\n    char msg[256];\\n    snprintf(msg, sizeof(msg), \\\"%s A %s %s %c %lld %lld L\\\",\\n              gSender.c_str(), feed.c_str(), orderId.c_str(), side, volume, price);\\n\\n    char subject[64];\\n    snprintf(subject, sizeof(subject), \\\"ex.req.%s\\\", gSender.c_str());\\n\\n    natsMsg* reply = nullptr;\\n    natsStatus s = natsConnection_RequestString(&reply, gConn, subject, msg, 2000);\\n    if (s != NATS_OK) {\\n        printf(\\\"[%s] addOrder request failed: %s\\\\n\\\", feed.c_str(), natsStatus_GetText(s));\\n        return false;\\n    }\\n    std::string replyStr(natsMsg_GetData(reply), natsMsg_GetDataLength(reply));\\n    natsMsg_Destroy(reply);\\n\\n    if (!replyStr.empty() && replyStr[0] == 'Y') return true;\\n    printf(\\\"[%s] addOrder rejected: %s\\\\n\\\", feed.c_str(), replyStr.c_str());\\n    return false;\\n}\\n\\n// Sends \\\"<SENDER> C <FEED> <id>\\\".\\nstatic bool cancelOrder(const std::string& feed, const std::string& orderId) {\\n    if (orderId.empty()) return true;\\n    char msg[256];\\n    snprintf(msg, sizeof(msg), \\\"%s C %s %s\\\", gSender.c_str(), feed.c_str(), orderId.c_str());\\n\\n    char subject[64];\\n    snprintf(subject, sizeof(subject), \\\"ex.req.%s\\\", gSender.c_str());\\n\\n    natsMsg* reply = nullptr;\\n    natsStatus s = natsConnection_RequestString(&reply, gConn, subject, replyStr(natsMsg_GetData(reply), natsMsg_GetDataLength(reply));\\n    natsMsg_Destroy(reply);\\n    return !replyStr.empty() && replyStr[0] == 'Y';\\n}\\n\\n// Cancel-and-replace both sides if the desired quote differs meaningfully\\n// from what's currently resting. Called on a timer, not per-tick.\\nstatic void requoteInstrument(InstrumentState& st) {\\n    Quote q = computeQuotes(st);\\n    if (!q.valid) return;\\n\\n    bool bidNeedsUpdate = (st.restingBidPx != q.bidPx);\\n    bool askNeedsUpdate = (st.restingAskPx != q.askPx);\\n\\n    if (bidNeedsUpdate) {\\n        cancelOrder(st.feed, st.restingBidId);\\n        std::string id = nextOrderId(st);\\n        if (addOrder(st.feed, id, 'B', q.vol, q.bidPx)) {\\n            st.restingBidId = id;\\n            st.restingBidPx = q.bidPx;\\n        } else {\\n            st.restingBidId.clear();\\n            st.restingBidPx = -1;\\n        }\\n    }\\n    if (askNeedsUpdate) {\\n        cancelOrder(st.feed, st.restingAskId);\\n        std::string id = nextOrderId(st);\\n        if (addOrder(st.feed, id, 'S', q.vol, q.askPx)) {\\n            st.restingAskId = id;\\n            st.restingAskPx = q.askPx;\\n        } else {\\n            st.restingAskId.clear();\\n            st.restingAskPx = -1;\\n        }\\n    }\\n}\\n\\n// ============================================================================\\n// NATS callbacks\\n// ============================================================================\\n\\nstatic void onBBO(natsConnection* nc, natsSubscription* sub, natsMsg* msg, void* closure) {\\n    (void)nc; (void)sub; (void)closure;\\n\\n    const char* data = natsMsg_GetData(msg);\\n    int len = natsMsg_GetDataLength(msg);\\n    const char* subject = natsMsg_GetSubject(msg);\\n\\n    std::vector<std::string> fields = splitFields(data, len);\\n    writeRow(\\\"BBO\\\", subject, fields);\\n\\n    // fields: [ts, FEED, bid_px, bid_vol, ask_px, ask_vol]\\n    if (fields.size() == 6) {\\n        std::string feed = fields[1];\\n        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(instrumentsMutex);\\n        auto it = instruments.find(feed);\\n        if (it != instruments.end()) {\\n            InstrumentState& st = it->second;\\n            st.bidPx  = (fields[2] == \\\"-\\\") ?                 "text": "They're a periodic heartbeat snapshot of each instrument's state, written every 250ms in the requote loop regardless of whether a fill happened \u2014 as opposed to `FILL` rows, which only fire when a trade actually occurs.\n\n**Why they exist:** between fills, your position can still be *bleeding* against you (price moving away from your average entry) or your rolling stats can be shifting in ways worth seeing, but nothing in `FILL` rows would capture that since there's no fill to log. The `PNL` row gives you a continuous timeline of `position`, `realizedPnL`, `pnlSinceRecalib`, `rollingMean`, `rollingStd`, `zscore`, `ref_price`, and your current resting bid/ask \u2014 sampled on a clock, not an event. That lets you plot \"what was our state at time T\" even during quiet stretches with no trades.\n\n**Important gap to know about:** the `PNL` rows in `bbo_data.csv` do **not** include unrealized PnL \u2014 only `realizedPnL` (locked in from closed trades) and `pnlSinceRecalib`. If you're trying to answer \"am I actually losing money right now,\" that's incomplete on its own, since a big open losing position won't show up as negative until you close it. That's specifically why `pnl.csv` (`writePnlRow`) exists separately \u2014 it computes `unrealizedPnL` (marking your open position against current mid) and gives you `total_pnl = realized + unrealized`, which is the number you actually want for \"how are we doing\" analysis.\n\nSo practically:\n- **`bbo_data.csv`'s `PNL` rows** \u2014 good for correlating rolling stats/quote levels against the BBO/MD data already in that file, same timeline, easy to join.\n- **`pnl.csv`** \u2014 the one to use for actual profit/loss analysis, since it's the only place `unrealized_pnl` and `total_pnl` live.\n\nThere's some redundancy between the two right now (`position`, `realizedPnL`, `pnlSinceRecalib` appear in both).                         "extracted_content": "# Exchange protocol v2.5\n\nThe exchange speaks **space-separated ASCII messages over NATS**. Fields never\ncontain spaces. There are three things to talk to:\n\n| What                 | NATS subject              | Mechanism            |\n|----------------------|---------------------------|----------------------|\n| Order entry          | `ex.req.<SENDER>`         | request / reply      |\n| Market data          | `ex.md.<FEED>.<SENDER>`   | publish (JetStream)  |\n| Best bid/offer       | `ex.bbo.<FEED>`           | publish (JetStream)  |\n| Instrument metadata  | KV bucket `EX_META`       | JetStream KV         |\n\n- A **`<FEED>`** (feedcode) is 4 chars: 2 for the underlying + 2 for the expiry,\n  e.g. `AAH6`. All feedcodes on the same underlying share the prefix (`AA`).\n- A **`<SENDER>`** is an 8-char identity tag you choose for your strategy.\n- An **order id** is 8 chars you choose, unique per sender. Publicly an order is\n  identified by the 17-char `sender:orderid`.\n- Prices and volumes are integers.\n\n## Order entry \u2014 `ex.req.<SENDER>` (request/reply)\n\nPublish your request to **`ex.req.<your-sender>`** (NATS request/reply; the reply\ncomes back on the inbox). The sender in the subject is what the exchange acts on,\nand it **must match** the `<SENDER>` at the start of your message \u2014 you can only\nenter and cancel orders for your own sender. Every request starts with your\n`<SENDER>` then a 1-char type.\n\n| Type | Meaning      | Fields after `<SENDER> <type>`                                   |\n|------|--------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `A`  | add order    | `<FEED> <id:8> <B\\|S> <volume> <price> <M\\|L\\|F>`                 |\n| `C`  | cancel order | `<FEED> <id:8>`                                                  |\n| `X`  | cancel many  | `<FEED> <B\\|S\\|X> <price>`  \u2014 see below                           |\n| `Q`  | enable STP   | `<FEED>`                                                         |\n| `W`  | disable STP  | `<FEED>`                                                          |\n\nOrder types: **`L`** = limit (rests on the book), **`M`** = market, **`F`** =\nfill-and-kill (executes what it can immediately, cancels the rest). Only `L`\nrests.\n\n**Replies** start with the exchange's tag, then:\n- `Y <n>` \u2014 accepted. For `A`, `<n>` is the volume that traded immediately. For\n  `C`/`X`, `<n>` is how many orders were cancelled.\n- `N <code> <text>` \u2014 rejected.\n\nReject codes are stable numbers with a short text. A few you will hit early:\n`100` malformed \u00b7 `202` bad feedcode \u00b7 `203` re-used order id. The rest are\nyours to catalogue by experiment.\n\n### `X` \u2014 cancel many\n\n`X <FEED> <B|S|X> <price>` cancels several of **your** resting orders at once and\nreplies `Y <n>` with the number cancelled. The `<FEED>` may also select more than\none expiry, price may select more than one price\n\n## Market data \u2014 `ex.md.<FEED>.<SENDER>`\n\nSubscribe to `ex.md.<FEED>.*` to see all market data for a contract, or to\n`ex.md.<FEED>.<your-sender>` for just your own. Every message is prefixed with an\n`int64` nanosecond timestamp.\n\n| Type | Fields after `<ts> <type>`                                          |\n|------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `A`  | `<id:17> <B\\|S> <volume> <price>`  \u2014 order added to the book          |\n| `E`  | `<incoming:17> <resting:17> <volume> <price> <matchid> <B\\|S>`        |\n| `C`  | `<id:17>`  \u2014 order removed from the book                              |\n| `T`  | same fields as `E`                                                    |\n\n- `E` is an **execution**. The trailing `B`/`S` is the **aggressor's side**. An\n  order may fill over **several** `E` messages \u2014 accumulate them.\n- `T` reports a **trade** \u2014 useful for watching trade flow.\n- Your own fills show up on `ex.md.<FEED>.<your-sender>`.\n\n## Best bid/offer \u2014 `ex.bbo.<FEED>`\n\n`<ts> <FEED> <bid_px> <bid_vol> <ask_px> <ask_vol>`, with `-` for an empty side.\nUpdated as the top of book changes.\n\n## Instrument metadata \u2014 KV `EX_META`\n\nKey = feedcode; value is `key=value` pairs: `ticksize`, `ref_price`, `band`\n(price band is `ref_price \u00b1 band`), `min_volume`, `max_volume`, `position_limit`,\n`max_tps`, `last_traded_price`. Read it to learn each contract's tick, price\nband, and limits.\n\n```bash\nnats kv ls  EX_META\nnats kv get EX_META AAH6\n```\n\n## Probing\n\nThe `nats` CLI is the fastest way to explore before you write code: `nats sub`\non the feeds above, `nats req` for order entry, `nats kv` for `EX_META`.\n"

JetStream context + EX_META KV read ---\n    if (s == NATS_OK) s = natsConnection_JetStream(&js, conn, nullptr);\n    if (s == NATS_OK) s = js_KeyValue(&kv, js, \"EX_META\");\n    if (s != NATS_OK) {\n        printf(\"JetStream/KV setup failed: %s\\n\", natsStatus_GetText(s));\n    } else {\n        s = kvStore_Get(&entry, kv, feed);\n        if (s == NATS_OK) {\n            printf(\"[EX_META %s] %s\\n\", feed, kvEntry_ValueString(entry));\n            kvEntry_Destroy(entry);\n        } else {\n            printf(\"kv get failed for %s: %s\\n\", feed, natsStatus_GetText(s));\n        }\n    }\n\n    // --- 3. Subscribe to BBO for the feed and print forever ---\n    char subject[64];\n    snprintf(subject, sizeof(subject), \"ex.bbo.%s\", feed);\n\n    if (s == NATS_OK) {\n        s = natsConnection_Subscribe(&sub, conn, subject, onBBO, nullptr);\n    }\n    if (s != NATS_OK) {\n        printf(\"subscribe failed: %s\\n\", natsStatus_GetText(s));\n    } else {\n        printf(\"subscribed to %s, printing updates (Ctrl+C to stop)...\\n\", subject);\n        // Keep the process alive; onBBO fires asynchronously on nats.c's\n        // internal thread. In the real strategy this loop becomes the\n        // event loop / gets replaced with proper shutdown handling.\n        while (true) {\n            nats_Sleep(1000);\n        }\n    }\n\n    // Cleanup (unreached in the loop above, but here for completeness /\n    // once we add signal handling for clean shutdown).\n    natsSubscription_Destroy(sub);\n    kvStore_Destroy(kv);\n    jsCtx_Destroy(js);\n    natsConnection_Destroy(conn);\n    nats_Close();\n\n    return (s == NATS_OK) ? 0 : 1;\n}\n"

                "text": "```bash\nmkdir build\n```\nMakes a new empty folder called `build`. This is just a convention \u2014 you keep generated build files (object files, makefiles, the compiled binary) separate from your source code, so they don't clutter things up and you can `rm -rf build` to start totally fresh anytime.\n\n```bash\ncd build\n```\nMoves you into that folder, because you're about to run CMake *from inside it* \u2014 that's what makes it an \"out-of-source build.\"\n\n```bash\ncmake ..\n```\nThis is the important one. CMake reads your `CMakeLists.txt` (which is one directory up \u2014 that's what `..` means) and figures out how to actually build the project on your specific machine: which compiler you have, where nats.c's source lives, what flags to use, etc. It doesn't compile anything yet \u2014 it just generates the actual build instructions (a bunch of Makefiles, by default) and drops them into the `build` folder you're standing in.\n\nIf this step fails, it's usually because something CMake needs is missing \u2014 a required library, the wrong CMake version, or a mistake in `CMakeLists.txt` itself.\n\n```bash\nmake\n```\nNow it actually compiles. `make` reads the Makefiles that `cmake` just generated and runs the real compiler (`g++`/`clang++`) on every source file \u2014 first building `nats.c` into a library (`nats_static`), then compiling `skeleton.cpp`, then linking them together into one executable called `skeleton`, which lands in the `build` folder.\n\nIf this step fails, it's a genuine compile or link error \u2014 missing header, wrong function name, etc. That's the output I actually want to see if something breaks, since it'll tell us exactly what's wrong with `skeleton.cpp` or the nats.c API calls.\n\nAfter both succeed, you'd have `build/skeleton` as a runnable binary.",

                "text": "**Flushing, explained:**\n\nWhen you write to a file with `std::ofstream`, the data doesn't necessarily go straight to disk right away \u2014 it usually sits in an internal memory buffer first, and gets written out in batches (either when the buffer fills up, or when the stream is closed/destroyed). This is normal and usually good for performance \u2014 writing to disk on every single line is slow.\n\nThe problem: if the program gets killed abruptly (you Ctrl+C the container, or `docker compose down` sends a kill signal) before that buffer gets written out, whatever's sitting in the buffer is lost \u2014 never made it to disk, even though your code \"wrote\" it as far as your C++ is concerned.\n\n`stream.flush()` forces whatever's currently buffered to actually hit disk immediately, on demand. Since you said you want all the data, call `.flush()` after every write (or every write to that BBO file specifically). It costs you some performance since you're bypassing the buffering benefit, but for a data-logging skeleton like this, correctness matters more than speed, and BBO messages aren't so frequent that per-line flushing will meaningfully slow anything down.\n\n**For #5 \u2014 getting the CSV out of the container:**\n\nAdd a bind mount to the `strategy` service in your `docker-compose.yml` so a folder inside the container maps to a real folder on your Mac. Something like:\n\n```yaml\nstrategy:\n  build: ./strategy\n  environment: *desk-env\n  depends_on:\n    - exchange\n  restart: on-failure\n  profiles:\n    - strategy\n  volumes:\n    - ./strategy/data:/data\n```\n\nThen in your C++, open the file at a path under `/data/`, e.g. `/data/bbo_log.csv` \u2014 since `/data` is mounted, anything you write there shows up live in `strategy/data/` on your actual Mac, survives the container being stopped/killed, and you can open it directly in pandas without extracting anything from Docker.\n\nCreate the local folder first so Docker doesn't complain:\n\n```bash\nmkdir -p strategy/data\n```\n\nGo ahead and write the logging code \u2014 parsing the line, opening/flushing the file, writing to `/data/bbo_log.csv`. This is normal and usually good for performance \u2014 writing to disk on every single line is slow.\n\nThe problem: if the program gets killed abruptly (you Ctrl+C the container, or `docker compose down` sends a kill signal) before that buffer gets written out, whatever's sitting in the buffer is lost \u2014 never made it to disk, even though your code \"wrote\" it as far as your C++ is concerned.\n\n`stream.flush()` forces whatever's currently buffered to actually hit disk immediately, on demand. Since you said you want all the data, call `.flush()` after every write (or every write to that BBO file specifically). It costs you some performance since you're bypassing the buffering benefit, but for a data-logging skeleton like this, correctness matters more than speed, and BBO messages aren't so frequent that per-line flushing will meaningfully slow anything down.\n\n**For #5 \u2014 getting the CSV out of the container:**\n\nAdd a bind mount to the `strategy` service in your `docker-compose.yml` so a folder inside the container maps to a real folder on your Mac. Something like:\n\n```yaml\nstrategy:\n  build: ./strategy\n  environment: *desk-env\n  depends_on:\n    - exchange\n  restart: on-failure\n  profiles:\n    - strategy\n  volumes:\n    - ./strategy/data:/data\n```\n\nThen in your C++, open the file at a path under `/data/`, e.g. `/data/bbo_log.csv` \u2014 since `/data` is mounted, anything you write there shows up live in `strategy/data/` on your actual Mac, survives the container being stopped/killed, and you can open it directly in pandas without extracting anything from Docker.\n\nCreate the local folder first so Docker doesn't complain:\n\n```bash\nmkdir -p strategy/data\n```\n\nGo ahead and write the logging code \u2014 parsing the line, opening/flushing the file, writing to `/data/bbo_log.csv`. Read EX_META for one feedcode via JetStream KV\n//   3. Subscribe to ex.bbo.<FEED> and print updates as they arrive\n//\n// No order entry, no strategy logic yet \u2014 this only exists to confirm\n// Docker + NATS + C++ actually talk to each other before building on top.\n//\n// Build: see CMakeLists.txt / Dockerfile (added once this compiles clean).\n\n#include <nats.h>\n#include <cstdio>\n#include <cstdlib>\n#include <cstring>\n#include <fstream>\n#include <vector>\n#include <string>\n#include <iostream>\n#include <sstream>\n\n// Reads env var with a fallback default, since the grading harness injects\n// real values but local dev needs something sane.\nstatic const char* envOr(const char* name, const char* fallback) {\n    const char* v = std::getenv(name);\n    return (v && v[0] != '\\0') ? v : fallback;\n}\n\n// Called for every message on ex.bbo.<FEED>.\nstatic void onBBO(natsConnection* nc, natsSubscription* sub, natsMsg* msg, void* closure) {\n    (void)nc; (void)sub; (void)closure;\n    std::ofstream* filePtr = static_cast<std::ofstream*>(closure);\n    // Message payload is the space-separated ASCII line described in\n    // PROTOCOL.md: \"<ts> <FEED> <bid_px> <bid_vol> <ask_px> <ask_vol>\"\n    const char* data = natsMsg_GetData(msg);\n    int len = natsMsg_GetDataLength(msg);\n    printf(\"[BBO] %.*s\\n\", len, data);\n    \n    std::string payload (data,len);\n    std::stringstream ss(payload);\n    std::vector<std::string> data_vector;\n    std::string word;\n\n    while (ss >> word) {\n        data_vector.push_back(word);\n    }\n\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < data_vector.size(); i++) {\n        *filePtr << data_vector[i];\n        if (i < data_vector.size() - 1) {\n            *filePtr << \",\";\n        }\n    }\n    *filePtr << \"\\n\";\n    filePtr->flush();\n    natsMsg_Destroy(msg);\n}\n\nint main(int argc, char** argv) {\n    std::ofstream file(\"/data/bbo_data.csv\");\n\n    if (!file.is_open()) {\n        std::cerr << \"Error! File Failed to open\" << std::endl;\n        return 1;\n    }\n\n    // FEED to probe \u2014 hardcoded for the skeleton, will become configurable\n    // once this is wired into the real strategy.\n    const char* feed = (argc > 1) ? argv[1] : \"AAH6\";\n\n    const char* natsUrl = envOr(\"NATS_URL\", \"nats://localhost:4222\");\n    const char* sender  = envOr(\"SENDER\", \"SKEL0001\"); // 8 chars, per PROTOCOL.md\n\n    printf(\"skeleton: connecting to %s as sender=%s, watching feed=%s\\n\",\n           natsUrl, sender, feed);\n\n    natsStatus s = NATS_OK;\n    natsConnection* conn = nullptr;\n    jsCtx* js = nullptr;\n    kvStore* kv = nullptr;\n    kvEntry* entry = nullptr;\n    natsSubscription* sub = nullptr;\n\n    // --- 1. Connect ---\n    s = natsConnection_ConnectTo(&conn, natsUrl);\n    if (s != NATS_OK) {\n        printf(\"connect failed: %s\\n\", natsStatus_GetText(s));\n        return 1;\n    }\n    printf(\"connected.\\n\");\n\n    // --- 2. JetStream context + EX_META KV read ---\n    if (s == NATS_OK) s = natsConnection_JetStream(&js, conn, nullptr);\n    if (s == NATS_OK) s = js_KeyValue(&kv, js, \"EX_META\");\n    if (s != NATS_OK) {\n        printf(\"JetStream/KV setup failed: %s\\n\", natsStatus_GetText(s));\n    } else {\n        s = kvStore_Get(&entry, kv, feed);\n        if (s == NATS_OK) {\n            printf(\"[EX_META %s] %s\\n\", feed, kvEntry_ValueString(entry));\n            kvEntry_Destroy(entry);\n        } else {\n            printf(\"kv get failed for %s: %s\\n\", feed, natsStatus_GetText(s));\n        }\n    }\n\n    // --- 3. Subscribe to BBO for the feed and print forever ---\n    char subject[64];\n    snprintf(subject, sizeof(subject), \"ex.bbo.%s\", feed);\n\n    if (s == NATS_OK) {\n        s = natsConnection_Subscribe(&sub, conn, subject, onBBO, &file);\n    }\n    if (s != NATS_OK) {\n        printf(\"subscribe failed: %s\\n\", natsStatus_GetText(s));\n    } else {\n        printf(\"subscribed to %s, printing updates (Ctrl+C to stop)...\\n\", subject);\n        // Keep the process alive; onBBO fires asynchronously on nats.c's\n        // internal thread. In the real strategy this loop becomes the\n        // event loop / gets replaced with proper shutdown handling.\n        while (true) {\n            nats_Sleep(1000);\n        }\n    }\n\n    // Cleanup (unreached in the loop above, but here for completeness /\n    // once we add signal handling for clean shutdown).\n    natsSubscription_Destroy(sub);\n    kvStore_Destroy(kv);\n    jsCtx_Destroy(js);\n    natsConnection_Destroy(conn);\n    nats_Close();\n\n    file.close();\n\n    std::cout << \"file created succesfully\" << std::endl;\n\n    return (s == NATS_OK) ? 0 : 1;\n}"

Resample by time instead of plotting every row.** You've got a nanosecond timestamp column \u2014 convert it to a proper pandas datetime, set it as the index, then resample to a coarser interval (e.g. every 100ms or 1s) and take the last value in each bucket, or the mean. This is usually the right move anyway since BBO updates arrive irregularly (bursts when the book's active, gaps when it's quiet) \u2014 resampling to fixed time buckets gives you an evenly-spaced series that's actually meaningful to look at, not just fewer points.\n\n```python\ndf['ts'] = pd.to_datetime(df['ts'], unit='ns')\ndf = df.set_index('ts')\nmid = ((df['bid_px'] + df['ask_px']) / 2).resample('1s').last()\nmid.plot()\n```\n\n**2. If you want every raw point but just need it to render fast**, use `matplotlib` with `plt.plot()` (a proper line plot, not `scatter`) \u2014 line plots handle hundreds of thousands of points fine, scatter plots get slow because every point is its own artist object. Also worth setting `rasterized=True` if you're going to export it as a vector format like SVG/PDF, otherwise the file itself gets huge.\n\n**3. Simple decimation** \u2014 just plot every Nth row (`df.iloc[::50]`) if you don't care about time-alignment and just want a quick visual sanity check. Fastest to write, crudest result \u2014 fine for \"does this look roughly like I expect\" but not for actually reading fine structure.\n\n**4. If you want to interactively zoom/pan** (useful for actually inspecting spread behavior around specific events), `plotly` handles this well but can get sluggish at 135k+ points unless you also downsample first \u2014 so combine plotly with option 1's resampling rather than throwing the raw data at it directly.\n\nFor what you're actually trying to learn (spread behavior, mid-price movement over the session), I'd start with option 1: resample to 1s bars, plot mid-price and bid-ask spread as two separate line charts.                 "text": "Reasonable, but scope it \u2014 you're not trying to build a general test suite, you're trying to answer two specific questions: \"is that spike a real market event or an artifact,\" and \"how should I characterize normal spread/price behavior for the quoter.\" A handful of targeted stats do that; you don't need exhaustiveness.\n\n**For classifying the spike:**\n- Compute spread's mean and standard deviation (or better, median and IQR, since a fat-tailed distribution will make mean/std misleading). Then check how many standard deviations (or IQRs) out that spike actually is \u2014 if it's a genuine 10+ sigma event, that's a strong signal it's either a real anomaly worth understanding or a data artifact, not just \"normal variance you haven't seen twice yet.\"\n- Look at how long it lasted \u2014 one resampled bucket, or several in a row? A single-bucket spike that instantly reverts looks different (probably a sweep, or a data gap) than a spike that persists for seconds (probably a real liquidity event).\n\n**For characterizing normal behavior (informs quoter design directly):**\n- **Spread distribution**: `df['spread'].describe()` plus a histogram \u2014 is it basically one fixed value (like `ticksize * N` most of the time) or does it have real variance? This tells you what spread you can realistically quote and expect to trade at.\n- **Mid-price returns**: compute `mid.diff()` or log returns, then look at their distribution and autocorrelation (`.autocorr()` or `statsmodels.tsa.stattools.acf`). If returns are close to uncorrelated (no autocorrelation), that supports \"random walk, no exploitable trend\" \u2014 good news for a pure market-making strategy, since you're not trying to predict direction, just capture spread.\n- **Volume at top of book**: distribution of `bid_vol`/`ask_vol` \u2014 tells you how much size you can expect to trade against without moving the market yourself.\n\nStart with those four, they're quick in pandas, and they'll tell you concretely whether the spike is an outlier worth a footnote in NOTES.md or something that changes your quoting logic (e.g. \"widen quotes if recent spread volatility spikes\").                         "extracted_content": "# Exchange protocol v2.5\n\nThe exchange speaks **space-separated ASCII messages over NATS**. Fields never\ncontain spaces. There are three things to talk to:\n\n| What                 | NATS subject              | Mechanism            |\n|----------------------|---------------------------|----------------------|\n| Order entry          | `ex.req.<SENDER>`         | request / reply      |\n| Market data          | `ex.md.<FEED>.<SENDER>`   | publish (JetStream)  |\n| Best bid/offer        | `ex.bbo.<FEED>`           | publish (JetStream)  |\n| Instrument metadata  | KV bucket `EX_META`       | JetStream KV         |\n\n- A **`<FEED>`** (feedcode) is 4 chars: 2 for the underlying + 2 for the expiry,\n  e.g. `AAH6`. All feedcodes on the same underlying share the prefix (`AA`).\n- A **`<SENDER>`** is an 8-char identity tag you choose for your strategy.\n- An **order id** is 8 chars you choose, unique per sender. Publicly an order is\n  identified by the 17-char `sender:orderid`.\n- Prices and volumes are integers.\n\n## Order entry \u2014 `ex.req.<SENDER>` (request/reply)\n\nPublish your request to **`ex.req.<your-sender>`** (NATS request/reply; the reply\ncomes back on the inbox). The sender in the subject is what the exchange acts on,\nand it **must match** the `<SENDER>` at the start of your message \u2014 you can only\nenter and cancel orders for your own sender. Every request starts with your\n`<SENDER>` then a 1-char type.\n\n| Type | Meaning      | Fields after `<SENDER> <type>`                                   |\n|------|--------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `A`  | add order    | `<FEED> <id:8> <B\\|S> <volume> <price> <M\\|L\\|F>`                 |\n| `C`  | cancel order | `<FEED> <id:8>`                                                  |\n| `X`  | cancel many  | `<FEED> <B\\|S\\|X> <price>`  \u2014 see below                           |\n| `Q`  | enable STP   | `<FEED>`                                                         |\n| `W`  | disable STP  | `<FEED>`                                                          |\n\nOrder types: **`L`** = limit (rests on the book), **`M`** = market, **`F`** =\nfill-and-kill (executes what it can immediately, cancels the rest). Only `L`\nrests.\n\n**Replies** start with the exchange's tag, then:\n- `Y <n>` \u2014 accepted. For `A`, `<n>` is the volume that traded immediately. For\n  `C`/`X`, `<n>` is how many orders were cancelled.\n- `N <code> <text>` \u2014 rejected.\n\nReject codes are stable numbers with a short text. A few you will hit early:\n`100` malformed \u00b7 `202` bad feedcode \u00b7 `203` re-used order id. The rest are\nyours to catalogue by experiment.\n\n### `X` \u2014 cancel many\n\n`X <FEED> <B|S|X> <price>` cancels several of **your** resting orders at once and\nreplies `Y <n>` with the number cancelled. The `<FEED>` may also select more than\none expiry, price may select more than one price\n\n## Market data \u2014 `ex.md.<FEED>.<SENDER>`\n\nSubscribe to `ex.md.<FEED>.*` to see all market data for a contract, or to\n`ex.md.<FEED>.<your-sender>` for just your own. Every message is prefixed with an\n`int64` nanosecond timestamp.\n\n| Type | Fields after `<ts> <type>`                                          |\n|------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `A`  | `<id:17> <B\\|S> <volume> <price>`  \u2014 order added to the book          |\n| `E`  | `<incoming:17> <resting:17> <volume> <price> <matchid> <B\\|S>`        |\n| `C`  | `<id:17>`  \u2014 order removed from the book                              |\n| `T`  | same fields as `E`                                                    |\n\n- `E` is an **execution**. The trailing `B`/`S` is the **aggressor's side**. An\n  order may fill over **several** `E` messages \u2014 accumulate them.\n- `T` reports a **trade** \u2014 useful for watching trade flow.\n- Your own fills show up on `ex.md.<FEED>.<your-sender>`.\n\n## Best bid/offer \u2014 `ex.bbo.<FEED>`\n\n`<ts> <FEED> <bid_px> <bid_vol> <ask_px> <ask_vol>`, with `-` for an empty side.\nUpdated as the top of book changes.\n\n## Instrument metadata \u2014 KV `EX_META`\n\nKey = feedcode; value is `key=value` pairs: `ticksize`, `ref_price`, `band`\n(price band is `ref_price \u00b1 band`), `min_volume`, `max_volume`, `position_limit`,\n`max_tps`, `last_traded_price`. Read it to learn each contract's tick, price\nband, and limits.\n\n```bash\nnats kv ls  EX_META\nnats kv get EX_META AAH6\n```\n\n## Probing\n\nThe `nats` CLI is the fastest way to explore before you write code: `nats sub`\non the feeds above, `nats req` for order entry, `nats kv` for `EX_META`.\n"

                "text": "No dumb question \u2014 worth nailing down before touching this task.\n\n**Docker**: a way to package an app plus everything it needs to run (code, dependencies, runtime, OS libraries) into a single portable unit called a **container**. Instead of \"install Python 3.11, then these 12 packages, then hope it works on your machine,\" you write a `Dockerfile` (a recipe), it builds an **image**, and that image runs identically anywhere \u2014 your laptop, a grading server, whatever. In this task, each of your three processes (taker, strategy, hedger) is its own container, and `docker compose` is the tool that starts them all together, wires up their networking, etc., based on a `docker-compose.yml` file.\n\nWhy it matters here: the exchange itself ships as a Docker image (you don't build it, just run it), and your `strategy/` and `hedger/` code needs a Dockerfile so it can be built and run the same way on the grading machine as on yours.\n\n**NATS**: a lightweight messaging system \u2014 think of it as a post office for programs. One process **publishes** a message to a named \"subject\" (like an address, e.g. `ex.md.AAH6.MYSENDER`), and any process **subscribed** to that subject receives it. There's no direct connection between sender and receiver; NATS just routes messages by subject name.\n\nTwo patterns used in this task:\n- **Publish/subscribe** \u2014 market data and BBO updates are published by the exchange; your strategy/hedger subscribe to hear about trades and book changes.\n- **Request/reply** \u2014 order entry: you publish a request to `ex.req.<SENDER>`, and NATS routes the response back to you specifically, like a function call over the network.\n\nSo concretely: the exchange (a Docker container) runs a NATS-speaking process. Your quoter and hedger (also Docker containers) connect to that same NATS server and talk to the exchange \u2014 and to each other, if you want \u2014 purely by publishing/subscribing to subjects. Nothing here is Python-specific or exchange-specific; NATS is a general tool, Docker is a general tool, both just happen to be how this simulated exchange is packaged and wired up.\n\nWant me to also explain how order books / market making actually work conceptually, or is the infra picture enough for now?",

                "text": "Good \u2014 most of that's solid. Let's fix the one piece that's off.\n\n**What's right:** Docker packages everything an app needs into a portable unit (container), Dockerfile is the self-assembly instructions, three separate processes need three separate Dockerfiles. All correct.\n\n**What's off:** \"put those three containers into one bigger container... arrive in same box\" \u2014 that's not quite it. `docker compose` doesn't merge them into one container. Each container stays its own separate, isolated thing \u2014 its own table, its own chair, sitting in its own spot in the room. What `docker compose` does is coordinate the *delivery and setup*: it starts all three at once, and it sets up a shared space (a network) so the table and chairs can \"see\" each other and talk, even though they're still separate physical objects.\n\nSo better analogy: it's not one box with three items in it \u2014 it's three separate boxes, delivered together by the same mover, who also sets up a group chat between them so they can coordinate once they're all in the room.\n\nPractically, for your task: your `strategy/` container and `hedger/` container are fully separate processes, each with its own filesystem, own code, own crash domain. If your hedger crashes, your strategy container keeps running untouched. They only interact through NATS messages \u2014 nothing else is shared between them.\n\nWant to try the NATS half back to me too, or is that one solid already?",

                "uuid": "01a04586-18ff-75aa-9980-05e8602d09bd",
                "text": "Good question \u2014 you actually can just bundle dependencies alongside your code (that's basically what a Python `requirements.txt` + venv, or a Node `package.json`, already does). Docker solves problems one level below that.\n\n**The gap those tools don't cover:** package managers handle *your language's* dependencies, but not everything your code needs to run. A few examples:\n\n- **The runtime itself.** `requirements.txt` doesn't specify \"and here's a working Python 3.11 interpreter\" \u2014 it assumes one already exists on the machine. If the grading machine has Python 3.9, or none at all, your bundle doesn't help.\n- **OS-level stuff.** Some libraries need system packages underneath them (compiled C libraries, specific OS versions, certain binaries on the `PATH`). Nothing in a `requirements.txt` captures \"and also `apt install libssl-dev`.\"\n- **Architecture.** Your task explicitly calls this out \u2014 grading runs on `linux/amd64`. If you're on an Apple Silicon Mac (arm64) and compile something locally, that binary literally won't run on the grading machine. Docker forces you to build *from source inside the container*, on the target architecture, so this can't silently break.\n- **\"Works on my machine.\"** Environment variables, file paths, other software installed on your laptop that you don't even realize you're relying on \u2014 all invisible dependencies that a Docker image eliminates by giving you a clean, fully-specified environment from scratch every time.\n\nSo the mental model: package managers solve \"which versions of these libraries\" within an assumed environment. Docker solves \"what *is* the environment\" \u2014 down to the OS and CPU architecture \u2014 so that assumption can't quietly be wrong.\n\nThat's exactly why your task's README calls out \"build from source inside the Dockerfile; don't `COPY` in binaries compiled on your machine\" \u2014 it's guarding against precisely this failure mode.",

You can spin up the same image into multiple containers if you want multiple identical tables.\n\nSo refining your line: it's not that the table builds itself fresh in *every* house.                 "uuid": "01a045d7-dee0-70f8-a922-8c6619a113d4",
                "text": "Good instinct to check, but no \u2014 STP here means **Self-Trade Prevention**, not stop-loss. It's a completely different concept from what \"stop\" might suggest.\n\n**The problem it solves:** you're running three separate processes (taker, strategy, hedger) all trading the same exchange, potentially on the same instrument. If your hedger places a sell order and your quoter's resting buy order is sitting right there at a matching price, without protection they could **trade against each other** \u2014 you'd buy from yourself, pay the exchange's fees (if any) twice, and accomplish literally nothing except moving your own money in a circle.\n\n**What STP does:** when enabled (`Q` in the protocol) for a given `<FEED>`, the exchange will detect if an incoming order would match against a resting order **from the same sender**, and prevent that match from happening (instead of executing it) \u2014 usually by cancelling one or both sides rather than filling them.\n\nTwo things worth noting for your task:\n1. STP is scoped **per sender**, not per desk. So if `taker`, `strategy`, and `hedger` use three different sender IDs (which they do \u2014 `$SENDER`, `$TAKER_SENDER`, `$HEDGER_SENDER`), enabling STP on the quoter's sender won't stop the quoter from accidentally trading against the *hedger's* orders \u2014 they're different senders as far as the exchange is concerned.\n2. That means if you're worried about your own desk's processes crossing each other, STP alone doesn't solve it \u2014 you'd likely need your own coordination logic (e.g., hedger checks the quoter's live orders before hedging, or you accept some self-crossing as a known cost).\n\nWorth digging into as you design the hedger: do you want it to actively avoid trading against your own quoter's resting orders, or is that an edge case you're fine ignoring for now?",

NATS exposes `nats://localhost:4222` \u2014 note the `nats://` protocol, not `http://`. That's a raw TCP socket speaking the NATS wire protocol, not a web server.                 "text": "That's something you build \u2014 the exchange doesn't hand you a PnL number anywhere in the protocol. What it gives you is raw fills, and PnL is a derived thing you compute from those.\n\n**The building blocks you have:**\n- Your own fills come through on `ex.md.<FEED>.<your-sender>` as `E` (execution) messages \u2014 side, volume, price. You already need to consume these for any position tracking anyway (hedger definitely needs it, quoter probably wants it too).\n- `EX_META`'s `last_traded_price`, or the live `ex.bbo.<FEED>` feed, gives you a current market reference price for anything you're still holding.\n\n**How PnL actually breaks down, conceptually:**\n\n1. **Realized PnL** \u2014 cash actually in/out from trades that have happened. Every time you buy, cash goes down by `price \u00d7 volume`; every time you sell, cash goes up. Sum it as fills arrive.\n2. **Unrealized PnL (mark-to-market)** \u2014 the value of whatever position you're still holding, valued at the *current* market price, not what you paid for it. `position \u00d7 current_price` gives you what it's \"worth\" right now on paper.\n3. **Total PnL** = realized + unrealized. This is the number that actually reflects \"am I making money,\" since a position that hasn't been closed still has real economic value that moves with the market.\n\nSince contracts here are cash-settled and worth exactly their listed price (per the README), this is fairly clean \u2014 no weird conversion, the price *is* the dollar value.\n\n**Practically for this task:** you'll likely want each seat (or a shared piece of logic) accumulating fills into a running position + cash, then computing mark-to-market against the latest BBO or last traded price whenever you want to check PnL \u2014 for your own monitoring/logging, and possibly for the hedger's risk decisions (e.g. hedge harder if unrealized PnL is moving against you, not just if position size is large).\n\nWorth tracking per-instrument if you end up quoting more than one feed, and probably worth logging/exposing somewhere so you can watch it live while the sim runs, not just compute it after the fact.",

                "text": "This is basically right \u2014 just two small refinements.\n\n**Docker:** everything you said is accurate, one nuance to sharpen. It's not \"a copy of how the desk would run on my computer\" \u2014 it's closer to \"a copy of how the desk *should* run, built fresh and correctly for the target machine, regardless of what your computer looks like.\" That distinction matters because of the amd64/arm64 thing you already hit: your computer is arm64, but the shipped container is built for amd64. If it were literally a copy of your machine's setup, it'd be the wrong architecture and would fail on TRV's grading server. Instead, the Dockerfile is a recipe that gets rebuilt from source, targeting `linux/amd64` specifically, independent of what you personally have installed or what chip you're on. So: not \"a copy of my setup,\" but \"a self-contained, correctly-targeted setup, built the same way every time regardless of whose machine builds it.\"\n\n**NATS:** solid, one word to tighten \u2014 \"central exchange\" is fine informally, but technically the exchange isn't special to NATS itself. NATS doesn't know or care that one of the participants is \"the exchange\" \u2014 it's just another process publishing/subscribing on subjects, same as your seats. It only *acts* central because everyone's agreed to treat `ex.req.*`/`ex.md.*`/`ex.bbo.*`/`EX_META` as \"the exchange's\" subjects by convention, and because it's the one actually matching orders. NATS itself is neutral plumbing \u2014 any process, including two of your own seats, is a peer on equal footing on that bus. Small distinction, but it matters once you're deciding how your seats coordinate: you're not routing hedger\u2192exchange\u2192quoter, you'd set up hedger\u2194quoter directly if you want that.\n\nEverything else \u2014 one script per seat, own dependencies, message protocol adherence, free choice on inter-seat wiring, needing that coordination to be fast \u2014 is correct.\n\nYou've got a solid grip on the architecture now.                 "text": "\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\nGood instinct \u2014 the analogy holds well, with one structural difference worth flagging up front.\n\n**Where it's the same:** in Prosperity you got market state (order depths) each tick and returned a list of orders \u2014 buy/sell, price, volume \u2014 as your quoting decision. Same conceptual job here: read the book/prices, decide what to quote, submit orders. The core skill you already have \u2014 fair value estimation, spread management, position-aware sizing \u2014 transfers directly.\n\n**Where it's different, and this matters a lot:** Prosperity was **tick-based** \u2014 you got called once per timestep, submitted your full order list, and the round advanced. This exchange is **event-driven and continuous** \u2014 there's no \"your turn,\" it's a live NATS feed streaming at you asynchronously, and your quoter is a long-running process reacting to events (BBO updates, executions, fills) whenever they happen, and managing its own resting orders over time (they don't get reset each \"tick\" \u2014 they sit on the book until filled or you cancel them). So the mental shift: instead of \"compute best orders this tick, submit, done,\" you're building something closer to a stateful loop that maintains live quotes, updates them as the market/your position moves, and reacts to fills \u2014 much closer to a real market-making bot than to a batch-processed competition submission.\n\n**On strategy substance**, given your Prosperity background (EMA fair value, passive market making \u00b1spread around a reference, position-aware skew), the natural quoter design here:\n1. Compute a fair value from `EX_META`'s `ref_price`/`last_traded_price` and/or the live BBO midpoint.\n2. Quote a bid and ask symmetrically around that fair value, spread wide enough to be profitable after adverse selection, narrow enough to actually get filled.\n3. Skew the quotes based on your current position \u2014 if you're long, shade your quotes down (sell more eagerly, buy less eagerly) to naturally mean-revert toward flat, exactly like Prosperity's inventory-aware market making.\n4. Respect `EX_META`'s `ticksize`, `band`, `min_volume`/`max_volume`, `position_limit` \u2014 reject risk otherwise.\n\nGiven point 2 (need to react continuously, maintain state, handle async events) \u2014 do you want to lock in the language first, since that'll shape how the event loop actually gets written? What are you comfortable in or want practice with \u2014 Go, Rust, C++, Java, TS/Node?",

                        "text": "Good instinct \u2014 the analogy holds well, with one structural difference worth flagging up front.\n\n**Where it's the same:** in Prosperity you got market state (order depths) each tick and returned a list of orders \u2014 buy/sell, price, volume \u2014 as your quoting decision. The core skill you already have \u2014 fair value estimation, spread management, position-aware sizing \u2014 transfers directly.\n\n**Where it's different, and this matters a lot:** Prosperity was **tick-based** \u2014 you got called once per timestep, submitted your full order list, and the round advanced. This exchange is **event-driven and continuous** \u2014 there's no \"your turn,\" it's a live NATS feed streaming at you asynchronously, and your quoter is a long-running process reacting to events (BBO updates, executions, fills) whenever they happen, and managing its own resting orders over time (they don't get reset each \"tick\" \u2014 they sit on the book until filled or you cancel them). So the mental shift: instead of \"compute best orders this tick, submit, done,\" you're building something closer to a stateful loop that maintains live quotes, updates them as the market/your position moves, and reacts to fills \u2014 much closer to a real market-making bot than to a batch-processed competition submission.\n\n**On strategy substance**, given your Prosperity background (EMA fair value, passive market making \u00b1spread around a reference, position-aware skew), the natural quoter design here:\n1. Compute a fair value from `EX_META`'s `ref_price`/`last_traded_price` and/or the live BBO midpoint.\n2. Quote a bid and ask symmetrically around that fair value, spread wide enough to be profitable after adverse selection, narrow enough to actually get filled.\n3. Skew the quotes based on your current position \u2014 if you're long, shade your quotes down (sell more eagerly, buy less eagerly) to naturally mean-revert toward flat, exactly like Prosperity's inventory-aware market making.\n4. Respect `EX_META`'s `ticksize`, `band`, `min_volume`/`max_volume`, `position_limit` \u2014 reject risk otherwise.\n\nGiven point 2 (need to react continuously, maintain state, handle async events) \u2014 do you want to lock in the language first, since that'll shape how the event loop actually gets written?                 "text": "Close, but one more correction on the exact phrase \"tick per tick\" \u2014 that's actually the thing that's *not* true here, and it's worth being precise since it changes how you write the code.\n\nThere's no \"tick\" in this system at all \u2014 that word implies a fixed, regular time unit (Prosperity: timestep N happens, everyone submits, timestep N+1 happens). This exchange has **no such heartbeat**. Things happen purely by **event**: a BBO update fires when the top of book changes, an execution message fires when a trade happens, and these arrive whenever the market produces them \u2014 could be microseconds apart, could be seconds apart, totally irregular. Your quoter doesn't get \"called\" on a schedule; it's sitting there subscribed, and it reacts whenever *something* arrives on the NATS subjects it's listening to.\n\nSo the more accurate version of what you said: submission is still the same idea (send buy/sell/price/volume), but instead of \"book management is up to me and I react tick per tick,\" it's \"book management is up to me, and I react **event per event**, whenever the market actually does something\" \u2014 not on any regular cadence at all.\n\nWhy this distinction actually matters practically: in Prosperity, your orders were implicitly wiped and reconsidered fresh every timestep. Here, an order you place with type `L` (limit) just **sits on the book indefinitely** until it either fills or you explicitly cancel it \u2014 nobody resets it for you. So part of your quoter's job is actively managing *when* to cancel/replace a stale quote (e.g., market moved but your resting order didn't), which didn't really exist as a concept in Prosperity at all.\n\nDoes that distinction make sense \u2014 the shift from \"regular scheduled snapshots\" to \"irregular reactive stream, with persistent state you must actively manage\"?",

So \"quoter to hedger to taker\" coordination isn't necessarily symmetric \u2014 it depends on whether the taker already publishes anything useful, or whether you need to modify it to participate in your custom coordination scheme.\n\nTwo scenarios:\n- If taker already publishes something on a custom subject (or you can identify its fills easily), the hedger can just consume that as-is.\n- If it doesn't, you have a choice: either modify `taker/` to publish position/fill updates on a subject your hedger listens to, or \u2014 simpler \u2014 have the hedger derive the taker's position purely by subscribing to `ex.md.<FEED>.<TAKER_SENDER>` (its execution feed) directly off the exchange, since `$TAKER_SENDER` is a known env var. That second option means you don't need to touch taker's code at all to know what it's doing \u2014 the exchange's own market data already tells you, since fills are per-sender and public-ish via the feed.\n\nActually \u2014 that logic extends to quoter and hedger too. You don't strictly *need* a custom coordination subject at all: since every seat's own fills show up on `ex.md.<FEED>.<sender>`, and everyone's sender IDs are known via env vars, the hedger could just subscribe to all three senders' feeds directly and compute combined position itself, without you inventing any custom protocol.\n\nThe custom coordination channel becomes valuable for stuff *not* derivable from fills alone \u2014 e.g. \"hedger, I'm about to widen my quotes, expect more inventory soon\" or intent/signals ahead of time, not just after-the-fact position state.\n\nWorth deciding: do you want the hedger computing combined position purely from subscribing to the three existing exchange fill-feeds (simpler, no taker/quoter code changes needed for coordination itself), or do you want an actual custom pub/sub channel between your own processes for richer signaling? Given time constraints on a take-home, the first is probably the pragmatic move \u2014 want to go with that?",
