The array positions **don't correspond to \"recency\" at all**; `bufferIndex` is just \"where to write next,\" not \"where the newest/oldest logically is.\"\n\nWalk through it concretely with a size-4 buffer (using 4 instead of 20 so it's easy to trace) and samples `A, B, C, D, E` arriving in that order:\n\n```\npush A: buffer = [A, _, _, _], index becomes 1\npush B: buffer = [A, B, _, _], index becomes 2\npush C: buffer = [A, B, C, _], index becomes 3\npush D: buffer = [A, B, C, D], index becomes 0   <- wrapped\npush E: buffer = [E, B, C, D], index becomes 1   <- E overwrote A, the oldest\n```\n\nAfter pushing E, the buffer holds `[E, B, C, D]` \u2014 that **is** correctly \"the last 4 samples\" (B, C, D, E), just not stored in chronological left-to-right order in the array. `A` (the oldest) got correctly evicted and replaced by `E` (the newest). Nothing about \"most recent\" requires the array to *read* in chronological order \u2014 for your stddev calculation, you're summing over all valid entries regardless of position, so the order they're stored in the array doesn't matter at all. You just need \"the 20 most recent values are in there\" \u2014 which they are.\n\nWhere order *would* matter: if you needed to know *which one is oldest vs newest* (e.g., to compute something like a trend or weighted-by-recency average). You don't need that for a plain rolling stddev \u2014 every sample in the buffer counts equally regardless of position.\n\nSo \u2014 is your concern actually about the stddev calc treating all entries equally regardless of age, or was it specifically about the array's storage order?                 "text": "No \u2014 `double midBuffer[20]` is a **plain C-style fixed-size array**, not a `std::vector`.\n\nKey differences:\n\n- **Fixed size, known at compile time.** `[20]` is baked into the type \u2014 it will always hold exactly 20 doubles, no more, no less. You can't resize it, push_back onto it, or ask it for its size at runtime (there's no `.size()` \u2014 `sizeof(midBuffer)/sizeof(double)` is the old C trick if you ever needed it, but here you don't since you're tracking `bufferCount` yourself).\n- **Lives inline inside the struct**, not on the heap. When you have `InstrumentState st;`, those 20 doubles are physically part of `st`'s memory, allocated wherever `st` itself is (stack or wherever the struct lives) \u2014 no separate heap allocation, no pointer indirection.\n- **No bounds checking.** If you ever wrote `midBuffer[20]` (one past the end) or a negative index, it's undefined behavior \u2014 silent memory corruption, not an exception like `std::vector::at()` would throw. This is exactly why the `% 20` wraparound in `pushSample` is load-bearing \u2014 nothing stops you from writing out of bounds if you get that arithmetic wrong.\n\n`std::vector<double> midBuffer;` would be the dynamically-resizable alternative \u2014 has `.push_back()`, `.size()`, grows/shrinks automatically, lives on the heap. For a fixed-size rolling buffer like this, the plain array is actually the more idiomatic choice \u2014 you know the size never changes, so paying for vector's resizing machinery would be unnecessary overhead. But it does mean you're fully responsible for not walking off the end yourself.",

Two concrete problems in it:\n\n**a) Dominant-aggressor logic conflates \"mover\" with \"driver\" incorrectly for multi-member clusters.** In `runDiscovery`, the singleton-rejection dominance check (`kMoverDominanceShare`) is only applied to `members.size() == 1`. Since `AAH6` (real driver) is unquoted-signal-only and piggybacks quote off it with a fixed lag, but the piggyback LPs' *repost* also correlates back-and-forth with the mover's *own* walk (mover trades against resting book depth, generating its own execution-driven bidask moves on AAH6 that get logged in `midHist` as bbo updates, not as \"who's the aggressor\") \u2014 `leadCount` can tip toward whichever instrument happens to update more frequently/with cleaner lag structure, not whichever is causally upstream. AAH6 updates far more often (mover ticks every 0.2s) than AAM6/AAU6 (which only requote on integer-crossing), so lag-correlation `r2` can look strong in *either* direction depending on noise, especially with only `kMinOverlapPoints = 20` required \u2014 that's a very low bar.\n\n**b) The aggressor-volume-based mover identification double-purposes as driver confirmation, but happens *after* clustering, not as an input to it.** `st.moverSender` and the dominance share are computed only for instruments already tagged `Role::DRIVER` by the clustering step. So if clustering picks e.g. AAM6 as the \"driver\" of its cluster (because of the lag-correlation noise above), you'll get `mover_identified` logs computing a share for the *wrong* instrument, and you'd never even see the correct dominance check run against AAH6 \u2014 the diagnostic (`[DISCOVERY][WARN] ... below dominance threshold`) doesn't fire on the pairs that actually matter.\n\n**c) There's also a units/timescale mismatch**: `kLagStepNanos = 100ms`, `kMaxLagNanos = 3s`, scanning both directions \u2014 this is checking whether AAH6 leads AAM6/AAU6 (or vice versa) at up to 3s lag, but per mem2.md the actual mechanism is **\"round(fv(driver)) crossing an integer\" as the piggyback's requote trigger**, which is not a fixed-lag linear relationship at all \u2014 it's a rounding/threshold nonlinearity. Pearson correlation over raw mid-price series at fixed lags is the wrong statistical tool for that relationship, and this is exactly the kind of correlation-based approach mem2.md records as abandoned in favor of just discovering driver/piggyback via requote-burst structure. Verified with `g++ -fsyntax-only -Wall -Wextra` against a stub `nats.h` \u2014 clean, no warnings.\n\nOne thing worth flagging: the new discovery logic assumes a driver's piggybacks share its 2-char underlying prefix (`AA`), which matches this sim's `AAH6/AAM6/AAU6` naming \u2014 but mem2.md notes the grading instrument set is deliberately unspecified. If the graded exchange doesn't follow that naming convention, the prefix-matching step needs a fallback (or you keep it opt-in via a flag).",

Two compounding effects, one is the actual PnL killer:\n\n## The cause\n\n`armEntry` posts entry orders as **marketable-crossing limit orders** \u2014 `entryPx` is deliberately placed on the far side of the mover's target (`targetPrice \u00b1 offset`) specifically so it crosses immediately and gets filled by the sweep. That's the whole point of the entry logic \u2014 it's designed to fill *instantly*, often fully, **in the same `A` reply**, per protocol:\n\n> `Y <n>` \u2014 accepted. For `A`, `<n>` is the volume that traded immediately.\n\nBut `addOrder` throws away `<n>`:\n\n```cpp\nbool ok = toks.size() >= 2 && toks[1] == \"Y\";\n```\n\nIt never reads `toks[2]`. So when an entry order fills entirely on the accept-reply itself (the normal case for a deliberately-marketable order), **no `E` message is ever generated for the resting side because there is no resting side \u2014 it never rests** (or rests only partially). The `handleOwnFill` code path that writes to `PnlFile` is only reachable via an `E` market-data message on `ex.md.<FEED>.*`. If the whole fill happened synchronously inside the request/reply, and no separate `E` shows up for your own side (order fully filled and done, nothing left resting to later report a cancel/fill against), **`st.entryFilled` stays 0, `st.position` never updates, and `PnlFile` never gets a line for that trade** \u2014 even though the trade happened and Cannon Capital's margin account changed.\n\nWhether an `E` is *also* published for your own synchronous fill (in addition to the reply's `<n>`) is actually the open question \u2014 PROTOCOL.md doesn't explicitly say fills-inside-the-reply are mirrored on `ex.md`.                 "text": "Right \u2014 that's exactly the failure mode. Let me walk through what's actually happening and what the async alternative looks like.\n\n## Why the stall happens\n\nYour architecture (per mem2.md's settled design) is: one NATS delivery thread does a bare `enqueue` in `onRawMsg`, and one consumer thread (`mainLoop`) drains `gQueue` and does everything else \u2014 parsing, state updates, decisions, **order entry** \u2014 in order, on that single thread.\n\n```cpp\nstatic void onRawMsg(natsConnection*, natsSubscription*, natsMsg* msg, void*) {\n    RawMsg rm;\n    ...\n    { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(gMutex); gQueue.push_back(std::move(rm)); }\n    gCv.notify_one();\n    natsMsg_Destroy(msg);\n}\n```\n\nThat's correctly non-blocking \u2014 NATS keeps delivering messages into the queue no matter what the consumer thread is doing.\n\nBut `natsConnection_RequestString` (inside `sendRequest`, called by `addOrder`) is a **blocking call**: it publishes your order, then synchronously waits (up to `kOrderTimeoutMs` = 2000ms) for the reply to come back, all on the *same consumer thread* that's supposed to be draining `gQueue`.\n\n```cpp\nstatic bool sendRequest(const std::string& body, std::string& replyOut) {\n    ...\n    natsStatus s = natsConnection_RequestString(&reply, gConn, subj.c_str(), body.c_str(), kOrderTimeoutMs);\n    // <-- consumer thread is frozen here, doing nothing else, for up to 2s\n    ...\n}\n```\n\nSo the call chain `dispatch \u2192 handleBbo \u2192 updateFv \u2192 armEntryFromZScore \u2192 addOrder \u2192 sendRequest` freezes the *only* thread that processes `gQueue`. Meanwhile `onRawMsg` keeps firing on every incoming bbo/md message from NATS's own internal I/O threads, and every one of those just piles into `gQueue` since nobody's draining it. When `sendRequest` finally returns, `mainLoop` wakes up and has to chew through however many messages piled up \u2014 and if a burst of bbo ticks each individually triggered another z-score check that also happened to want to enter, you can even get **queued-up stale decisions** (an order posted off a z-score that's now several hundred milliseconds and several ticks out of date by the time it's finally processed).\n\n## The async alternative\n\nInstead of blocking request/reply, use **fire-and-forget publish**, and correlate the reply asynchronously via a subscription \u2014 which is actually closer to what the protocol already supports, since `ex.req.<SENDER>` replies come back on an inbox subject regardless of whether you use the blocking helper or not.\n\nConcretely, this means:\n\n1. **Publish the order request without waiting.** `natsConnection_PublishRequest` (publish with a reply-to inbox you generate) instead of `natsConnection_RequestString`.\n2. **Subscribe once, up front, to your own inbox pattern** (or use NATS's async request API if the C client exposes one \u2014 `natsConnection_RequestMsg` has async variants in some client versions, but the simplest portable approach is manual inbox pub/sub).\n3. **When the reply arrives, it comes back through `onRawMsg` like any other message** (if you subscribe the inbox through the same subscription mechanism) \u2014 or through a small dedicated reply-handling queue \u2014 and gets matched back to the order via the order id you already generate.\n4. **The consumer thread never blocks.** It fires the order, updates state to \"order X pending, awaiting ack,\" moves on to the next queue item immediately, and finishes booking the fill/rejection whenever the async reply shows up later \u2014 processed just like any other queued event.\n\nThe shape of it:\n\n```cpp\nstruct PendingOrder {\n    std::string feed;\n    char side;\n    long long price;\n    long long size;\n    long long sentNs;\n};\nstatic std::unordered_map<std::string, PendingOrder> gPendingOrders; // keyed by orderId\n\nstatic void sendOrderAsync(InstrumentState& st, char side, long long vol, long long price) {\n    std::string id = genOrderId(side == 'B' ? 'B' : 'A', st);\n    std::ostringstream body;\n    body << gSender << \" A \" << st.feed << \" \" << id << \" \" << side << \" \" << vol << \" \" << price << \" L\";\n\n    gPendingOrders[id] = {st.feed, side, price, vol, nowNs()};\n\n    // async publish \u2014 does NOT block waiting for the reply\n    natsConnection_PublishString(gConn, (\"ex.req.\" + gSender).c_str(), body.str().c_str());\n    // reply will arrive on the request's auto-generated inbox subject, or\n    // on a fixed inbox you subscribed once at startup, and gets routed\n    // through the normal message queue/dispatch path just like bbo/md\n}\n```\n\nThen in `dispatch` (or a new handler), when the order-entry reply arrives, you look up `gPendingOrders[id]`, book the immediate-fill volume exactly the way `armEntry`/`armEntryFromZScore` do now, and erase the pending entry.\n\n## Trade-offs, honestly\n\n- **This is a real rewrite**, not a small patch \u2014 the whole \"wait for `addOrder` to return true/false right there in `armEntry`\" control flow goes away. `armEntry` becomes \"fire order, mark state as pending,\" and the actual booking logic moves to wherever the async reply is handled.\n- **You lose the synchronous \"did it work\" check inline.** Right now `armEntry` only sets `st.entryActive = true` *if* `addOrder` returned true. Async, you either optimistically set pending state and roll it back on a later rejection, or you track a distinct \"awaiting ack\" state (mem2.md's rel-recovery thread actually mentions exactly this pattern being considered \u2014 \"per-instrument awaiting own cancel ack flag\" \u2014 same idea, different action).\n- **NATS's C client may or may not give you a clean async request helper** depending on the version pinned in `third_party/nats.c` \u2014 worth checking before committing to hand-rolling inbox subscriptions.\n\nGiven you're mid-build and this touches `addOrder`, `armEntry`, `armEntryFromZScore`, and `postExitLadder` all at once, do you want me to actually do this rewrite now, or do you want to sit with the design first (e.g. decide the pending-order state shape) before I touch the code?",

Let me walk through what's actually happening and what the async alternative looks like.\n\n## Why the stall happens\n\nYour architecture (per mem2.md's settled design) is: one NATS delivery thread does a bare `enqueue` in `onRawMsg`, and one consumer thread (`mainLoop`) drains `gQueue` and does everything else \u2014 parsing, state updates, decisions, **order entry** \u2014 in order, on that single thread.\n\n```cpp\nstatic void onRawMsg(natsConnection*, natsSubscription*, natsMsg* msg, void*) {\n    RawMsg rm;\n    ...\n    { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(gMutex); gQueue.push_back(std::move(rm)); }\n    gCv.notify_one();\n    natsMsg_Destroy(msg);\n}\n```\n\nThat's correctly non-blocking \u2014 NATS keeps delivering messages into the queue no matter what the consumer thread is doing.\n\nBut `natsConnection_RequestString` (inside `sendRequest`, called by `addOrder`) is a **blocking call**: it publishes your order, then synchronously waits (up to `kOrderTimeoutMs` = 2000ms) for the reply to come back, all on the *same consumer thread* that's supposed to be draining `gQueue`.\n\n```cpp\nstatic bool sendRequest(const std::string& body, std::string& replyOut) {\n    ...\n    natsStatus s = natsConnection_RequestString(&reply, gConn, subj.c_str(), body.c_str(), kOrderTimeoutMs);\n    // <-- consumer thread is frozen here, doing nothing else, for up to 2s\n    ...\n}\n```\n\nSo the call chain `dispatch \u2192 handleBbo \u2192 updateFv \u2192 armEntryFromZScore \u2192 addOrder \u2192 sendRequest` freezes the *only* thread that processes `gQueue`. Meanwhile `onRawMsg` keeps firing on every incoming bbo/md message from NATS's own internal I/O threads, and every one of those just piles into `gQueue` since nobody's draining it. When `sendRequest` finally returns, `mainLoop` wakes up and has to chew through however many messages piled up \u2014 and if a burst of bbo ticks each individually triggered another z-score check that also happened to want to enter, you can even get **queued-up stale decisions** (an order posted off a z-score that's now several hundred milliseconds and several ticks out of date by the time it's finally processed).\n\n## The async alternative\n\nInstead of blocking request/reply, use **fire-and-forget publish**, and correlate the reply asynchronously via a subscription \u2014 which is actually closer to what the protocol already supports, since `ex.req.<SENDER>` replies come back on an inbox subject regardless of whether you use the blocking helper or not.\n\nConcretely, this means:\n\n1. **Publish the order request without waiting.** `natsConnection_PublishRequest` (publish with a reply-to inbox you generate) instead of `natsConnection_RequestString`.\n2. **Subscribe once, up front, to your own inbox pattern** (or use NATS's async request API if the C client exposes one \u2014 `natsConnection_RequestMsg` has async variants in some client versions, but the simplest portable approach is manual inbox pub/sub).\n3. **When the reply arrives, it comes back through `onRawMsg` like any other message** (if you subscribe the inbox through the same subscription mechanism) \u2014 or through a small dedicated reply-handling queue \u2014 and gets matched back to the order via the order id you already generate.\n4. **The consumer thread never blocks.** It fires the order, updates state to \"order X pending, awaiting ack,\" moves on to the next queue item immediately, and finishes booking the fill/rejection whenever the async reply shows up later \u2014 processed just like any other queued event.\n\nThe shape of it:\n\n```cpp\nstruct PendingOrder {\n    std::string feed;\n    char side;\n    long long price;\n    long long size;\n    long long sentNs;\n};\nstatic std::unordered_map<std::string, PendingOrder> gPendingOrders; // keyed by orderId\n\nstatic void sendOrderAsync(InstrumentState& st, char side, long long vol, long long price) {\n    std::string id = genOrderId(side == 'B' ? 'B' : 'A', st);\n    std::ostringstream body;\n    body << gSender << \" A \" << st.feed << \" \" << id << \" \" << side << \" \" << vol << \" \" << price << \" L\";\n\n    gPendingOrders[id] = {st.feed, side, price, vol, nowNs()};\n\n    // async publish \u2014 does NOT block waiting for the reply\n    natsConnection_PublishString(gConn, (\"ex.req.\" + gSender).c_str(), body.str().c_str());\n    // reply will arrive on the request's auto-generated inbox subject, or\n    // on a fixed inbox you subscribed once at startup, and gets routed\n    // through the normal message queue/dispatch path just like bbo/md\n}\n```\n\nThen in `dispatch` (or a new handler), when the order-entry reply arrives, you look up `gPendingOrders[id]`, book the immediate-fill volume exactly the way `armEntry`/`armEntryFromZScore` do now, and erase the pending entry.\n\n## Trade-offs, honestly\n\n- **This is a real rewrite**, not a small patch \u2014 the whole \"wait for `addOrder` to return true/false right there in `armEntry`\" control flow goes away. `armEntry` becomes \"fire order, mark state as pending,\" and the actual booking logic moves to wherever the async reply is handled.\n- **You lose the synchronous \"did it work\" check inline.** Right now `armEntry` only sets `st.entryActive = true` *if* `addOrder` returned true. Async, you either optimistically set pending state and roll it back on a later rejection, or you track a distinct \"awaiting ack\" state (mem2.md's rel-recovery thread actually mentions exactly this pattern being considered \u2014 \"per-instrument awaiting own cancel ack flag\" \u2014 same idea, different action).\n- **NATS's C client may or may not give you a clean async request helper** depending on the version pinned in `third_party/nats.c` \u2014 worth checking before committing to hand-rolling inbox subscriptions.\n\nGiven you're mid-build and this touches `addOrder`, `armEntry`, `armEntryFromZScore`, and `postExitLadder` all at once, do you want me to actually do this rewrite now, or do you want to sit with the design first (e.g. decide the pending-order state shape) before I touch the code?",

That fully explains \">2 seconds\" \u2014 it's not one timeout, it's several stacked in a row, all triggered by one price event.\n\nTo directly answer your question: no, the queue emptying isn't causing the silence \u2014 the silence is the *cause* of the queue backing up. Queued through\n// the existing per-instrument actionQueue, so this is 4 sequential ops\n// (cancel bid, cancel ask, add bid, add ask) each waiting on the previous\n// ack \u2014 same pipeline the driver's exit ladder already uses, just a\n// different ReqKind pair.\n\nstatic constexpr long long kPiggybackSize = 3;\n\nstatic void onPiggybackCenterChanged(InstrumentState& pst) {\n    // Cancel existing resting quotes, if any. Uses the same ENTRY_CANCEL/\n    // EXIT_CANCEL kinds as the driver path \u2014 repurposed here rather than\n    // adding new ReqKind values, since the cancel/ack bookkeeping is\n    // identical (fire, wait for ack, move on). pgBidId/pgAskId need adding\n    // to InstrumentState (see below) to track piggyback quote ids\n    // separately from the driver's entryId/exitLadder.\n    if (!pst.pgBidId.empty()) {\n        requestCancel(pst, pst.pgBidId, ReqKind::ENTRY_CANCEL);\n        pst.pgBidId.clear();\n    }\n    if (!pst.pgAskId.empty()) {\n        requestCancel(pst, pst.pgAskId, ReqKind::EXIT_CANCEL);\n        pst.pgAskId.clear();\n    }\n\n    // \u00a75.1: one tick inside live best bid/ask; fall back to cEst +/- 1 if a\n    // side of the book is currently empty.\n    long long tick = pst.meta.ticksize > 0 ? pst.askPx - tick\n                                        : static_cast<long long>(std::llround(*pst.cEst)) + tick;\n    bidPx = clampToBand(bidPx, pst.meta);\n    askPx = clampToBand(askPx, pst.meta);\n\n    // Queued behind the two cancels above via the same awaitingAck gate \u2014\n    // requestAdd already handles \"queue if busy\" so no extra logic needed\n    // here, just call in the order we want them to eventually fire.\n    requestAdd(pst, 'B', bidPx, kPiggybackSize, ReqKind::ENTRY_ADD);\n    requestAdd(pst, 'S', askPx, kPiggybackSize, ReqKind::EXIT_ADD);\n\n    DiscoveryLog << nowNs() << \",piggyback_requote,\" << pst.feed << \",cEst=\" << *pst.cEst\n                 << \" bid=\" << bidPx << \" ask=\" << askPx << \"\\n\";\n}\n\n\n// --- InstrumentState additions ----------------------------------------------\n// Piggyback's own resting quote ids \u2014 separate from entryId/exitLadder\n// (driver-only fields) since a piggyback's two sides aren't an entry/exit\n// pair, they're just two independent standing quotes.\n\n    std::string pgBidId;\n    std::string pgAskId;\n```\n\nOne thing worth flagging, not a style choice: repurposing `ReqKind::ENTRY_ADD`/`EXIT_ADD`/`ENTRY_CANCEL`/`EXIT_CANCEL` for piggyback quotes means `handleOrderReply` and `handleOwnFill` \u2014 which currently branch on those exact kinds assuming driver semantics (`st.entryActive`, `st.exitLadder`, PnL sign conventions tied to entry/exit) \u2014 will misfire when a piggyback's ack comes back tagged `ENTRY_ADD`.
